title: Variance and covariance
text:
DefDefinition 1 (Deviation)






Definition 1 (Deviation) A deviation is the difference between a value and a reference value. For any quantity \(z\) and reference value \(r\), the deviation of \(z\) from \(r\) is:
\[z - r\]










RemarkRemark






Remark. In probability and statistics, “deviation” usually means deviation from a population mean.
See: Wikipedia: Deviation (statistics)










ExmExample 1 (Deviation from a reference weight)






Example 1 (Deviation from a reference weight) A newborn weighing 3,200 g deviates from a reference weight of 3,500 g by \(3200 - 3500 = -300\) g.










DefDefinition 2 (Deviation from a population or subpopulation mean)






Definition 2 (Deviation from a population or subpopulation mean) The deviation from the mean of a random variable \(Y\) is its deviation from its expectation:
\[\delta(Y) \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}Y - {\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[Y\right]\mathclose{}}\]
For a realized observation \(y\):
\[\delta(y) \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}y - {\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[Y\right]\mathclose{}}\]










RemarkRemark






Remark. Other sources often call this quantity an error or noise term [1]. In regression settings, the reference mean is often conditional on covariates: \(\delta(y_i) \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}y_i - {\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[Y_i \mid X_i = x_i\right]\mathclose{}}\).
These notes prefer “deviation” for this mean-deviation quantity; “error” and “noise” are common aliases. The Morrison Lab’s regression notes use “residual” (defined in their Linear regression chapter) for deviations from fitted values, write \(\delta(\cdot)\) for these model/data deviations, and reserve \({\varepsilon\mathopen{}\left(\cdot\right)\mathclose{}}\) for estimator-to-estimand deviations (see Estimation).
See:

Wikipedia: Errors and residuals
Wikipedia: Deviation (statistics)
Wikipedia: Linear regression — Notation and terminology











ExmExample 2 (Deviation of a die roll from its mean)






Example 2 (Deviation of a die roll from its mean) A fair die roll \(Y\) has \({\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[Y\right]\mathclose{}} = 3.5\) (computed on the expectation page), so a roll of \(y = 5\) has deviation
\[
\begin{aligned}
\delta(5) &= 5 - 3.5 \\
&= 1.5,
\end{aligned}
\]
and a roll of \(y = 2\) has deviation
\[
\begin{aligned}
\delta(2) &= 2 - 3.5 \\
&= -1.5.
\end{aligned}
\]






Measurement noise is almost always modeled as a random variable \(\varepsilon\) with mean zero and variance \(\sigma^2\).






RemarkRemark 1 (Mean zero is a parametrization choice)






Remark 1 (Mean zero is a parametrization choice). Mean zero is a parametrization choice, not a substantive assumption. In \(Y = f(x) + \varepsilon\), moving a constant from \(\varepsilon\) into \(f(x)\) changes the split but not the distribution of \(Y\), so the data identify only the sum \(f(x) + {\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[\varepsilon\right]\mathclose{}}\), the mean of \(Y\) at \(x\). Requiring \({\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[\varepsilon\right]\mathclose{}} = 0\) picks the one split in which \(f(x)\) is that mean. This loses no generality when the model for \(f\) can absorb a constant, as any model with an intercept can. It restricts the model only when \(f\) cannot absorb one, as in a regression through the origin.




Mean zero gives one identity, used repeatedly across statistical modeling and machine learning.






ExrExercise 1 (The average squared error of pure noise)






Exercise 1 (The average squared error of pure noise) Let \(\varepsilon\) be a random variable with \(\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon] = 0\) and \({\operatorname{Var}\mathopen{}\left(\varepsilon\right)\mathclose{}} = \sigma^2\).
Find \(\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon^2]\) in terms of \(\sigma^2\), and say which earlier result you used.










SolutionSolution 1






Solution 1. Theorem 3 says \({\operatorname{Var}\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}} = \mathbb{E}[X^2] - (\mathbb{E}[X])^2\) for any \(X\). Taking \(X = \varepsilon\) and substituting \(\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon] = 0\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon^2]
&= {\operatorname{Var}\mathopen{}\left(\varepsilon\right)\mathclose{}} + 0^2 \\
&= \sigma^2
\end{aligned}
\tag{1}\]
so for mean-zero noise the average squared value is the variance.
The identity looks slight and does a lot of work. Equation 1 is the step that produces the irreducible error term in regression and statistical modeling: it converts a statement about the spread of the noise, which is what a model of the world gives you, into a statement about squared error, which is what the fitting objective measures.










LemTheorem 1 (The second moment of mean-zero noise)






Theorem 1 (The second moment of mean-zero noise) Let \(\varepsilon\) be a random variable with \(\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon] = 0\) and \({\operatorname{Var}\mathopen{}\left(\varepsilon\right)\mathclose{}} = \sigma^2\). Then
\[\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon^2] = \sigma^2\]










ProofProof






Proof. This is the solution to Exercise 1, worked in Solution 1. It rearranges Theorem 3, using \(\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon] = 0\).

title: Variance and covariance
Variance and covariance
text:
3 The best constant prediction






LemTheorem 5 (Expected squared error of a constant prediction)






Theorem 5 (Expected squared error of a constant prediction) Let \(Y\) be a random variable with mean \(\mu\) and finite variance. Then for every number \(c\),
\[
{\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[{\mathopen{}\left(Y - c\right)\mathclose{}}^{2}\right]\mathclose{}} = {\operatorname{Var}\mathopen{}\left(Y\right)\mathclose{}} + {\mathopen{}\left(\mu- c\right)\mathclose{}}^{2}.
\tag{2}\]










ProofProof






Proof. Add and subtract \(\mu\) inside the square, expand it, and take the expectation term by term:
\[
\begin{aligned}
{\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[{\mathopen{}\left(Y - c\right)\mathclose{}}^{2}\right]\mathclose{}}
&= {\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[{\mathopen{}\left((Y - \mu) + (\mu- c)\right)\mathclose{}}^{2}\right]\mathclose{}}
&& \text{(add and subtract } \mu\text{)} \\
&= {\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[{\mathopen{}\left(Y - \mu\right)\mathclose{}}^{2} + 2(\mu- c)(Y - \mu) + {\mathopen{}\left(\mu- c\right)\mathclose{}}^{2}\right]\mathclose{}}
&& \text{(expand the square of a sum)} \\
&= {\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[{\mathopen{}\left(Y - \mu\right)\mathclose{}}^{2}\right]\mathclose{}} + 2(\mu- c){\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[Y - \mu\right]\mathclose{}} + {\mathopen{}\left(\mu- c\right)\mathclose{}}^{2}
&& \text{(linearity of expectation; } \mu\text{ and } c \text{ are constants)} \\
&= {\operatorname{Var}\mathopen{}\left(Y\right)\mathclose{}} + 2(\mu- c){\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[Y - \mu\right]\mathclose{}} + {\mathopen{}\left(\mu- c\right)\mathclose{}}^{2}
&& \text{(variance as expected squared deviation)} \\
&= {\operatorname{Var}\mathopen{}\left(Y\right)\mathclose{}} + 2(\mu- c) \cdot 0 + {\mathopen{}\left(\mu- c\right)\mathclose{}}^{2}
&& \text{(} {\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[Y - \mu\right]\mathclose{}} = {\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[Y\right]\mathclose{}} - \mu= 0 \text{)} \\
&= {\operatorname{Var}\mathopen{}\left(Y\right)\mathclose{}} + {\mathopen{}\left(\mu- c\right)\mathclose{}}^{2}
&& \text{(zero times a number)}
\end{aligned}
\]










CorCorollary 1 (The mean is the best constant prediction under squared error)






Corollary 1 (The mean is the best constant prediction under squared error) Under the assumptions of Theorem 5,
\[
\arg \min_{c \in \mathbb{R}} {\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[{\mathopen{}\left(Y - c\right)\mathclose{}}^{2}\right]\mathclose{}} = {\mathopen{}\left\{\mu\right\}\mathclose{}}
\quad \text{and} \quad
\min_{c \in \mathbb{R}} {\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[{\mathopen{}\left(Y - c\right)\mathclose{}}^{2}\right]\mathclose{}} = {\operatorname{Var}\mathopen{}\left(Y\right)\mathclose{}},
\]
where \(\arg \min\) is the set of minimizers.










ProofProof






Proof. In Equation 2 the first term, \({\operatorname{Var}\mathopen{}\left(Y\right)\mathclose{}}\), does not depend on \(c\). The second term, \({\mathopen{}\left(\mu- c\right)\mathclose{}}^{2}\), is a square, so it is never negative, and it is zero exactly when \(c = \mu\). So \(c = \mu\) minimizes the expected squared error and no other number does, and at \(c = \mu\) the expected squared error is \({\operatorname{Var}\mathopen{}\left(Y\right)\mathclose{}}\).










ExmExample 9 (The best constant prediction of fuel economy)






Example 9 (The best constant prediction of fuel economy) Take the 392 cars in the Auto data described on the limit theorems page as the whole population, and predict the fuel economy (mpg) of a car drawn at random with one number \(c\). The code below computes the expected squared error of three constants, and sets each beside the right side of Equation 2.

mpg <- read.csv("data/auto.csv")$mpg
mu <- mean(mpg)
sigma2 <- mean((mpg - mu)^2)

c_values <- c(mean = mu, median = median(mpg), twenty = 20)
data.frame(
  c = c_values,
  expected_squared_error = sapply(c_values, function(cc) mean((mpg - cc)^2)),
  decomposition = sigma2 + (mu - c_values)^2
)


  



The two columns agree, as Theorem 5 says. The mean, 23.45, has the smallest expected squared error, 60.76, which is the variance of mpg over these cars (divisor the number of cars, not one fewer), as Corollary 1 says; the median and \(c = 20\) are each worse by \({\mathopen{}\left(\mu- c\right)\mathclose{}}^{2}\).

title: Probability basics
text:
DefDefinition 1 (Step)






Definition 1 (Step) A step is the carrying out of one instruction.










ExmExample 1 (Steps of a die roll)






Example 1 (Steps of a die roll) Carrying out the instruction “roll a six-sided die once” is one step. Carrying out the instruction “read the number facing up” is another step.










DefDefinition 2 (Procedure)






Definition 2 (Procedure) A procedure is a list of instructions that can be followed, one step at a time, until they are finished.










ExmExample 2 (Rolling a die once)






Example 2 (Rolling a die once) The instructions “roll a six-sided die once, then read the number facing up” comprise a procedure. Following the procedure takes the two steps in Example 1, and then it is finished.










DefDefinition 3 (Outcome)






Definition 3 (Outcome) An outcome is a single, fully specified way that a procedure can end, recorded as one value.










ExmExample 3 (Outcomes of a die roll)






Example 3 (Outcomes of a die roll) The procedure in Example 2 ends with one number facing up. Each of the numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 is an outcome, and one roll ends in exactly one of them.










DefDefinition 4 (Random experiment)






Definition 4 (Random experiment) A random experiment is a procedure that ends in exactly one outcome that we have not determined in advance [1].










RemarkRemark






Remark. The possible outcomes are collected in the sample space. Physical procedures, such as rolling a die, and sampling procedures, such as picking a unit from a data set without looking, are both random experiments.










ExmExample 4 (Rolling a die as a random experiment)






Example 4 (Rolling a die as a random experiment) The procedure in Example 2 is a random experiment: it ends in exactly one of the outcomes 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 or 6 (Example 3), and we do not determine in advance which outcome the procedure will produce.










ExmExample 5 (Picking a car model from the Auto data)






Example 5 (Picking a car model from the Auto data) The Auto data record the number of engine cylinders and the fuel economy (miles per gallon) of 392 car models sold between 1970 and 1982. They come from the StatLib library at Carnegie Mellon University and ship with the book An Introduction to Statistical Learning and the R package ISLR2 (ISLR2::Auto). This site has a copy at data/auto.csv.
Pick one car model from the data without looking, and record its number of cylinders. Which model comes up is not determined in advance, so this procedure is a random experiment. Its possible outcomes are the cylinder counts that occur in the data:

# read the local copy of the Auto data (one row per car model):
auto <- read.csv("data/auto.csv")

# the possible outcomes are the distinct cylinder counts in the data:
sort(unique(auto$cylinders))
#> [1] 3 4 5 6 8











DefDefinition 5 (Sample space)






Definition 5 (Sample space) The sample space of a random experiment, denoted \(\Omega\), is the set of all of its possible outcomes [2].










ExmExample 6 (Sample space of a die roll)






Example 6 (Sample space of a die roll) Rolling a six-sided die once has sample space \(\Omega= {\mathopen{}\left\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\right\}\mathclose{}}\).










DefDefinition 6 (Event)






Definition 6 (Event) An event is a subset of the sample space \(\Omega\) [3]: a set of outcomes.










RemarkRemark






Remark. When \(\Omega\) is uncountable, such as an interval of real numbers, only the subsets in a designated \(\sigma\)-algebra \(\mathcal{S}\) on \(\Omega\) count as events (some sources call a \(\sigma\)-algebra a Borel field [4], Def. 1.2.1); every set that arises in these notes is in \(\mathcal{S}\). When \(\Omega\) is finite or countably infinite, every subset of \(\Omega\) can be an event, because the collection of all subsets of \(\Omega\) is a \(\sigma\)-algebra (all subsets form a \(\sigma\)-algebra), as in \(\sigma\)-algebras for die rolls.










ExmExample 7 (Rolling an even number)






Example 7 (Rolling an even number) In Example 6, the event “the roll is even” is \(A = {\mathopen{}\left\{2, 4, 6\right\}\mathclose{}}\).










DefDefinition 7 (Occurrence of an event)






Definition 7 (Occurrence of an event) An event \(A\) occurs when the outcome of the experiment is in \(A\), and does not occur when the outcome is not in \(A\).










ExmExample 8 (Rolling a 4)






Example 8 (Rolling a 4) In Example 7, if the die shows 4, the event “the roll is even”, \({\mathopen{}\left\{2, 4, 6\right\}\mathclose{}}\), occurs, because \(4 \in {\mathopen{}\left\{2, 4, 6\right\}\mathclose{}}\), and the event “the roll is at most 2”, \({\mathopen{}\left\{1, 2\right\}\mathclose{}}\), does not occur.










DefDefinition 8 (Complement of an event)






Definition 8 (Complement of an event) The complement of an event \(A\), denoted \(\neg A\), is the event that \(A\) does not occur: the set of outcomes in the sample space \(\Omega\) that are not in \(A\).
\[\neg A \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}\Omega\setminus A\]










RemarkRemark






Remark. Other sources write \(A^c\) or \(\bar{A}\).










ExmExample 9 (Rolling an odd number)






Example 9 (Rolling an odd number) In Example 7, the complement of the event “the roll is even”, \(A = {\mathopen{}\left\{2, 4, 6\right\}\mathclose{}}\), is the event “the roll is odd”, \(\neg A = {\mathopen{}\left\{1, 3, 5\right\}\mathclose{}}\).










DefDefinition 9 (Mutually exclusive events (disjoint, pairwise disjoint, mutually disjoint))






Definition 9 (Mutually exclusive events (disjoint, pairwise disjoint, mutually disjoint)) Finitely or countably many sets \(A_1, A_2, \ldots\), such as events, are mutually exclusive (also called disjoint, pairwise disjoint, or mutually disjoint) when no two of them share an element:
\[A_i \cap A_j = \emptyset \quad \text{for all } i \neq j\]










RemarkRemark






Remark. The math notes define the same property for sets in general, as pairwise disjoint.










ExmExample 10 (Low and high rolls)






Example 10 (Low and high rolls) In Example 6, the events “the roll is at most 2”, \({\mathopen{}\left\{1, 2\right\}\mathclose{}}\), and “the roll is at least 5”, \({\mathopen{}\left\{5, 6\right\}\mathclose{}}\), are mutually exclusive: no roll is in both. The events “the roll is even”, \({\mathopen{}\left\{2, 4, 6\right\}\mathclose{}}\), and “the roll is at most 2”, \({\mathopen{}\left\{1, 2\right\}\mathclose{}}\), are not mutually exclusive: a roll of 2 is in both.










DefDefinition 10 (Partition of an event)






Definition 10 (Partition of an event) A partition of an event \(A\) is a finite or countably infinite collection of events \(A_1, A_2, \ldots\) that satisfies:

The events \(A_1, A_2, \ldots\) are mutually exclusive.
Their union is \(A\): \(\bigcup_{i} A_i = A\).











RemarkRemark 1 (A partition of the sample space)






Remark 1 (A partition of the sample space). A partition of the sample space is the case \(A = \Omega\).










RemarkRemark






Remark. Some sources also require each piece \(A_i\) to contain at least one outcome.










ExmExample 11 (Partitioning the die roll)






Example 11 (Partitioning the die roll) In Example 6, the events “the roll is even”, \({\mathopen{}\left\{2, 4, 6\right\}\mathclose{}}\), and “the roll is odd”, \({\mathopen{}\left\{1, 3, 5\right\}\mathclose{}}\), are mutually exclusive, and their union is \(\Omega\), so they partition the sample space. So do the six single-outcome events \({\mathopen{}\left\{1\right\}\mathclose{}}, {\mathopen{}\left\{2\right\}\mathclose{}}, \ldots, {\mathopen{}\left\{6\right\}\mathclose{}}\). The events \({\mathopen{}\left\{1, 2\right\}\mathclose{}}\) and \({\mathopen{}\left\{5, 6\right\}\mathclose{}}\) from Example 10 do not partition \(\Omega\): their union leaves out 3 and 4.










DefDefinition 11 (Probability measure (probability function))






Definition 11 (Probability measure (probability function)) A probability measure (also called a probability function [4], Definition 1.2.4) on a sample space \(\Omega\), often denoted \(\Pr()\) or \(\mathbb{P}()\), is a measure on the events of \(\Omega\) that gives the whole sample space probability 1 [5]:
\[\Pr(\Omega) = 1\]










ExmExample 12 (Probability measure for a fair die)






Example 12 (Probability measure for a fair die) For the die roll in Example 6, define \(\Pr(A) \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}\mathopen{}\left|A\right|\mathclose{} / 6\), where \(\mathopen{}\left|A\right|\mathclose{}\) is the number of outcomes in \(A\). This function is \(1/6\) times the counting measure \(\mu(A) = \mathopen{}\left|A\right|\mathclose{}\) on the die rolls (counting elements is a measure), so it is a measure on the events of \(\Omega\), and it gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Pr(\Omega) &= 6/6 \\
&= 1.
\end{aligned}
\]
The event “the roll is even” from Example 7 has probability
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Pr({\mathopen{}\left\{2, 4, 6\right\}\mathclose{}}) &= 3/6 \\
&= 1/2.
\end{aligned}
\]










CorCorollary 1 (Probability measures are finitely additive)






Corollary 1 (Probability measures are finitely additive) Every probability measure is finitely additive: for any mutually exclusive events \(A_1, \ldots, A_n\),
\[\Pr(A_1 \cup \cdots \cup A_n) = \sum_{i=1}^n\Pr(A_i)\]










ProofProof






Proof. A probability measure is a measure (Definition 11), so measures are finitely additive applies to it.










LemTheorem 1 (Continuity of probability)






Theorem 1 (Continuity of probability) If \(A_1 \supseteq A_2 \supseteq \cdots\) are events with \(\bigcap_{i=1}^{\infty} A_i = \emptyset\), then:
\[\lim_{n \to \infty} \Pr(A_n) = 0\]










ProofProof






Proof. For each \(i\), let \(B_i \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}A_i \setminus A_{i+1}\), the outcomes in \(A_i\) but not in \(A_{i+1}\). Each \(B_i = A_i \cap (\Omega\setminus A_{i+1})\) is an event, by closure properties of a \(\sigma\)-algebra.
The \(B_i\) are pairwise disjoint. For \(i < j\), \(B_j \subseteq A_j \subseteq A_{i+1}\), while \(B_i\) has no outcomes in \(A_{i+1}\), so \(B_i \cap B_j = \emptyset\).
\(A_n = \bigcup_{i=n}^{\infty} B_i\) for each \(n\). For \(i \ge n\), \(B_i \subseteq A_i \subseteq A_n\), so the union is contained in \(A_n\). Conversely, let \(\omega\in A_n\). Since \(\bigcap_{i} A_i = \emptyset\), \(\omega\) is not in every \(A_i\); since the \(A_i\) are nested, the indices \(i\) with \(\omega\in A_i\) are \(1, \ldots, m\) for some \(m \ge n\). Then \(\omega\in A_m\) and \(\omega\notin A_{m+1}\), so \(\omega\in B_m\).
\(\Pr(A_1)\) is finite. The events \(A_1\) and \(\Omega\setminus A_1\) are disjoint with union \(\Omega\), so Corollary 1 applies to them:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Pr(A_1)
&\le \Pr(A_1) + \Pr(\Omega\setminus A_1)
&& \text{(} \Pr(\Omega\setminus A_1) \ge 0 \text{)} \\
&= \Pr(\Omega)
&& \text{(finite additivity of } \Pr \text{)} \\
&= 1
&& \text{(definition of a probability measure)}
\end{aligned}
\]
The limit. For each \(n\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Pr(A_n)
&= {\Pr\mathopen{}\left(\bigcup_{i=n}^{\infty} B_i\right)\mathclose{}}
&& \text{(} A_n = \bigcup_{i=n}^{\infty} B_i \text{)} \\
&= \sum_{i=n}^{\infty} \Pr(B_i)
&& \text{(countable additivity; the } B_i \text{ are pairwise disjoint)}
\end{aligned}
\]
With \(n = 1\), this says the series \(\sum_{i=1}^{\infty} \Pr(B_i)\) has the finite total \(\Pr(A_1)\). So, for \(n \ge 2\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Pr(A_n)
&= \sum_{i=1}^{\infty} \Pr(B_i) - \sum_{i=1}^{n-1} \Pr(B_i)
&& \text{(split off the first } n - 1 \text{ terms; the total is finite)} \\
&= \Pr(A_1) - \sum_{i=1}^{n-1} \Pr(B_i)
&& \text{(the case } n = 1 \text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]
As \(n \to \infty\), the partial sums \(\sum_{i=1}^{n-1} \Pr(B_i)\) converge to the total \(\Pr(A_1)\), so \(\Pr(A_n) \to \Pr(A_1) - \Pr(A_1) = 0\).










RemarkRemark






Remark. Requiring countable additivity, not just finite additivity, enables results such as Theorem 1, and it is what makes sums over countably infinite partitions valid.










LemTheorem 2 (Kolmogorov axioms)






Theorem 2 (Kolmogorov axioms) A function \(\Pr\) that assigns a real number \(\Pr(A)\) to each event \(A\) of a sample space \(\Omega\) is a probability measure if and only if it satisfies:

For any event \(A\), \(\Pr(A) \ge 0\).
The probability of the whole sample space is 1: \[\Pr(\Omega) = 1\]
\(\Pr\) is countably additive: for any mutually exclusive events \(A_1, A_2, \ldots\), \[{\Pr\mathopen{}\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^{\infty} A_i\right)\mathclose{}} = \sum_{i=1}^{\infty} \Pr(A_i)\]











ProofProof






Proof. Suppose \(\Pr\) is a probability measure. It is a measure, so its values lie in the extended non-negative reals \([0, \infty]\), which gives axiom 1, and it is countably additive, which is axiom 3. Axiom 2 is the condition \(\Pr(\Omega) = 1\) in Definition 11.
Conversely, suppose \(\Pr\) satisfies the three axioms. By axiom 1, \(\Pr\) takes values in \([0, \infty]\), so axiom 3 says \(\Pr\) is countably additive in the sense of the definition of countable additivity. Then, by countable additivity and the empty set, \(\Pr(\emptyset)\) is 0 or \(\infty\); \(\Pr(\emptyset)\) is a real number, so \(\Pr(\emptyset) = 0\). So \(\Pr\) satisfies both conditions of the definition of a measure (\(\Pr(\emptyset) = 0\) and countable additivity) and is a measure on the events of \(\Omega\). With axiom 2, \(\Pr\) is a probability measure (Definition 11).










RemarkRemark






Remark. Many sources define a probability measure by these three axioms instead; the theorem shows that the two definitions agree. The axioms are named for Kolmogorov, who introduced them in 1933 [6]. The axiom form does not list \(\Pr(\emptyset) = 0\); the proof above derives it.










LemTheorem 3 (Probability of a subset’s intersection)






Theorem 3 (Probability of a subset’s intersection) If \(A\) and \(B\) are events and \(A\subseteq B\), then \(\Pr(A \cap B) = \Pr(A)\).










ProofProof






Proof. Since \(A \subseteq B\), every outcome in \(A\) is also in \(B\), so \(A \cap B = A\), and therefore \(\Pr(A \cap B) = \Pr(A)\).










LemTheorem 4 (An event and its complement sum to 1)






Theorem 4 (An event and its complement sum to 1) For any event \(A\) and its complement \(\neg A\):
\[\Pr(A) + \Pr(\neg A) = 1\]










ProofProof






Proof. The events \(A\) and \(\neg A\) are disjoint, and their union is \(\Omega\).
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Pr(A) + \Pr(\neg A)
&= \Pr(A \cup \neg A)
&& \text{(additivity of probability for disjoint events)} \\
&= \Pr(\Omega)
&& \text{(} A \cup \neg A = \Omega\text{)} \\
&= 1
&& \text{(probability of the sample space is 1)}
\end{aligned}
\]










CorCorollary 2 (Complement rule)






Corollary 2 (Complement rule) For any event \(A\):
\[\Pr(\neg A) = 1 - \Pr(A)\]










ProofProof






Proof. Subtract \(\Pr(A)\) from both sides of Theorem 4.










CorCorollary 3 (Complement rule in probability (\(\pi\)) notation)






Corollary 3 (Complement rule in probability (\(\pi\)) notation) If the probability of an event \(A\) is \(\Pr(A)=\pi\), then the probability that \(A\) does not occur is:
\[\Pr(\neg A)= 1 - \pi\]










ProofProof






Proof. \[
\begin{aligned}
\Pr(\neg A) &= 1 - \Pr(A)
&& \text{(complement rule)} \\
&= 1 - \pi
&& \text{(substitute } \Pr(A) = \pi\text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]










ExmExample 13 (Probability of not rolling a six)






Example 13 (Probability of not rolling a six) For a fair die, the event “the roll is a six” has probability \(\pi= 1/6\), so by Corollary 3 the probability of not rolling a six is \(1 - 1/6 = 5/6\).










DefDefinition 12 (Choosing at random)






Definition 12 (Choosing at random) Let \(S\) be a set with a measure \(\mu\) such that \(0 < \mu(S) < \infty\). To choose an element of \(S\) at random is to run a random experiment whose sample space is \(S\) and whose probability measure is the uniform distribution on \(S\).










ExmExample 14 (Choosing at random from a finite set and from an interval)






Example 14 (Choosing at random from a finite set and from an interval) For a finite set \(S\), let \(\mu(A) = \mathopen{}\left|A\right|\mathclose{}\) be the counting measure. Then \(\Pr(A) = \mathopen{}\left|A\right|\mathclose{} / \mathopen{}\left|S\right|\mathclose{}\), so every element of \(S\) has the same probability \(1/\mathopen{}\left|S\right|\mathclose{}\).
For the interval \(S = [0, 1]\), let \(\mu(A)\) be the length of \(A\). Then \(\Pr(A)\) is the length of \(A\), so the probability that the chosen number lies in \([0.2, 0.5]\) is \(0.3\). The chosen number has the \(\text{Uniform}(0, 1)\) distribution.
The integers have infinite counting measure, so they have no choice at random in this sense.










ExmExample 15 (Choosing a car at random from the Auto data)






Example 15 (Choosing a car at random from the Auto data) The Auto data of Example 5 have 392 car models. Let \(S\) be the set of car models in the data. Choosing a car at random from \(S\) (Definition 12), with the counting measure, gives each car probability \(1/\mathopen{}\left|S\right|\mathclose{}\), so the probability that the car has four cylinders is the fraction of cars with four cylinders:

# read the local copy of the Auto data (one row per car model):
auto <- read.csv("data/auto.csv")

# the event "four cylinders" is the set of rows where cylinders == 4;
# the mean of the logical vector is |A| / |S|, the probability in
# the definition of choosing at random:
mean(auto$cylinders == 4)
#> [1] 0.5076531

title: Probability basics
text:
DefDefinition 1 (Step)






Definition 1 (Step) A step is the carrying out of one instruction.










ExmExample 1 (Steps of a die roll)






Example 1 (Steps of a die roll) Carrying out the instruction “roll a six-sided die once” is one step. Carrying out the instruction “read the number facing up” is another step.










DefDefinition 2 (Procedure)






Definition 2 (Procedure) A procedure is a list of instructions that can be followed, one step at a time, until they are finished.










ExmExample 2 (Rolling a die once)






Example 2 (Rolling a die once) The instructions “roll a six-sided die once, then read the number facing up” comprise a procedure. Following the procedure takes the two steps in Example 1, and then it is finished.










DefDefinition 3 (Outcome)






Definition 3 (Outcome) An outcome is a single, fully specified way that a procedure can end, recorded as one value.










ExmExample 3 (Outcomes of a die roll)






Example 3 (Outcomes of a die roll) The procedure in Example 2 ends with one number facing up. Each of the numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 is an outcome, and one roll ends in exactly one of them.










DefDefinition 4 (Random experiment)






Definition 4 (Random experiment) A random experiment is a procedure that ends in exactly one outcome that we have not determined in advance [1].










RemarkRemark






Remark. The possible outcomes are collected in the sample space. Physical procedures, such as rolling a die, and sampling procedures, such as picking a unit from a data set without looking, are both random experiments.










ExmExample 4 (Rolling a die as a random experiment)






Example 4 (Rolling a die as a random experiment) The procedure in Example 2 is a random experiment: it ends in exactly one of the outcomes 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 or 6 (Example 3), and we do not determine in advance which outcome the procedure will produce.










ExmExample 5 (Picking a car model from the Auto data)






Example 5 (Picking a car model from the Auto data) The Auto data record the number of engine cylinders and the fuel economy (miles per gallon) of 392 car models sold between 1970 and 1982. They come from the StatLib library at Carnegie Mellon University and ship with the book An Introduction to Statistical Learning and the R package ISLR2 (ISLR2::Auto). This site has a copy at data/auto.csv.
Pick one car model from the data without looking, and record its number of cylinders. Which model comes up is not determined in advance, so this procedure is a random experiment. Its possible outcomes are the cylinder counts that occur in the data:

# read the local copy of the Auto data (one row per car model):
auto <- read.csv("data/auto.csv")

# the possible outcomes are the distinct cylinder counts in the data:
sort(unique(auto$cylinders))
#> [1] 3 4 5 6 8











DefDefinition 5 (Sample space)






Definition 5 (Sample space) The sample space of a random experiment, denoted \(\Omega\), is the set of all of its possible outcomes [2].










ExmExample 6 (Sample space of a die roll)






Example 6 (Sample space of a die roll) Rolling a six-sided die once has sample space \(\Omega= {\mathopen{}\left\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\right\}\mathclose{}}\).










DefDefinition 6 (Event)






Definition 6 (Event) An event is a subset of the sample space \(\Omega\) [3]: a set of outcomes.










RemarkRemark






Remark. When \(\Omega\) is uncountable, such as an interval of real numbers, only the subsets in a designated \(\sigma\)-algebra \(\mathcal{S}\) on \(\Omega\) count as events (some sources call a \(\sigma\)-algebra a Borel field [4], Def. 1.2.1); every set that arises in these notes is in \(\mathcal{S}\). When \(\Omega\) is finite or countably infinite, every subset of \(\Omega\) can be an event, because the collection of all subsets of \(\Omega\) is a \(\sigma\)-algebra (all subsets form a \(\sigma\)-algebra), as in \(\sigma\)-algebras for die rolls.










ExmExample 7 (Rolling an even number)






Example 7 (Rolling an even number) In Example 6, the event “the roll is even” is \(A = {\mathopen{}\left\{2, 4, 6\right\}\mathclose{}}\).










DefDefinition 7 (Occurrence of an event)






Definition 7 (Occurrence of an event) An event \(A\) occurs when the outcome of the experiment is in \(A\), and does not occur when the outcome is not in \(A\).










ExmExample 8 (Rolling a 4)






Example 8 (Rolling a 4) In Example 7, if the die shows 4, the event “the roll is even”, \({\mathopen{}\left\{2, 4, 6\right\}\mathclose{}}\), occurs, because \(4 \in {\mathopen{}\left\{2, 4, 6\right\}\mathclose{}}\), and the event “the roll is at most 2”, \({\mathopen{}\left\{1, 2\right\}\mathclose{}}\), does not occur.










DefDefinition 8 (Complement of an event)






Definition 8 (Complement of an event) The complement of an event \(A\), denoted \(\neg A\), is the event that \(A\) does not occur: the set of outcomes in the sample space \(\Omega\) that are not in \(A\).
\[\neg A \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}\Omega\setminus A\]










RemarkRemark






Remark. Other sources write \(A^c\) or \(\bar{A}\).










ExmExample 9 (Rolling an odd number)






Example 9 (Rolling an odd number) In Example 7, the complement of the event “the roll is even”, \(A = {\mathopen{}\left\{2, 4, 6\right\}\mathclose{}}\), is the event “the roll is odd”, \(\neg A = {\mathopen{}\left\{1, 3, 5\right\}\mathclose{}}\).










DefDefinition 9 (Mutually exclusive events (disjoint, pairwise disjoint, mutually disjoint))






Definition 9 (Mutually exclusive events (disjoint, pairwise disjoint, mutually disjoint)) Finitely or countably many sets \(A_1, A_2, \ldots\), such as events, are mutually exclusive (also called disjoint, pairwise disjoint, or mutually disjoint) when no two of them share an element:
\[A_i \cap A_j = \emptyset \quad \text{for all } i \neq j\]










RemarkRemark






Remark. The math notes define the same property for sets in general, as pairwise disjoint.










ExmExample 10 (Low and high rolls)






Example 10 (Low and high rolls) In Example 6, the events “the roll is at most 2”, \({\mathopen{}\left\{1, 2\right\}\mathclose{}}\), and “the roll is at least 5”, \({\mathopen{}\left\{5, 6\right\}\mathclose{}}\), are mutually exclusive: no roll is in both. The events “the roll is even”, \({\mathopen{}\left\{2, 4, 6\right\}\mathclose{}}\), and “the roll is at most 2”, \({\mathopen{}\left\{1, 2\right\}\mathclose{}}\), are not mutually exclusive: a roll of 2 is in both.










DefDefinition 10 (Partition of an event)






Definition 10 (Partition of an event) A partition of an event \(A\) is a finite or countably infinite collection of events \(A_1, A_2, \ldots\) that satisfies:

The events \(A_1, A_2, \ldots\) are mutually exclusive.
Their union is \(A\): \(\bigcup_{i} A_i = A\).











RemarkRemark 1 (A partition of the sample space)






Remark 1 (A partition of the sample space). A partition of the sample space is the case \(A = \Omega\).










RemarkRemark






Remark. Some sources also require each piece \(A_i\) to contain at least one outcome.










ExmExample 11 (Partitioning the die roll)






Example 11 (Partitioning the die roll) In Example 6, the events “the roll is even”, \({\mathopen{}\left\{2, 4, 6\right\}\mathclose{}}\), and “the roll is odd”, \({\mathopen{}\left\{1, 3, 5\right\}\mathclose{}}\), are mutually exclusive, and their union is \(\Omega\), so they partition the sample space. So do the six single-outcome events \({\mathopen{}\left\{1\right\}\mathclose{}}, {\mathopen{}\left\{2\right\}\mathclose{}}, \ldots, {\mathopen{}\left\{6\right\}\mathclose{}}\). The events \({\mathopen{}\left\{1, 2\right\}\mathclose{}}\) and \({\mathopen{}\left\{5, 6\right\}\mathclose{}}\) from Example 10 do not partition \(\Omega\): their union leaves out 3 and 4.










DefDefinition 11 (Probability measure (probability function))






Definition 11 (Probability measure (probability function)) A probability measure (also called a probability function [4], Definition 1.2.4) on a sample space \(\Omega\), often denoted \(\Pr()\) or \(\mathbb{P}()\), is a measure on the events of \(\Omega\) that gives the whole sample space probability 1 [5]:
\[\Pr(\Omega) = 1\]










ExmExample 12 (Probability measure for a fair die)






Example 12 (Probability measure for a fair die) For the die roll in Example 6, define \(\Pr(A) \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}\mathopen{}\left|A\right|\mathclose{} / 6\), where \(\mathopen{}\left|A\right|\mathclose{}\) is the number of outcomes in \(A\). This function is \(1/6\) times the counting measure \(\mu(A) = \mathopen{}\left|A\right|\mathclose{}\) on the die rolls (counting elements is a measure), so it is a measure on the events of \(\Omega\), and it gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Pr(\Omega) &= 6/6 \\
&= 1.
\end{aligned}
\]
The event “the roll is even” from Example 7 has probability
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Pr({\mathopen{}\left\{2, 4, 6\right\}\mathclose{}}) &= 3/6 \\
&= 1/2.
\end{aligned}
\]










CorCorollary 1 (Probability measures are finitely additive)






Corollary 1 (Probability measures are finitely additive) Every probability measure is finitely additive: for any mutually exclusive events \(A_1, \ldots, A_n\),
\[\Pr(A_1 \cup \cdots \cup A_n) = \sum_{i=1}^n\Pr(A_i)\]










ProofProof






Proof. A probability measure is a measure (Definition 11), so measures are finitely additive applies to it.










LemTheorem 1 (Continuity of probability)






Theorem 1 (Continuity of probability) If \(A_1 \supseteq A_2 \supseteq \cdots\) are events with \(\bigcap_{i=1}^{\infty} A_i = \emptyset\), then:
\[\lim_{n \to \infty} \Pr(A_n) = 0\]










ProofProof






Proof. For each \(i\), let \(B_i \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}A_i \setminus A_{i+1}\), the outcomes in \(A_i\) but not in \(A_{i+1}\). Each \(B_i = A_i \cap (\Omega\setminus A_{i+1})\) is an event, by closure properties of a \(\sigma\)-algebra.
The \(B_i\) are pairwise disjoint. For \(i < j\), \(B_j \subseteq A_j \subseteq A_{i+1}\), while \(B_i\) has no outcomes in \(A_{i+1}\), so \(B_i \cap B_j = \emptyset\).
\(A_n = \bigcup_{i=n}^{\infty} B_i\) for each \(n\). For \(i \ge n\), \(B_i \subseteq A_i \subseteq A_n\), so the union is contained in \(A_n\). Conversely, let \(\omega\in A_n\). Since \(\bigcap_{i} A_i = \emptyset\), \(\omega\) is not in every \(A_i\); since the \(A_i\) are nested, the indices \(i\) with \(\omega\in A_i\) are \(1, \ldots, m\) for some \(m \ge n\). Then \(\omega\in A_m\) and \(\omega\notin A_{m+1}\), so \(\omega\in B_m\).
\(\Pr(A_1)\) is finite. The events \(A_1\) and \(\Omega\setminus A_1\) are disjoint with union \(\Omega\), so Corollary 1 applies to them:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Pr(A_1)
&\le \Pr(A_1) + \Pr(\Omega\setminus A_1)
&& \text{(} \Pr(\Omega\setminus A_1) \ge 0 \text{)} \\
&= \Pr(\Omega)
&& \text{(finite additivity of } \Pr \text{)} \\
&= 1
&& \text{(definition of a probability measure)}
\end{aligned}
\]
The limit. For each \(n\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Pr(A_n)
&= {\Pr\mathopen{}\left(\bigcup_{i=n}^{\infty} B_i\right)\mathclose{}}
&& \text{(} A_n = \bigcup_{i=n}^{\infty} B_i \text{)} \\
&= \sum_{i=n}^{\infty} \Pr(B_i)
&& \text{(countable additivity; the } B_i \text{ are pairwise disjoint)}
\end{aligned}
\]
With \(n = 1\), this says the series \(\sum_{i=1}^{\infty} \Pr(B_i)\) has the finite total \(\Pr(A_1)\). So, for \(n \ge 2\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Pr(A_n)
&= \sum_{i=1}^{\infty} \Pr(B_i) - \sum_{i=1}^{n-1} \Pr(B_i)
&& \text{(split off the first } n - 1 \text{ terms; the total is finite)} \\
&= \Pr(A_1) - \sum_{i=1}^{n-1} \Pr(B_i)
&& \text{(the case } n = 1 \text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]
As \(n \to \infty\), the partial sums \(\sum_{i=1}^{n-1} \Pr(B_i)\) converge to the total \(\Pr(A_1)\), so \(\Pr(A_n) \to \Pr(A_1) - \Pr(A_1) = 0\).










RemarkRemark






Remark. Requiring countable additivity, not just finite additivity, enables results such as Theorem 1, and it is what makes sums over countably infinite partitions valid.










LemTheorem 2 (Kolmogorov axioms)






Theorem 2 (Kolmogorov axioms) A function \(\Pr\) that assigns a real number \(\Pr(A)\) to each event \(A\) of a sample space \(\Omega\) is a probability measure if and only if it satisfies:

For any event \(A\), \(\Pr(A) \ge 0\).
The probability of the whole sample space is 1: \[\Pr(\Omega) = 1\]
\(\Pr\) is countably additive: for any mutually exclusive events \(A_1, A_2, \ldots\), \[{\Pr\mathopen{}\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^{\infty} A_i\right)\mathclose{}} = \sum_{i=1}^{\infty} \Pr(A_i)\]











ProofProof






Proof. Suppose \(\Pr\) is a probability measure. It is a measure, so its values lie in the extended non-negative reals \([0, \infty]\), which gives axiom 1, and it is countably additive, which is axiom 3. Axiom 2 is the condition \(\Pr(\Omega) = 1\) in Definition 11.
Conversely, suppose \(\Pr\) satisfies the three axioms. By axiom 1, \(\Pr\) takes values in \([0, \infty]\), so axiom 3 says \(\Pr\) is countably additive in the sense of the definition of countable additivity. Then, by countable additivity and the empty set, \(\Pr(\emptyset)\) is 0 or \(\infty\); \(\Pr(\emptyset)\) is a real number, so \(\Pr(\emptyset) = 0\). So \(\Pr\) satisfies both conditions of the definition of a measure (\(\Pr(\emptyset) = 0\) and countable additivity) and is a measure on the events of \(\Omega\). With axiom 2, \(\Pr\) is a probability measure (Definition 11).










RemarkRemark






Remark. Many sources define a probability measure by these three axioms instead; the theorem shows that the two definitions agree. The axioms are named for Kolmogorov, who introduced them in 1933 [6]. The axiom form does not list \(\Pr(\emptyset) = 0\); the proof above derives it.










LemTheorem 3 (Probability of a subset’s intersection)






Theorem 3 (Probability of a subset’s intersection) If \(A\) and \(B\) are events and \(A\subseteq B\), then \(\Pr(A \cap B) = \Pr(A)\).










ProofProof






Proof. Since \(A \subseteq B\), every outcome in \(A\) is also in \(B\), so \(A \cap B = A\), and therefore \(\Pr(A \cap B) = \Pr(A)\).










LemTheorem 4 (An event and its complement sum to 1)






Theorem 4 (An event and its complement sum to 1) For any event \(A\) and its complement \(\neg A\):
\[\Pr(A) + \Pr(\neg A) = 1\]










ProofProof






Proof. The events \(A\) and \(\neg A\) are disjoint, and their union is \(\Omega\).
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Pr(A) + \Pr(\neg A)
&= \Pr(A \cup \neg A)
&& \text{(additivity of probability for disjoint events)} \\
&= \Pr(\Omega)
&& \text{(} A \cup \neg A = \Omega\text{)} \\
&= 1
&& \text{(probability of the sample space is 1)}
\end{aligned}
\]










CorCorollary 2 (Complement rule)






Corollary 2 (Complement rule) For any event \(A\):
\[\Pr(\neg A) = 1 - \Pr(A)\]










ProofProof






Proof. Subtract \(\Pr(A)\) from both sides of Theorem 4.










CorCorollary 3 (Complement rule in probability (\(\pi\)) notation)






Corollary 3 (Complement rule in probability (\(\pi\)) notation) If the probability of an event \(A\) is \(\Pr(A)=\pi\), then the probability that \(A\) does not occur is:
\[\Pr(\neg A)= 1 - \pi\]










ProofProof






Proof. \[
\begin{aligned}
\Pr(\neg A) &= 1 - \Pr(A)
&& \text{(complement rule)} \\
&= 1 - \pi
&& \text{(substitute } \Pr(A) = \pi\text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]










ExmExample 13 (Probability of not rolling a six)






Example 13 (Probability of not rolling a six) For a fair die, the event “the roll is a six” has probability \(\pi= 1/6\), so by Corollary 3 the probability of not rolling a six is \(1 - 1/6 = 5/6\).










DefDefinition 12 (Choosing at random)






Definition 12 (Choosing at random) Let \(S\) be a set with a measure \(\mu\) such that \(0 < \mu(S) < \infty\). To choose an element of \(S\) at random is to run a random experiment whose sample space is \(S\) and whose probability measure is the uniform distribution on \(S\).










ExmExample 14 (Choosing at random from a finite set and from an interval)






Example 14 (Choosing at random from a finite set and from an interval) For a finite set \(S\), let \(\mu(A) = \mathopen{}\left|A\right|\mathclose{}\) be the counting measure. Then \(\Pr(A) = \mathopen{}\left|A\right|\mathclose{} / \mathopen{}\left|S\right|\mathclose{}\), so every element of \(S\) has the same probability \(1/\mathopen{}\left|S\right|\mathclose{}\).
For the interval \(S = [0, 1]\), let \(\mu(A)\) be the length of \(A\). Then \(\Pr(A)\) is the length of \(A\), so the probability that the chosen number lies in \([0.2, 0.5]\) is \(0.3\). The chosen number has the \(\text{Uniform}(0, 1)\) distribution.
The integers have infinite counting measure, so they have no choice at random in this sense.










ExmExample 15 (Choosing a car at random from the Auto data)






Example 15 (Choosing a car at random from the Auto data) The Auto data of Example 5 have 392 car models. Let \(S\) be the set of car models in the data. Choosing a car at random from \(S\) (Definition 12), with the counting measure, gives each car probability \(1/\mathopen{}\left|S\right|\mathclose{}\), so the probability that the car has four cylinders is the fraction of cars with four cylinders:

# read the local copy of the Auto data (one row per car model):
auto <- read.csv("data/auto.csv")

# the event "four cylinders" is the set of rows where cylinders == 4;
# the mean of the logical vector is |A| / |S|, the probability in
# the definition of choosing at random:
mean(auto$cylinders == 4)
#> [1] 0.5076531

title: Probability basics
text:
2 Odds







DefDefinition 13 (Odds)






Definition 13 (Odds) Let \(A\) be an event with probability \(\mathbb{P}(A) \in (0, 1)\). The odds of \(A\) are [7]
\[\omega\stackrel{\text{def}}{=}\frac{\mathbb{P}(A)}{1 - \mathbb{P}(A)} \in (0, \infty).\]










ExmExample 16 (Odds that a car in the Auto data is American)






Example 16 (Odds that a car in the Auto data is American) In the Auto data of Example 5, let \(A\) be the event that a car chosen at random is American, which the data code as origin == 1. Its probability is the fraction of American cars, as in Example 15, and its odds follow from Definition 13:

auto <- read.csv("data/auto.csv")
p_american <- mean(auto$origin == 1)
c(probability = p_american, odds = p_american / (1 - p_american))
#> probability        odds 
#>    0.625000    1.666667

The odds 1.67 say that an American car is about 1.7 times as likely as a car of non-American origin.










DefDefinition 14 (Log-odds (also called the logit))






Definition 14 (Log-odds (also called the logit)) The log-odds, also called the logit, of an event \(A\) with probability \(\mathbb{P}(A) \in (0, 1)\) are the natural logarithm of its odds [8]:
\[\eta\stackrel{\text{def}}{=}{\operatorname{log}\mathopen{}\left\{\omega\right\}\mathclose{}} = {\operatorname{log}\mathopen{}\left\{\frac{\mathbb{P}(A)}{1 - \mathbb{P}(A)}\right\}\mathclose{}} \in \mathbb{R}.\]










ExmExample 17 (Log-odds that a car in the Auto data is American)






Example 17 (Log-odds that a car in the Auto data is American) For the event \(A\) of Example 16, the log-odds of Definition 14 are:

log(p_american / (1 - p_american))
#> [1] 0.5108256

The log-odds are positive because the odds exceed 1: an American car is more likely than not.

title: Probability basics
text:
3 Conditional probability







DefDefinition 15 (Conditional probability)






Definition 15 (Conditional probability) For two events \(A\) and \(B\) with \(\Pr(B) > 0\), the conditional probability of \(A\) given \(B\) [9], denoted \(\Pr(A \mid B)\), is:
\[\Pr(A \mid B) \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}\frac{\Pr(A \cap B)}{\Pr(B)}\]










RemarkRemark






Remark. Geometrically and computationally, conditioning on an event \(B\) can be viewed as slicing the sample space to retain only the outcomes compatible with \(B\), and then renormalizing the remaining probabilities (dividing by \(\Pr(B)\)) so that they sum to 1 [10, Sec. 2.7.4].










ExmExample 18 (Rolling a six, given an even roll)






Example 18 (Rolling a six, given an even roll) For a fair die (Example 12), let \(A = {\mathopen{}\left\{6\right\}\mathclose{}}\) and \(B = {\mathopen{}\left\{2, 4, 6\right\}\mathclose{}}\). Then \(A \cap B = {\mathopen{}\left\{6\right\}\mathclose{}}\), so:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Pr(A \mid B)
&= \frac{\Pr(A \cap B)}{\Pr(B)}
&& \text{(definition of conditional probability)} \\
&= \frac{1/6}{3/6}
&& \text{(substitute the probabilities)} \\
&= \frac{1}{3}
&& \text{(simplify)}
\end{aligned}
\]










LemTheorem 5 (Law of conditional probability)






Theorem 5 (Law of conditional probability) For any two events \(A\) and \(B\) with \(\Pr(B) > 0\):
\[\Pr(A \cap B) = \Pr(A \mid B) \cdot\Pr(B)\]










ProofProof






Proof. Rearranging Definition 15:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Pr(A \mid B) &= \frac{\Pr(A \cap B)}{\Pr(B)} && \text{(definition of conditional probability)}
\\ \Pr(A \cap B) &= \Pr(A \mid B) \cdot\Pr(B) && \text{(multiply both sides by } \Pr(B) \text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]










ExmExample 19 (Applying the law of conditional probability)






Example 19 (Applying the law of conditional probability) Suppose 30% of adults exercise regularly (\(\Pr(E) = 0.30\)), and among adults who exercise regularly, 60% have low blood pressure (\(\Pr(L \mid E) = 0.60\)).
Then, by Theorem 5, the probability that a randomly selected adult both exercises regularly and has low blood pressure is:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Pr(L \cap E) &= \Pr(L \mid E) \cdot\Pr(E)
&& \text{(law of conditional probability)} \\
&= 0.60 \cdot 0.30
&& \text{(substitute the given values)} \\
&= 0.18
&& \text{(multiply)}
\end{aligned}
\]










LemTheorem 6 (Law of total probability)






Theorem 6 (Law of total probability) If \(B_1, B_2, \ldots\) is a partition of the sample space, with \(\Pr(B_i) > 0\) for every \(i\), then for any event \(A\) [11]:
\[\Pr(A) = \sum_{i=1}^{\infty} \Pr(A \mid B_i) \cdot\Pr(B_i)\]










ProofProof






Proof. Since \(B_1, B_2, \ldots\) partition the sample space, the events \(A \cap B_1, A \cap B_2, \ldots\) are mutually exclusive and their union is \(A\). By countable additivity, and then by Theorem 5:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Pr(A)
&= \sum_{i=1}^{\infty} \Pr(A \cap B_i) && \text{(countable additivity for partition of } A \text{)}
\\&= \sum_{i=1}^{\infty} \Pr(A \mid B_i) \cdot\Pr(B_i) && \text{(law of conditional probability; } \Pr(B_i) > 0 \text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]










LemTheorem 7 (Bayes’ theorem)






Theorem 7 (Bayes’ theorem) For any two events \(A\) and \(B\) with \(\Pr(A) > 0\) and \(\Pr(B) > 0\) [12]:
\[\Pr(A \mid B) = \frac{\Pr(B \mid A) \cdot\Pr(A)}{\Pr(B)}\]










ProofProof






Proof. By Definition 15 and Theorem 5:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Pr(A \mid B)
&= \frac{\Pr(A \cap B)}{\Pr(B)}
&& \text{(definition of conditional probability)} \\
&= \frac{\Pr(B \cap A)}{\Pr(B)}
&& \text{(intersection is commutative: } A \cap B = B \cap A \text{)} \\
&= \frac{\Pr(B \mid A) \cdot\Pr(A)}{\Pr(B)}
&& \text{(law of conditional probability applied to } \Pr(B \cap A) \text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]










ExmExample 20 (Positive predictive value of a medical test)






Example 20 (Positive predictive value of a medical test) Suppose a disease test has 99% sensitivity and 99% specificity, and the prevalence of the disease in the population is 7%.
Let \(D\) be the event “person has the disease” and \({+}\) be the event “test is positive”. Then:

\(\Pr({+}\mid D) = 0.99\) (sensitivity)
\(\Pr({-}\mid \neg D) = 0.99\) (specificity), so the false positive rate is
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Pr({+}\mid \neg D) &= 1 - 0.99 \\
&= 0.01
\end{aligned}
\]
\(\Pr(D) = 0.07\) (prevalence)

By Theorem 7, with the denominator expanded by the law of total probability over the partition \(\{D, \neg D\}\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Pr(D \mid {+})
&= \frac{\Pr({+}\mid D) \cdot\Pr(D)}{\Pr({+})}
&& \text{(Bayes' theorem)} \\
&= \frac{\Pr({+}\mid D) \cdot\Pr(D)}{\Pr({+}\mid D) \cdot\Pr(D) + \Pr({+}\mid \neg D) \cdot\Pr(\neg D)}
&& \text{(law of total probability)} \\
&= \frac{0.99 \cdot 0.07}{0.99 \cdot 0.07 + 0.01 \cdot 0.93}
&& \text{(substitute the given values)} \\
&= \frac{0.0693}{0.0693 + 0.0093}
&& \text{(multiply each term in the numerator and denominator)} \\
&= \frac{0.0693}{0.0786}
&& \text{(add the denominator's two terms)} \\
&\approx 0.88
&& \text{(divide)}
\end{aligned}
\]
Even with a highly accurate test (99% sensitive and 99% specific), only about 88% of people who test positive actually have the disease, because the disease prevalence is relatively low (7%).










ExrExercise 1 (Turn a conditional around)






Exercise 1 (Turn a conditional around) Definition 15 defines \(\Pr(A \mid B)\) in terms of \(\Pr(A \cap B)\). Write the same definition with \(A\) and \(B\) swapped, then eliminate \(\Pr(A \cap B)\) between the two.
Your result should express \(\Pr(A \mid B)\) using \(\Pr(B \mid A)\), \(\Pr(A)\) and \(\Pr(B)\), and none of them jointly.










SolutionSolution 1






Solution 1. Multiplying Definition 15 through by its denominator, in each direction,
\[\Pr(A \cap B) = \Pr(A \mid B)\,\Pr(B),
\qquad
\Pr(A \cap B) = \Pr(B \mid A)\,\Pr(A)\]
The left-hand sides are the same quantity, so the right-hand sides are equal. Dividing by \(\Pr(B)\) gives Bayes’ rule (Theorem 7):
\[\Pr(A \mid B) = \frac{\Pr(B \mid A)\,\Pr(A)}{\Pr(B)} \tag{1}\]
Nothing was assumed beyond \(\Pr(A) > 0\) and \(\Pr(B) > 0\), which the two conditionals need in order to be defined at all.
As Hutchinson emphasizes [13], each component carries standard Bayesian terminology:

\(\Pr(A \mid B)\) is the posterior probability of \(A\) given the observed evidence \(B\).
\(\Pr(B \mid A)\) is the likelihood of the evidence \(B\) given \(A\).
\(\Pr(A)\) is the prior probability of \(A\) before seeing \(B\).
\(\Pr(B)\) is the marginal probability of the evidence.

From this formula, the direction of effects is transparent: increasing the prior \(\Pr(A)\) or the likelihood \(\Pr(B \mid A)\) increases the posterior \(\Pr(A \mid B)\), while increasing the probability of the evidence \(\Pr(B)\) decreases it.










ExrExercise 2 (A test that is right 99% of the time)






Exercise 2 (A test that is right 99% of the time) A screening test for a disease is positive for \(99\%\) of people who have it and negative for \(99\%\) of people who do not. One person in a thousand has the disease.
A randomly screened person tests positive. What is the probability that they have the disease? Guess first, then compute it with Equation 1.










SolutionSolution 2






Solution 2. Write \(S\) for having the disease and \({+}\) for a positive test. The three given numbers are
\[\Pr({+}\mid S) = 0.99, \qquad \Pr({+}\mid \text{not } S) = 0.01, \qquad \Pr(S) = 0.001\]
Equation 1 needs \(\Pr({+})\), the overall chance of a positive result. Assemble it with Theorem 6, splitting on whether the person is sick:
\[\begin{aligned}
\Pr({+}) &= \Pr({+}\mid S)\Pr(S) + \Pr({+}\mid \text{not } S)\Pr(\text{not } S) \\
&= (0.99)(0.001) + (0.01)(0.999) \\
&= 0.00099 + 0.00999 \\
&= 0.01098
\end{aligned}\]
Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Pr(S \mid {+})
&= \frac{\Pr({+}\mid S)\,\Pr(S)}{\Pr({+})} \\
&= \frac{0.00099}{0.01098} \\
&\approx 0.0902
\end{aligned}
\]
About 9%, not the \(99\%\) most people guess.
The reason is the base rate [14]. Out of \(100{,}000\) people screened, about \(100\) have the disease and \(99\) of them test positive, while \(99{,}900\) do not have it and about \(999\) of them test positive anyway. The false positives outnumber the true positives ten to one, because there are a thousand times more people available to produce them.
The base rate is fundamental to evaluating screening tests and binary classifiers, and it illustrates why raw accuracy can be misleading on rare events.






Show code
brPost = (prev) => brSens * prev / (brSens * prev + (1 - brSpec) * (1 - prev))
// The same people as counts, out of 100,000 screened.
brN = 100000
brSick = brN * brPrev
brTP = brSick * brSens
brFP = (brN - brSick) * (1 - brSpec)












































Show code
viewof brSens = Inputs.range([0.5, 1], {value: 0.99, step: 0.001, label: "P(+ | S), sensitivity"})
viewof brSpec = Inputs.range([0.5, 1], {value: 0.99, step: 0.001, label: "P(\u2212 | not S), specificity"})
viewof brPrev = Inputs.range([0.0001, 0.5], {value: 0.001, transform: Math.log, format: d3.format(".4~f"), label: "P(S), prevalence"})


Show code
{
  const n = (v) => Math.round(v).toLocaleString("en-US");
  return md`Out of ${n(brN)} people screened, ${n(brSick)} have the disease and ${n(brTP)} of them test positive;
of the ${n(brN - brSick)} who do not, ${n(brFP)} test positive anyway.
So of the ${n(brTP + brFP)} positives, ${n(brTP)} are sick:
P(S | +) = **${(100 * brPost(brPrev)).toFixed(1)}%**.`;
}


Show code
Plot.plot({
  ariaLabel: 'Of 100,000 people screened, ' +
    'the ones who test positive, ' +
    'as one bar split into the sick, ' +
    'in orange, ' +
    'and the healthy, ' +
    'in blue.',
  width: 380, height: 120, marginLeft: 10, marginRight: 20,
  x: {label: "people who test positive, out of 100,000 screened"},
  color: {domain: ["sick", "not sick"], range: ["#ff7f0e", "#1f77b4"], legend: true},

    Plot.barX([{who: "sick", n: brTP}, {who: "not sick", n: brFP}],
              {x: "n", fill: "who", insetTop: 10, insetBottom: 10}),

  ]
})


Show code
Plot.plot({
  ariaLabel: 'The chance of disease after a positive test, ' +
    'plotted against the prevalence on a log scale, ' +
    'for the chosen sensitivity and specificity, ' +
    'with the chosen prevalence marked.',
  width: 380, height: 230, grid: true,
  x: {type: "log", domain: [0.0001, 0.5], label: "P(S), prevalence (log scale)",
      ticks: [0.0001, 0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 0.5], tickFormat: d3.format(".2~%")},
  y: {domain: [0, 1], label: "P(S | +)"},

    Plot.line(d3.range(-4, Math.log10(0.5) + 0.001, 0.02).map((e) => 10 ** e),

})




Figure 1: The chance of disease after a positive test, as counts out of 100,000 people screened and as a function of the prevalence.

title: Limit theorems
text:
RemarkRemark






Remark. The sample mean of many independent random variables, none of which dominates the others, has a distribution that is approximately bell-shaped, whatever the distributions of the individual variables. Theorem 1 makes this precise.










LemTheorem 1 (Central Limit Theorem)






Theorem 1 (Central Limit Theorem) Let \(X_1, X_2, \ldots\) be IID random variables with population mean \(\mu\) and finite variance \(\sigma^2> 0\), and let \({{\bar{X}}_{n}} \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^nX_i\). Then for every real number \(z\) [1]:
\[
\lim_{n \to \infty} {\Pr\mathopen{}\left(\frac{\sqrt{n}\,({{\bar{X}}_{n}} - \mu)}{\sigma} \le z\right)\mathclose{}} = \Phi(z)
\]
where \(\Phi(z) \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}\int_{-\infty}^{z} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \text{e}^{-u^2/2}\,du\) is the CDF of the standard normal distribution \({\operatorname{N}\mathopen{}\left(0, 1\right)\mathclose{}}\).










RemarkRemark






Remark. This version is the Lindeberg–Lévy CLT; its proof is beyond these notes’ scope [2], Theorem 27.1. Other versions relax the IID assumption, which is why the informal statement asks only that no summand dominate.










CorCorollary 1 (Central Limit Theorem for a sum)






Corollary 1 (Central Limit Theorem for a sum) Let \(X_1, X_2, \ldots\) be IID random variables with population mean \(\mu\) and finite variance \(\sigma^2> 0\), and let \(S_n \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}\sum_{i=1}^nX_i\). Then for every real number \(z\):
\[
\lim_{n \to \infty} {\Pr\mathopen{}\left(\frac{S_n - n\mu}{\sigma\sqrt{n}} \le z\right)\mathclose{}} = \Phi(z)
\]










ProofProof






Proof. Since \(S_n = n{{\bar{X}}_{n}}\),
\[
\frac{S_n - n\mu}{\sigma\sqrt{n}}
= \frac{n({{\bar{X}}_{n}} - \mu)}{\sigma\sqrt{n}}
= \frac{\sqrt{n}\,({{\bar{X}}_{n}} - \mu)}{\sigma},
\]
so the event in this corollary is the event in Theorem 1, and the limits agree.










LemTheorem 2 (Mean and variance of a sum of IID random variables)






Theorem 2 (Mean and variance of a sum of IID random variables) Let \(X_1, \ldots, X_n\) be IID random variables, each discrete or continuous, with population mean \(\mu\) and finite variance \(\sigma^2\), and let \(S_n \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}\sum_{i=1}^nX_i\). Then, by linearity of expectation for finite sums and the variance of a linear combination:
\[
\begin{aligned}
{\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[S_n\right]\mathclose{}} &= n\mu\\
{\operatorname{Var}\mathopen{}\left(S_n\right)\mathclose{}} &= n\sigma^2
\end{aligned}
\]










ProofProof






Proof. For the mean, apply linearity of expectation for finite sums with every \(a_i = 1\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
{\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[S_n\right]\mathclose{}}
&= {\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[\sum_{i=1}^n1 \cdot X_i\right]\mathclose{}}
&& \text{(} 1 \cdot v = v \text{)} \\
&= \sum_{i=1}^n1 \cdot{\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[X_i\right]\mathclose{}}
&& \text{(linearity of expectation for finite sums, all } a_i = 1 \text{)} \\
&= \sum_{i=1}^n{\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[X_i\right]\mathclose{}}
&& \text{(} 1 \cdot v = v \text{)} \\
&= n\mu
&& \text{(each } X_i \text{ has mean } \mu\text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]
For the variance, apply the variance of a linear combination with every \(a_i = 1\). For \(i \ne j\), \(X_i\) and \(X_j\) are independent (take \(A_k = \mathbb{R}\) for every other \(k\) in the definition of independence), so \({\operatorname{Cov}\mathopen{}\left(X_i, X_j\right)\mathclose{}} = 0\) for independent summands; and \({\operatorname{Cov}\mathopen{}\left(X_i, X_i\right)\mathclose{}} = {\operatorname{Var}\mathopen{}\left(X_i\right)\mathclose{}}\) (covariance of a variable with itself):
\[
\begin{aligned}
{\operatorname{Var}\mathopen{}\left(S_n\right)\mathclose{}}
&= \sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^n {\operatorname{Cov}\mathopen{}\left(X_i, X_j\right)\mathclose{}}
&& \text{(variance of a linear combination, all } a_i = 1 \text{)} \\
&= \sum_{i=1}^n{\operatorname{Cov}\mathopen{}\left(X_i, X_i\right)\mathclose{}} + \sum_{\substack{i, j = 1 \\ i \ne j}}^n {\operatorname{Cov}\mathopen{}\left(X_i, X_j\right)\mathclose{}}
&& \text{(split off the terms with } i = j \text{)} \\
&= \sum_{i=1}^n{\operatorname{Var}\mathopen{}\left(X_i\right)\mathclose{}} + 0
&& \text{(covariance with itself; independent summands)} \\
&= n\sigma^2
&& \text{(each } X_i \text{ has variance } \sigma^2\text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]










CorCorollary 2 (Mean and variance of a sample mean of IID random variables)






Corollary 2 (Mean and variance of a sample mean of IID random variables) Let \(X_1, \ldots, X_n\) be IID random variables, each discrete or continuous, with population mean \(\mu\) and finite variance \(\sigma^2\), and let \({{\bar{X}}_{n}} \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^nX_i\). Then:
\[
\begin{aligned}
{\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[{{\bar{X}}_{n}}\right]\mathclose{}} &= \mu\\
{\operatorname{Var}\mathopen{}\left({{\bar{X}}_{n}}\right)\mathclose{}} &= \frac{\sigma^2}{n}
\end{aligned}
\]










ProofProof






Proof. Let \(S_n \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}\sum_{i=1}^nX_i\), so \({{\bar{X}}_{n}} = S_n / n\). By Theorem 2, \({\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[S_n\right]\mathclose{}} = n\mu\) and \({\operatorname{Var}\mathopen{}\left(S_n\right)\mathclose{}} = n\sigma^2\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
{\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[{{\bar{X}}_{n}}\right]\mathclose{}}
&= {\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[\frac{S_n}{n}\right]\mathclose{}}
&& \text{(definition of sample mean)}\\
&= \frac{1}{n}{\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[S_n\right]\mathclose{}}
&& \text{(linearity of expectation)}\\
&= \frac{1}{n} \cdot n\mu
&& \text{(mean of a sum of IID variables)}\\
&= \mu
&& \text{(cancel $n$)}\\
{\operatorname{Var}\mathopen{}\left({{\bar{X}}_{n}}\right)\mathclose{}}
&= {\operatorname{Var}\mathopen{}\left(\frac{S_n}{n}\right)\mathclose{}}
&& \text{(definition of sample mean)}\\
&= \frac{1}{n^2}{\operatorname{Var}\mathopen{}\left(S_n\right)\mathclose{}}
&& \text{(variance of a constant multiple)}\\
&= \frac{1}{n^2} \cdot n\sigma^2
&& \text{(variance of a sum of IID variables)}\\
&= \frac{\sigma^2}{n}
&& \text{(cancel one factor of $n$)}
\end{aligned}
\]










RemarkRemark






Remark. In practice, Theorem 1 justifies approximating \({{\bar{X}}_{n}}\) by a normal distribution with mean \(\mu\) and variance \(\sigma^2/n\), and Corollary 1 justifies approximating \(S_n\) by a normal distribution with mean \(n\mu\) and variance \(n\sigma^2\). By Theorem 2, these are exactly the means and variances of \({{\bar{X}}_{n}} = S_n/n\) and \(S_n\).










ExmExample 1 (The sum of five dice)






Example 1 (The sum of five dice) A single fair die roll has the discrete uniform distribution on \({\mathopen{}\left\{1, \ldots, 6\right\}\mathclose{}}\), which is flat, not bell-shaped (Figure 1). Its mean is \(\mu= 3.5\), and its variance is
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sigma^2&= \sum_{x=1}^{6} (x - 3.5)^2 / 6 \\
&= 35/12.
\end{aligned}
\]


Show code
dice_sum_pmf <- function(n_dice) {
  totals <- rowSums(expand.grid(rep(list(1:6), n_dice)))
  probs <- prop.table(table(totals))
  tibble::tibble(total = as.numeric(names(probs)), p = as.vector(probs))
}

dice_plot <-
  ggplot2::ggplot(mapping = ggplot2::aes(x = total, y = p)) +
  ggplot2::xlab("sum of dice (x)") +
  ggplot2::ylab("Probability of outcome, Pr(X=x)") +
  ggplot2::expand_limits(y = 0)

dice_plot + ggplot2::geom_col(data = dice_sum_pmf(1))











Figure 1: Distribution of the outcome of one die











The sum of five independent rolls, \(S_5\), is already close to bell-shaped (Figure 2).


Show code
pmf_five_dice <- dice_sum_pmf(5)
dice_plot + ggplot2::geom_col(data = pmf_five_dice)











Figure 2: Distribution of the sum of five dice











For example, the exact probability that five dice total at most 15 is \(\Pr(S_5 \le 15) = 0.3052\). The normal approximation that Corollary 1 suggests, with mean \(5 \cdot 3.5 = 17.5\) and variance \(5 \cdot 35/12 \approx 14.58\), evaluated at \(15.5\) to account for \(S_5\) taking only integer values, gives \(\Phi\mathopen{}\left((15.5 - 17.5)/\sqrt{14.58}\right)\mathclose{} \approx 0.3002\).










ExmExample 2 (Sample means of car horsepower)






Example 2 (Sample means of car horsepower) The Auto data record the horsepower and fuel economy of 392 car models sold between 1970 and 1982. They come from the StatLib library at Carnegie Mellon University and ship with the book An Introduction to Statistical Learning, in the Python package ISLP (ISLP.load_data("Auto")) and the R package ISLR2 (ISLR2::Auto). This site has a copy at data/auto.csv, and both code tabs below read that file.
Horsepower is not bell-shaped: a few powerful cars give it a long right tail. To apply Theorem 1, treat each draw of one car at random as one IID observation \(X_i\), so that \(\mu\) and \(\sigma^2\) are the population mean and variance of the 392 horsepower values. The sample mean \({{\bar{X}}_{n}} = S_n/n\), where \(S_n = \sum_{i=1}^nX_i\), has mean \(\mu\) and standard deviation \(\sigma/\sqrt{n}\), because \(S_n\) has mean \(n\mu\) and variance \(n\sigma^2\) by Theorem 2. The code below draws 10,000 random samples of each size \(n \in {\mathopen{}\left\{1, 5, 30\right\}\mathclose{}}\), with replacement, and computes each sample’s sample mean.

PythonR



import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

hp = pd.read_csv("data/auto.csv")["horsepower"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
mu, sigma = hp.mean(), hp.std(ddof=0)

rng = np.random.default_rng(571)
sizes = [1, 5, 30]
sample_means = {n: rng.choice(hp, size=(10_000, n)).mean(axis=1) for n in sizes}

def skewness(x):
    return np.mean(((x - x.mean()) / x.std()) ** 3)

pd.DataFrame({
    "n": sizes,
    "sd of sample means": [sample_means[n].std(ddof=1) for n in sizes],
    "sigma / sqrt(n)": [sigma / np.sqrt(n) for n in sizes],
    "skewness of sample means": [skewness(sample_means[n]) for n in sizes],
})
#>     n  sd of sample means  sigma / sqrt(n)  skewness of sample means
#> 0   1           38.691521        38.442033                  1.080767
#> 1   5           17.265666        17.191800                  0.522243
#> 2  30            6.971269         7.018523                  0.164940




hp <- read.csv("data/auto.csv")$horsepower
mu <- mean(hp)
sigma <- sqrt(mean((hp - mu)^2))

set.seed(571)
sizes <- c(1, 5, 30)
sample_means <- lapply(sizes, function(n) {
  replicate(10000, mean(sample(hp, n, replace = TRUE)))
})

skewness <- function(x) mean(((x - mean(x)) / sqrt(mean((x - mean(x))^2)))^3)

data.frame(
  n = sizes,
  sd_of_sample_means = sapply(sample_means, sd),
  sigma_over_root_n = sigma / sqrt(sizes),
  skewness_of_sample_means = sapply(sample_means, skewness)
)


  






Figure 3 shows a histogram of the 10,000 sample means for each \(n\), with the normal density \({\operatorname{N}\mathopen{}\left(\mu, \sigma^2/n\right)\mathclose{}}\) from Theorem 1 drawn over it.


Show code

means_long <- tibble::tibble(
  n = factor(
    rep(n_labels, each = length(sample_means[[1]])),
    levels = n_labels
  ),
  sample_mean = unlist(sample_means)
)
normal_curves <- seq_along(sizes) |>
  lapply(function(k) {
    se <- sigma / sqrt(sizes[k])
    grid <- seq(mu - 4 * se, mu + 4 * se, length.out = 200)
    tibble::tibble(
      n = factor(n_labels[k], levels = n_labels),
      sample_mean = grid,
      density = dnorm(grid, mu, se)
    )
  }) |>
  dplyr::bind_rows()

ggplot2::ggplot(means_long, ggplot2::aes(x = sample_mean)) +
  ggplot2::geom_histogram(
    ggplot2::aes(y = ggplot2::after_stat(density)),
    bins = 40,
    fill = "grey70",
    color = "white"
  ) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(
    ggplot2::aes(y = density),
    data = normal_curves,
    linewidth = 1
  ) +
  ggplot2::facet_wrap(ggplot2::vars(n), scales = "free") +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "sample mean of horsepower", y = "density") +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal()











Figure 3: Histograms of 10,000 sample means of horsepower, for samples of n = 1, 5 and 30 cars drawn with replacement from the Auto data. The curve is the normal density with mean mu and standard deviation sigma over the square root of n.











The sample means for \(n = 1\) are just single cars, so they are skewed. By \(n = 30\) the histogram is close to the normal curve. The standard deviation of the sample means is within 1.2% of \(\sigma/\sqrt{n}\) at every \(n\), as Theorem 2 predicts. The skewness of the sample means, which is zero for a normal distribution, falls from 1.07 at \(n = 1\) to 0.48 at \(n = 5\) and 0.2 at \(n = 30\).

title: Limit theorems
text:
RemarkRemark






Remark. The sample mean of many independent random variables, none of which dominates the others, has a distribution that is approximately bell-shaped, whatever the distributions of the individual variables. Theorem 1 makes this precise.










LemTheorem 1 (Central Limit Theorem)






Theorem 1 (Central Limit Theorem) Let \(X_1, X_2, \ldots\) be IID random variables with population mean \(\mu\) and finite variance \(\sigma^2> 0\), and let \({{\bar{X}}_{n}} \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^nX_i\). Then for every real number \(z\) [1]:
\[
\lim_{n \to \infty} {\Pr\mathopen{}\left(\frac{\sqrt{n}\,({{\bar{X}}_{n}} - \mu)}{\sigma} \le z\right)\mathclose{}} = \Phi(z)
\]
where \(\Phi(z) \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}\int_{-\infty}^{z} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \text{e}^{-u^2/2}\,du\) is the CDF of the standard normal distribution \({\operatorname{N}\mathopen{}\left(0, 1\right)\mathclose{}}\).










RemarkRemark






Remark. This version is the Lindeberg–Lévy CLT; its proof is beyond these notes’ scope [2], Theorem 27.1. Other versions relax the IID assumption, which is why the informal statement asks only that no summand dominate.










CorCorollary 1 (Central Limit Theorem for a sum)






Corollary 1 (Central Limit Theorem for a sum) Let \(X_1, X_2, \ldots\) be IID random variables with population mean \(\mu\) and finite variance \(\sigma^2> 0\), and let \(S_n \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}\sum_{i=1}^nX_i\). Then for every real number \(z\):
\[
\lim_{n \to \infty} {\Pr\mathopen{}\left(\frac{S_n - n\mu}{\sigma\sqrt{n}} \le z\right)\mathclose{}} = \Phi(z)
\]










ProofProof






Proof. Since \(S_n = n{{\bar{X}}_{n}}\),
\[
\frac{S_n - n\mu}{\sigma\sqrt{n}}
= \frac{n({{\bar{X}}_{n}} - \mu)}{\sigma\sqrt{n}}
= \frac{\sqrt{n}\,({{\bar{X}}_{n}} - \mu)}{\sigma},
\]
so the event in this corollary is the event in Theorem 1, and the limits agree.










LemTheorem 2 (Mean and variance of a sum of IID random variables)






Theorem 2 (Mean and variance of a sum of IID random variables) Let \(X_1, \ldots, X_n\) be IID random variables, each discrete or continuous, with population mean \(\mu\) and finite variance \(\sigma^2\), and let \(S_n \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}\sum_{i=1}^nX_i\). Then, by linearity of expectation for finite sums and the variance of a linear combination:
\[
\begin{aligned}
{\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[S_n\right]\mathclose{}} &= n\mu\\
{\operatorname{Var}\mathopen{}\left(S_n\right)\mathclose{}} &= n\sigma^2
\end{aligned}
\]










ProofProof






Proof. For the mean, apply linearity of expectation for finite sums with every \(a_i = 1\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
{\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[S_n\right]\mathclose{}}
&= {\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[\sum_{i=1}^n1 \cdot X_i\right]\mathclose{}}
&& \text{(} 1 \cdot v = v \text{)} \\
&= \sum_{i=1}^n1 \cdot{\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[X_i\right]\mathclose{}}
&& \text{(linearity of expectation for finite sums, all } a_i = 1 \text{)} \\
&= \sum_{i=1}^n{\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[X_i\right]\mathclose{}}
&& \text{(} 1 \cdot v = v \text{)} \\
&= n\mu
&& \text{(each } X_i \text{ has mean } \mu\text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]
For the variance, apply the variance of a linear combination with every \(a_i = 1\). For \(i \ne j\), \(X_i\) and \(X_j\) are independent (take \(A_k = \mathbb{R}\) for every other \(k\) in the definition of independence), so \({\operatorname{Cov}\mathopen{}\left(X_i, X_j\right)\mathclose{}} = 0\) for independent summands; and \({\operatorname{Cov}\mathopen{}\left(X_i, X_i\right)\mathclose{}} = {\operatorname{Var}\mathopen{}\left(X_i\right)\mathclose{}}\) (covariance of a variable with itself):
\[
\begin{aligned}
{\operatorname{Var}\mathopen{}\left(S_n\right)\mathclose{}}
&= \sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^n {\operatorname{Cov}\mathopen{}\left(X_i, X_j\right)\mathclose{}}
&& \text{(variance of a linear combination, all } a_i = 1 \text{)} \\
&= \sum_{i=1}^n{\operatorname{Cov}\mathopen{}\left(X_i, X_i\right)\mathclose{}} + \sum_{\substack{i, j = 1 \\ i \ne j}}^n {\operatorname{Cov}\mathopen{}\left(X_i, X_j\right)\mathclose{}}
&& \text{(split off the terms with } i = j \text{)} \\
&= \sum_{i=1}^n{\operatorname{Var}\mathopen{}\left(X_i\right)\mathclose{}} + 0
&& \text{(covariance with itself; independent summands)} \\
&= n\sigma^2
&& \text{(each } X_i \text{ has variance } \sigma^2\text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]










CorCorollary 2 (Mean and variance of a sample mean of IID random variables)






Corollary 2 (Mean and variance of a sample mean of IID random variables) Let \(X_1, \ldots, X_n\) be IID random variables, each discrete or continuous, with population mean \(\mu\) and finite variance \(\sigma^2\), and let \({{\bar{X}}_{n}} \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^nX_i\). Then:
\[
\begin{aligned}
{\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[{{\bar{X}}_{n}}\right]\mathclose{}} &= \mu\\
{\operatorname{Var}\mathopen{}\left({{\bar{X}}_{n}}\right)\mathclose{}} &= \frac{\sigma^2}{n}
\end{aligned}
\]










ProofProof






Proof. Let \(S_n \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}\sum_{i=1}^nX_i\), so \({{\bar{X}}_{n}} = S_n / n\). By Theorem 2, \({\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[S_n\right]\mathclose{}} = n\mu\) and \({\operatorname{Var}\mathopen{}\left(S_n\right)\mathclose{}} = n\sigma^2\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
{\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[{{\bar{X}}_{n}}\right]\mathclose{}}
&= {\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[\frac{S_n}{n}\right]\mathclose{}}
&& \text{(definition of sample mean)}\\
&= \frac{1}{n}{\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[S_n\right]\mathclose{}}
&& \text{(linearity of expectation)}\\
&= \frac{1}{n} \cdot n\mu
&& \text{(mean of a sum of IID variables)}\\
&= \mu
&& \text{(cancel $n$)}\\
{\operatorname{Var}\mathopen{}\left({{\bar{X}}_{n}}\right)\mathclose{}}
&= {\operatorname{Var}\mathopen{}\left(\frac{S_n}{n}\right)\mathclose{}}
&& \text{(definition of sample mean)}\\
&= \frac{1}{n^2}{\operatorname{Var}\mathopen{}\left(S_n\right)\mathclose{}}
&& \text{(variance of a constant multiple)}\\
&= \frac{1}{n^2} \cdot n\sigma^2
&& \text{(variance of a sum of IID variables)}\\
&= \frac{\sigma^2}{n}
&& \text{(cancel one factor of $n$)}
\end{aligned}
\]










RemarkRemark






Remark. In practice, Theorem 1 justifies approximating \({{\bar{X}}_{n}}\) by a normal distribution with mean \(\mu\) and variance \(\sigma^2/n\), and Corollary 1 justifies approximating \(S_n\) by a normal distribution with mean \(n\mu\) and variance \(n\sigma^2\). By Theorem 2, these are exactly the means and variances of \({{\bar{X}}_{n}} = S_n/n\) and \(S_n\).










ExmExample 1 (The sum of five dice)






Example 1 (The sum of five dice) A single fair die roll has the discrete uniform distribution on \({\mathopen{}\left\{1, \ldots, 6\right\}\mathclose{}}\), which is flat, not bell-shaped (Figure 1). Its mean is \(\mu= 3.5\), and its variance is
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sigma^2&= \sum_{x=1}^{6} (x - 3.5)^2 / 6 \\
&= 35/12.
\end{aligned}
\]


Show code
dice_sum_pmf <- function(n_dice) {
  totals <- rowSums(expand.grid(rep(list(1:6), n_dice)))
  probs <- prop.table(table(totals))
  tibble::tibble(total = as.numeric(names(probs)), p = as.vector(probs))
}

dice_plot <-
  ggplot2::ggplot(mapping = ggplot2::aes(x = total, y = p)) +
  ggplot2::xlab("sum of dice (x)") +
  ggplot2::ylab("Probability of outcome, Pr(X=x)") +
  ggplot2::expand_limits(y = 0)

dice_plot + ggplot2::geom_col(data = dice_sum_pmf(1))











Figure 1: Distribution of the outcome of one die











The sum of five independent rolls, \(S_5\), is already close to bell-shaped (Figure 2).


Show code
pmf_five_dice <- dice_sum_pmf(5)
dice_plot + ggplot2::geom_col(data = pmf_five_dice)











Figure 2: Distribution of the sum of five dice











For example, the exact probability that five dice total at most 15 is \(\Pr(S_5 \le 15) = 0.3052\). The normal approximation that Corollary 1 suggests, with mean \(5 \cdot 3.5 = 17.5\) and variance \(5 \cdot 35/12 \approx 14.58\), evaluated at \(15.5\) to account for \(S_5\) taking only integer values, gives \(\Phi\mathopen{}\left((15.5 - 17.5)/\sqrt{14.58}\right)\mathclose{} \approx 0.3002\).










ExmExample 2 (Sample means of car horsepower)






Example 2 (Sample means of car horsepower) The Auto data record the horsepower and fuel economy of 392 car models sold between 1970 and 1982. They come from the StatLib library at Carnegie Mellon University and ship with the book An Introduction to Statistical Learning, in the Python package ISLP (ISLP.load_data("Auto")) and the R package ISLR2 (ISLR2::Auto). This site has a copy at data/auto.csv, and both code tabs below read that file.
Horsepower is not bell-shaped: a few powerful cars give it a long right tail. To apply Theorem 1, treat each draw of one car at random as one IID observation \(X_i\), so that \(\mu\) and \(\sigma^2\) are the population mean and variance of the 392 horsepower values. The sample mean \({{\bar{X}}_{n}} = S_n/n\), where \(S_n = \sum_{i=1}^nX_i\), has mean \(\mu\) and standard deviation \(\sigma/\sqrt{n}\), because \(S_n\) has mean \(n\mu\) and variance \(n\sigma^2\) by Theorem 2. The code below draws 10,000 random samples of each size \(n \in {\mathopen{}\left\{1, 5, 30\right\}\mathclose{}}\), with replacement, and computes each sample’s sample mean.

PythonR

import pandas as pd

hp = pd.read_csv("data/auto.csv")["horsepower"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
mu, sigma = hp.mean(), hp.std(ddof=0)

rng = np.random.default_rng(571)
sizes = [1, 5, 30]
sample_means = {n: rng.choice(hp, size=(10_000, n)).mean(axis=1) for n in sizes}

def skewness(x):
    return np.mean(((x - x.mean()) / x.std()) ** 3)

pd.DataFrame({
    "n": sizes,
    "sd of sample means": [sample_means[n].std(ddof=1) for n in sizes],
    "sigma / sqrt(n)": [sigma / np.sqrt(n) for n in sizes],
    "skewness of sample means": [skewness(sample_means[n]) for n in sizes],
})

#> 0   1           38.691521        38.442033                  1.080767
#> 1   5           17.265666        17.191800                  0.522243

data.frame(
  n = sizes,
  sd_of_sample_means = sapply(sample_means, sd),
  sigma_over_root_n = sigma / sqrt(sizes),
  skewness_of_sample_means = sapply(sample_means, skewness)
