title: Expectation
Expectation
Expectation
text:
3 Loss and risk







DefDefinition 9 (Prediction)






Definition 9 (Prediction) A prediction of a random variable \(Y\) is a constant \(\hat y\), or a function \(\hat{Y} \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}g(X)\) of another observable random variable \(X\), used as a guess for the value \(Y\) takes:
\[\hat y\quad \text{or} \quad \hat{Y} \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}g(X)\]










ExmExample 22 (Predictions of a die roll)






Example 22 (Predictions of a die roll) Let \(Y\) be the number shown by a fair six-sided die. The constant \(\hat y= 3\) is a prediction of \(Y\).
Let \(X\) be the indicator that \(Y\) is even. The function \(g(X) = 2 + 2X\) is also a prediction of \(Y\): it guesses \(2\) when \(Y\) is odd and \(4\) when \(Y\) is even.










RemarkRemark 1 (A prediction from a random input is random)






Remark 1 (A prediction from a random input is random). When no covariate or feature is available, a prediction is a single number \(\hat y\) (such as a constant \(c\)). When an informative random variable \(X\) is observed, a prediction is a function \(g(X)\), which is itself a random variable because \(X\) is random.










DefDefinition 10 (Loss function)






Definition 10 (Loss function) A loss function \(L(y, \hat y)\) is a rule that gives a number that is 0 or larger: the cost of predicting \(\hat y\) when the true value is \(y\) [12].










ExmExample 23 (A loss function that charges more for overpredicting)






Example 23 (A loss function that charges more for overpredicting) Let \(L(y, \hat y)\) cost \(2\) per unit of overprediction and \(1\) per unit of underprediction:
\[
L(y, \hat y) =
\begin{cases}
2\mathopen{}\left(\hat y- y\right)\mathclose{} & \text{if } \hat y> y \\
y - \hat y& \text{if } \hat y\le y.
\end{cases}
\]
This is a loss function because it is never negative. For the true value \(y = 2\) and the prediction \(\hat y= 7\), the loss is \(L(2, 7) = 2 \cdot 5 = 10\). For \(y = 7\) and \(\hat y= 2\), the loss is \(L(7, 2) = 5\).










DefDefinition 11 (Squared error loss)






Definition 11 (Squared error loss) The squared error loss is the loss function that charges the square of the difference between the true value \(y\) and the prediction \(\hat y\):
\[L(y, \hat y) \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}{\mathopen{}\left(y - \hat y\right)\mathclose{}}^{2}\]










ExmExample 24 (Squared error loss for one prediction)






Example 24 (Squared error loss for one prediction) For the true value \(y = 2\) and the prediction \(\hat y= 7\), the squared error loss is
\[{\mathopen{}\left(2 - 7\right)\mathclose{}}^{2} = 25.\]










DefDefinition 12 (Absolute error loss)






Definition 12 (Absolute error loss) The absolute error loss is the loss function that charges the absolute value of the difference between the true value \(y\) and the prediction \(\hat y\):
\[L(y, \hat y) \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}\mathopen{}\left|y - \hat y\right|\mathclose{}\]










ExmExample 25 (Absolute error loss for one prediction)






Example 25 (Absolute error loss for one prediction) For the true value \(y = 2\) and the prediction \(\hat y= 7\), the absolute error loss is
\[\mathopen{}\left|2 - 7\right|\mathclose{} = 5.\]










RemarkRemark 2 (Squared error loss is the most common choice)






Remark 2 (Squared error loss is the most common choice). Hastie et al. [13, p. 18] call squared error loss “by far the most common and convenient” choice.










DefDefinition 13 (Risk (expected loss))






Definition 13 (Risk (expected loss)) For a random variable \(Y\) and a prediction \(\hat y\) (a constant, or a function \(g(X)\) of a random input \(X\)), the risk is the expectation of the loss [14]:
\[R \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}{\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[L(Y, \hat y)\right]\mathclose{}}\]










ExmExample 26 (Risk of a constant prediction)






Example 26 (Risk of a constant prediction) Let \(Y\) be a random variable with \(\mathbb{P}(Y = 0) = 0.5\) and \(\mathbb{P}(Y = 2) = 0.5\), and use the constant prediction \(\hat y= 0\). The risk under squared error loss is
\[
\begin{aligned}
{\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[{\mathopen{}\left(Y - 0\right)\mathclose{}}^{2}\right]\mathclose{}}
&= 0.5 \cdot{\mathopen{}\left(0 - 0\right)\mathclose{}}^{2} + 0.5 \cdot{\mathopen{}\left(2 - 0\right)\mathclose{}}^{2} \\
&= 2.
\end{aligned}
\]
The risk under absolute error loss is
\[
\begin{aligned}
{\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[\mathopen{}\left|Y - 0\right|\mathclose{}\right]\mathclose{}}
&= 0.5 \cdot\mathopen{}\left|0 - 0\right|\mathclose{} + 0.5 \cdot\mathopen{}\left|2 - 0\right|\mathclose{} \\
&= 1.
\end{aligned}
\]










RemarkRemark 3 (Risk measures the quality of a prediction)






Remark 3 (Risk measures the quality of a prediction). The quality of a prediction is evaluated using a loss function and its expected value, the risk.










ExrExercise 6 (Squared and absolute loss)






Exercise 6 (Squared and absolute loss)  

For a true value \(y = 3\) and a prediction \(\hat y= 5\), compute the squared error loss \({\mathopen{}\left(y - \hat y\right)\mathclose{}}^{2}\) and the absolute error loss \(\mathopen{}\left|y - \hat y\right|\mathclose{}\).
A random variable \(Y\) has \(\mathbb{P}(Y = 0) = 0.5\) and \(\mathbb{P}(Y = 4) = 0.5\). For the constant prediction \(c = 1\), compute the risk under squared error loss \({\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[{\mathopen{}\left(Y - c\right)\mathclose{}}^{2}\right]\mathclose{}}\) and the risk under absolute error loss \({\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[\mathopen{}\left|Y - c\right|\mathclose{}\right]\mathclose{}}\).
Repeat part 2 for \(c = 2\).
Which of \(c = 1\) and \(c = 2\) gives the smaller risk under each loss?











SolutionSolution 2






Solution 2. 

For squared error loss: \[{\mathopen{}\left(3 - 5\right)\mathclose{}}^{2} = 4\] For absolute error loss: \[\mathopen{}\left|3 - 5\right|\mathclose{} = 2\]
For \(c = 1\): The risk under squared error loss is: \[
\begin{aligned}
{\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[{\mathopen{}\left(Y - 1\right)\mathclose{}}^{2}\right]\mathclose{}}
&= 0.5 \cdot{\mathopen{}\left(0 - 1\right)\mathclose{}}^{2} + 0.5 \cdot{\mathopen{}\left(4 - 1\right)\mathclose{}}^{2} \\
&= 0.5 \cdot 1 + 0.5 \cdot 9 \\
&= 5
\end{aligned}
\] The risk under absolute error loss is: \[
\begin{aligned}
{\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[\mathopen{}\left|Y - 1\right|\mathclose{}\right]\mathclose{}}
&= 0.5 \cdot\mathopen{}\left|0 - 1\right|\mathclose{} + 0.5 \cdot\mathopen{}\left|4 - 1\right|\mathclose{} \\
&= 0.5 \cdot 1 + 0.5 \cdot 3 \\
&= 2
\end{aligned}
\]
For \(c = 2\): The risk under squared error loss is: \[
\begin{aligned}
{\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[{\mathopen{}\left(Y - 2\right)\mathclose{}}^{2}\right]\mathclose{}}
&= 0.5 \cdot{\mathopen{}\left(0 - 2\right)\mathclose{}}^{2} + 0.5 \cdot{\mathopen{}\left(4 - 2\right)\mathclose{}}^{2} \\
&= 0.5 \cdot 4 + 0.5 \cdot 4 \\
&= 4
\end{aligned}
\] The risk under absolute error loss is: \[
\begin{aligned}
{\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[\mathopen{}\left|Y - 2\right|\mathclose{}\right]\mathclose{}}
&= 0.5 \cdot\mathopen{}\left|0 - 2\right|\mathclose{} + 0.5 \cdot\mathopen{}\left|4 - 2\right|\mathclose{} \\
&= 0.5 \cdot 2 + 0.5 \cdot 2 \\
&= 2
\end{aligned}
\]
The prediction \(c = 2\) has the smaller risk under squared error loss (\(4\) versus \(5\)). The two predictions have the same risk under absolute error loss (\(2\)), so under absolute error loss this exercise does not choose one of them. The prediction \(c = 2\) equals the expectation: \[
\begin{aligned}
{\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[Y\right]\mathclose{}}
&= 0.5 \cdot 0 + 0.5 \cdot 4 \\
&= 2
\end{aligned}
\]











RemarkRemark 4 (The best prediction depends on the loss)






Remark 4 (The best prediction depends on the loss). In Exercise 6 (parts 2 and 3), the risk of the prediction \(c = 1\) is \(5\) for squared error loss and \(2\) for absolute error loss. The risk of the prediction \(c = 2\) is \(4\) for squared error loss and \(2\) for absolute error loss.
The prediction with the smallest risk depends on the loss. In Exercise 6, every constant \(c\) from \(0\) to \(4\) has absolute error risk \(2\), because
\[
\begin{aligned}
{\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[\mathopen{}\left|Y - c\right|\mathclose{}\right]\mathclose{}} &= 0.5\,c + 0.5\,(4 - c) \\
&= 2.
\end{aligned}
\]
Only \(c = 2\) has the smallest squared error risk. Under squared error loss, the prediction function that minimizes risk is the conditional mean \({\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[Y \mid X\right]\mathclose{}}\), proved below (Theorem 13). Hastie et al. [13, p. 20] state that, for absolute error loss, the best prediction function is the conditional median instead of the conditional mean. This statement is given here without proof.










ExrExercise 7 (Comparing prediction functions under squared-error loss)






Exercise 7 (Comparing prediction functions under squared-error loss) Let \((X, Y)\) be jointly distributed discrete random variables. \(X\) takes values in \(\{0, 1\}\) with \(\mathbb{P}(X= 0) = 0.5\) and \(\mathbb{P}(X= 1) = 0.5\). Given \(X= 0\), \(Y\) takes values in \(\{0, 2\}\) with conditional probabilities \(\mathbb{P}(Y= 0 \mid X= 0) = 0.5\) and \(\mathbb{P}(Y= 2 \mid X= 0) = 0.5\). Given \(X= 1\), \(Y\) takes values in \(\{4, 6\}\) with conditional probabilities \(\mathbb{P}(Y= 4 \mid X= 1) = 0.5\) and \(\mathbb{P}(Y= 6 \mid X= 1) = 0.5\).

Compute the marginal mean \({\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[Y\right]\mathclose{}}\) and the conditional expectation function \({f^*\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}} \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}{\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[Y\mid X\right]\mathclose{}}\).
Consider the constant prediction \(f_1\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{} \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}{\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[Y\right]\mathclose{}} = 3\), which ignores \(X\). Compute its squared-error risk \({\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[{\mathopen{}\left(Y- f_1\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}\right)\mathclose{}}^{2}\right]\mathclose{}}\).
Consider the alternate prediction \(f_2\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{} \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}4X\). Compute its squared-error risk \({\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[{\mathopen{}\left(Y- f_2\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}\right)\mathclose{}}^{2}\right]\mathclose{}}\).
Compute the squared-error risk \({\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[{\mathopen{}\left(Y- {f^*\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}}\right)\mathclose{}}^{2}\right]\mathclose{}}\) of the conditional mean predictor \({f^*\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}}\). Which of \(f_1\), \(f_2\), and \(f^*\) achieves the lowest risk?











SolutionSolution 3






Solution 3. 

For each value of \(X\), compute the conditional expectation: \[
\begin{aligned}
{\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[Y\mid X= 0\right]\mathclose{}}
&= 0 \cdot 0.5 + 2 \cdot 0.5 \\
&= 1
\end{aligned}
\] \[
\begin{aligned}
{\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[Y\mid X= 1\right]\mathclose{}}
&= 4 \cdot 0.5 + 6 \cdot 0.5 \\
&= 5
\end{aligned}
\] By the law of iterated expectations (Theorem 10), the marginal mean is: \[
\begin{aligned}
{\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[Y\right]\mathclose{}}
&= {\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[{\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[Y\mid X\right]\mathclose{}}\right]\mathclose{}} \\
&= 1 \cdot 0.5 + 5 \cdot 0.5 \\
&= 3
\end{aligned}
\] The conditional expectation function is \({f^*\mathopen{}\left(0\right)\mathclose{}} = 1\) and \({f^*\mathopen{}\left(1\right)\mathclose{}} = 5\), which can also be written \({f^*\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}} = 1 + 4X\).
For the constant prediction \(f_1\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{} = 3\): Given \(X= 0\): \[
\begin{aligned}
{\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[{\mathopen{}\left(Y- 3\right)\mathclose{}}^{2} \mid X= 0\right]\mathclose{}}
&= {\mathopen{}\left(0 - 3\right)\mathclose{}}^{2} \cdot 0.5 + {\mathopen{}\left(2 - 3\right)\mathclose{}}^{2} \cdot 0.5 \\
&= 9 \cdot 0.5 + 1 \cdot 0.5 \\
&= 5
\end{aligned}
\] Given \(X= 1\): \[
\begin{aligned}
{\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[{\mathopen{}\left(Y- 3\right)\mathclose{}}^{2} \mid X= 1\right]\mathclose{}}
&= {\mathopen{}\left(4 - 3\right)\mathclose{}}^{2} \cdot 0.5 + {\mathopen{}\left(6 - 3\right)\mathclose{}}^{2} \cdot 0.5 \\
&= 1 \cdot 0.5 + 9 \cdot 0.5 \\
&= 5
\end{aligned}
\] By the law of iterated expectations (Theorem 10): \[
\begin{aligned}
{\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[{\mathopen{}\left(Y- f_1\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}\right)\mathclose{}}^{2}\right]\mathclose{}}
&= {\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[{\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[{\mathopen{}\left(Y- 3\right)\mathclose{}}^{2} \mid X\right]\mathclose{}}\right]\mathclose{}} \\
&= 5 \cdot 0.5 + 5 \cdot 0.5 \\
&= 5
\end{aligned}
\]
For the prediction \(f_2\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{} = 4X\): Here \(f_2\mathopen{}\left(0\right)\mathclose{} = 0\) and \(f_2\mathopen{}\left(1\right)\mathclose{} = 4\). Given \(X= 0\): \[
\begin{aligned}
{\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[{\mathopen{}\left(Y- 0\right)\mathclose{}}^{2} \mid X= 0\right]\mathclose{}}
&= {\mathopen{}\left(0 - 0\right)\mathclose{}}^{2} \cdot 0.5 + {\mathopen{}\left(2 - 0\right)\mathclose{}}^{2} \cdot 0.5 \\
&= 0 \cdot 0.5 + 4 \cdot 0.5 \\
&= 2
\end{aligned}
\] Given \(X= 1\): \[
\begin{aligned}
{\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[{\mathopen{}\left(Y- 4\right)\mathclose{}}^{2} \mid X= 1\right]\mathclose{}}
&= {\mathopen{}\left(4 - 4\right)\mathclose{}}^{2} \cdot 0.5 + {\mathopen{}\left(6 - 4\right)\mathclose{}}^{2} \cdot 0.5 \\
&= 0 \cdot 0.5 + 4 \cdot 0.5 \\
&= 2
\end{aligned}
\] By Theorem 10: \[
\begin{aligned}
{\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[{\mathopen{}\left(Y- f_2\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}\right)\mathclose{}}^{2}\right]\mathclose{}}
&= 2 \cdot 0.5 + 2 \cdot 0.5 \\
&= 2
\end{aligned}
\]
For the conditional mean predictor \({f^*\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}} = {\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[Y\mid X\right]\mathclose{}}\): Given \(X= 0\), \({f^*\mathopen{}\left(0\right)\mathclose{}} = 1\): \[
\begin{aligned}
{\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[{\mathopen{}\left(Y- 1\right)\mathclose{}}^{2} \mid X= 0\right]\mathclose{}}
&= {\mathopen{}\left(0 - 1\right)\mathclose{}}^{2} \cdot 0.5 + {\mathopen{}\left(2 - 1\right)\mathclose{}}^{2} \cdot 0.5 \\
&= 1 \cdot 0.5 + 1 \cdot 0.5 \\
&= 1
\end{aligned}
\] Given \(X= 1\), \({f^*\mathopen{}\left(1\right)\mathclose{}} = 5\): \[
\begin{aligned}
{\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[{\mathopen{}\left(Y- 5\right)\mathclose{}}^{2} \mid X= 1\right]\mathclose{}}
&= {\mathopen{}\left(4 - 5\right)\mathclose{}}^{2} \cdot 0.5 + {\mathopen{}\left(6 - 5\right)\mathclose{}}^{2} \cdot 0.5 \\
&= 1 \cdot 0.5 + 1 \cdot 0.5 \\
&= 1
\end{aligned}
\] By Theorem 10: \[
\begin{aligned}
{\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[{\mathopen{}\left(Y- {f^*\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}}\right)\mathclose{}}^{2}\right]\mathclose{}}
&= 1 \cdot 0.5 + 1 \cdot 0.5 \\
&= 1
\end{aligned}
\] The conditional mean predictor \(f^*\) achieves the lowest risk (\(1\)), strictly outperforming \(f_2\) (\(2\)) and the constant prediction \(f_1\) (\(5\)).











DefDefinition 14 (Outcome)






Definition 14 (Outcome) The outcome \(Y\) of a data point is the random variable whose value a prediction tries to guess.










ExmExample 27 (The outcome in the best-predictor exercise)






Example 27 (The outcome in the best-predictor exercise) In Exercise 7, the outcome \(Y\) takes the values \(0\) and \(2\) when the input is \(0\), and the values \(4\) and \(6\) when the input is \(1\).










DefDefinition 15 (Input)






Definition 15 (Input) The input \(X\) of a data point (also called its predictor or covariate) is the observed random variable from which a prediction of its outcome is computed.










ExmExample 28 (The input in the best-predictor exercise)






Example 28 (The input in the best-predictor exercise) In Exercise 7, the input \(X\) takes the values \(0\) and \(1\), each with probability \(0.5\).










DefDefinition 16 (New observation)






Definition 16 (New observation) A new observation is an input and outcome pair \((X, Y)\) with the same joint distribution as the observations used to choose the prediction, statistically independent of them, whose input is observed and whose outcome is not yet observed.










ExmExample 29 (A new observation in the best-predictor exercise)






Example 29 (A new observation in the best-predictor exercise) In Exercise 7, suppose the new observation \((X, Y)\) satisfies the suppositions of its definition, with the joint distribution given in the exercise as the population it is drawn from. Suppose also that its input is observed to be \(X= 1\). Then its unobserved outcome is \(4\) or \(6\) with equal probability, and a prediction of \(5\) is a guess for that outcome.










DefDefinition 17 (Prediction error)






Definition 17 (Prediction error) A prediction function \({f\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}}\) has as its estimand the observed outcome \(Y\) of a new observation with input \(X\), not the conditional mean of that outcome. The prediction error of \(f\) is the prediction minus that outcome:
\[{{\varepsilon_{\text{pred}}}\mathopen{}\left(f\right)\mathclose{}} \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}{f\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}} - Y\]










ExmExample 30 (Prediction error in the best-predictor exercise)






Example 30 (Prediction error in the best-predictor exercise) In Exercise 7, consider the constant prediction \(f_1\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{} = 3\). Its prediction error is \({{\varepsilon_{\text{pred}}}\mathopen{}\left(f_1\right)\mathclose{}} = 3 - Y\). This is \(3\) when \(Y= 0\). It is \(-3\) when \(Y= 6\).










DefDefinition 18 (Squared-error risk (expected prediction error))






Definition 18 (Squared-error risk (expected prediction error)) The squared-error risk of a prediction function \({f\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}}\), also called its expected prediction error [13, p. 18], is the expected square of its prediction error:
\[{R\mathopen{}\left(f\right)\mathclose{}} \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}{\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[{\mathopen{}\left({{\varepsilon_{\text{pred}}}\mathopen{}\left(f\right)\mathclose{}}\right)\mathclose{}}^{2}\right]\mathclose{}}\]










ExmExample 31 (Squared-error risk in the best-predictor exercise)






Example 31 (Squared-error risk in the best-predictor exercise) In Exercise 7, consider the constant prediction \(f_1\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{} = 3\). Its squared-error risk is \({R\mathopen{}\left(f_1\right)\mathclose{}} = 5\).










RemarkRemark 5 (The squared-error risk is a risk)






Remark 5 (The squared-error risk is a risk). The squared-error risk is the risk under squared error loss.










LemLemma 2 (Prediction error splits at the conditional mean)






Lemma 2 (Prediction error splits at the conditional mean) Let \({\mu\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}} \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}{\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[Y\mid X\right]\mathclose{}}\) be the conditional expectation function of \(Y\) given \(X\). For any prediction function \({f\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}}\), the prediction error splits as:
\[{{\varepsilon_{\text{pred}}}\mathopen{}\left(f\right)\mathclose{}} = {{\varepsilon_{\text{pred}}}\mathopen{}\left(\mu\right)\mathclose{}} + \mathopen{}\left({f\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}} - {\mu\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}}\right)\mathclose{}\]










ProofProof






Proof. \[
\begin{aligned}
{{\varepsilon_{\text{pred}}}\mathopen{}\left(f\right)\mathclose{}}
&= {f\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}} - Y
&& \text{(definition of } {{\varepsilon_{\text{pred}}}\mathopen{}\left(f\right)\mathclose{}} \text{)} \\
&= \mathopen{}\left({\mu\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}} - Y\right)\mathclose{} + \mathopen{}\left({f\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}} - {\mu\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}}\right)\mathclose{}
&& \text{(add and subtract } {\mu\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}} \text{)} \\
&= {{\varepsilon_{\text{pred}}}\mathopen{}\left(\mu\right)\mathclose{}} + \mathopen{}\left({f\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}} - {\mu\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}}\right)\mathclose{}
&& \text{(definition of } {{\varepsilon_{\text{pred}}}\mathopen{}\left(\mu\right)\mathclose{}} \text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]










ExmExample 32 (The split in the best-predictor exercise)






Example 32 (The split in the best-predictor exercise) In Exercise 7, when \(X= 0\) and \(Y= 0\), the constant prediction \(f_1\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{} = 3\) has prediction error \({{\varepsilon_{\text{pred}}}\mathopen{}\left(f_1\right)\mathclose{}} = 3\). The conditional mean is \({\mu\mathopen{}\left(0\right)\mathclose{}} = 1\), so \({{\varepsilon_{\text{pred}}}\mathopen{}\left(\mu\right)\mathclose{}} = 1\) and \(f_1\mathopen{}\left(0\right)\mathclose{} - {\mu\mathopen{}\left(0\right)\mathclose{}} = 2\), and \(3 = 1 + 2\).










LemLemma 3 (The conditional mean’s error is uncorrelated with any function of the input)






Lemma 3 (The conditional mean’s error is uncorrelated with any function of the input) Let \({\mu\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}} \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}{\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[Y\mid X\right]\mathclose{}}\) be the conditional expectation function of \(Y\) given \(X\). For any prediction function \({f\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}}\) with \({\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[{f\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}}^2\right]\mathclose{}} < \infty\):
\[{\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[{{\varepsilon_{\text{pred}}}\mathopen{}\left(\mu\right)\mathclose{}} \cdot\mathopen{}\left({f\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}} - {\mu\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}}\right)\mathclose{}\right]\mathclose{}} = 0\]










ProofProof






Proof. Because \({f\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}} - {\mu\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}}\) is a function of \(X\), by Theorem 8 it factors out of the conditional expectation:
\[
\begin{aligned}
{\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[{{\varepsilon_{\text{pred}}}\mathopen{}\left(\mu\right)\mathclose{}}\mathopen{}\left({f\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}} - {\mu\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}}\right)\mathclose{} \mid X\right]\mathclose{}}
&= \mathopen{}\left({f\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}} - {\mu\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}}\right)\mathclose{} \cdot{\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[{{\varepsilon_{\text{pred}}}\mathopen{}\left(\mu\right)\mathclose{}} \mid X\right]\mathclose{}}
&& \text{(a function of } X\text{ factors out)} \\
&= \mathopen{}\left({f\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}} - {\mu\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}}\right)\mathclose{} \cdot{\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[{\mu\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}} - Y\mid X\right]\mathclose{}}
&& \text{(definition of } {{\varepsilon_{\text{pred}}}\mathopen{}\left(\mu\right)\mathclose{}} \text{)} \\
&= \mathopen{}\left({f\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}} - {\mu\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}}\right)\mathclose{} \cdot\mathopen{}\left({\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[{\mu\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}} \mid X\right]\mathclose{}} - {\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[Y\mid X\right]\mathclose{}}\right)\mathclose{}
&& \text{(linearity of conditional expectation)} \\
&= \mathopen{}\left({f\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}} - {\mu\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}}\right)\mathclose{} \cdot\mathopen{}\left({\mu\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}} - {\mu\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}}\right)\mathclose{}
&& \text{(a function of } X\text{ is its own conditional mean, and definition of } {\mu\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}} \text{)} \\
&= 0
&& \text{(evaluate)}
\end{aligned}
\]
By the law of iterated expectations (Theorem 10):
\[
\begin{aligned}
{\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[{{\varepsilon_{\text{pred}}}\mathopen{}\left(\mu\right)\mathclose{}}\mathopen{}\left({f\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}} - {\mu\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}}\right)\mathclose{}\right]\mathclose{}}
&= {\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[{\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[{{\varepsilon_{\text{pred}}}\mathopen{}\left(\mu\right)\mathclose{}}\mathopen{}\left({f\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}} - {\mu\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}}\right)\mathclose{} \mid X\right]\mathclose{}}\right]\mathclose{}}
&& \text{(law of iterated expectations)} \\
&= {\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[0\right]\mathclose{}}
&& \text{(the conditional expectation is } 0 \text{)} \\
&= 0
&& \text{(expectation of a constant)}
\end{aligned}
\]










ExmExample 33 (The vanishing cross term in the best-predictor exercise)






Example 33 (The vanishing cross term in the best-predictor exercise) In Exercise 7, take the constant prediction \(f_1\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{} = 3\). When \(X= 0\), \({\mu\mathopen{}\left(0\right)\mathclose{}} = 1\), so \(f_1\mathopen{}\left(0\right)\mathclose{} - {\mu\mathopen{}\left(0\right)\mathclose{}} = 2\), and \({{\varepsilon_{\text{pred}}}\mathopen{}\left(\mu\right)\mathclose{}} = 1 - Y\) is \(1\) or \(-1\) with equal probability, so the product has conditional mean \(0\). The same cancellation happens when \(X= 1\), so the expectation of the product is \(0\).










LemTheorem 12 (Squared-error risk decomposition)






Theorem 12 (Squared-error risk decomposition) Let \({\mu\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}} \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}{\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[Y\mid X\right]\mathclose{}}\) be the conditional expectation function of \(Y\) given \(X\). For any prediction function \({f\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}}\) with \({\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[{f\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}}^2\right]\mathclose{}} < \infty\):
\[{R\mathopen{}\left(f\right)\mathclose{}} = {R\mathopen{}\left(\mu\right)\mathclose{}} + {\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[{\mathopen{}\left({f\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}} - {\mu\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}}\right)\mathclose{}}^{2}\right]\mathclose{}}\]










ProofProof






Proof. The steps use the squared-error risk definition, Lemma 2, Lemma 3, and Theorem 4:
\[
\begin{aligned}
{R\mathopen{}\left(f\right)\mathclose{}}
&= {\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[{\mathopen{}\left({{\varepsilon_{\text{pred}}}\mathopen{}\left(f\right)\mathclose{}}\right)\mathclose{}}^{2}\right]\mathclose{}}
&& \text{(definition of the squared-error risk)} \\
&= {\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[{\mathopen{}\left({{\varepsilon_{\text{pred}}}\mathopen{}\left(\mu\right)\mathclose{}} + {\mathopen{}\left({f\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}} - {\mu\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}}\right)\mathclose{}}\right)\mathclose{}}^{2}\right]\mathclose{}}
&& \text{(the prediction error splits at } \mu\text{)} \\
&= {\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[{\mathopen{}\left({{\varepsilon_{\text{pred}}}\mathopen{}\left(\mu\right)\mathclose{}}\right)\mathclose{}}^{2}\right]\mathclose{}}
+ 2 \cdot{\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[{{\varepsilon_{\text{pred}}}\mathopen{}\left(\mu\right)\mathclose{}} \cdot{\mathopen{}\left({f\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}} - {\mu\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}}\right)\mathclose{}}\right]\mathclose{}}
+ {\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[{\mathopen{}\left({\mathopen{}\left({f\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}} - {\mu\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}}\right)\mathclose{}}\right)\mathclose{}}^{2}\right]\mathclose{}}
&& \text{(expand the square; linearity of expectation)} \\
&= {\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[{\mathopen{}\left({{\varepsilon_{\text{pred}}}\mathopen{}\left(\mu\right)\mathclose{}}\right)\mathclose{}}^{2}\right]\mathclose{}}
+ 2 \cdot 0
+ {\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[{\mathopen{}\left({\mathopen{}\left({f\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}} - {\mu\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}}\right)\mathclose{}}\right)\mathclose{}}^{2}\right]\mathclose{}}
&& \text{(the cross term is } 0 \text{)} \\
&= {R\mathopen{}\left(\mu\right)\mathclose{}}
+ {\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[{\mathopen{}\left({\mathopen{}\left({f\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}} - {\mu\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}}\right)\mathclose{}}\right)\mathclose{}}^{2}\right]\mathclose{}}
&& \text{(definition of the squared-error risk of } \mu\text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]










ExmExample 34 (The risk decomposition in the best-predictor exercise)






Example 34 (The risk decomposition in the best-predictor exercise) In Exercise 7, the constant prediction \(f_1\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{} = 3\) has squared-error risk \({R\mathopen{}\left(f_1\right)\mathclose{}} = 5\), which Theorem 12 splits as \(5 = 1 + 4\): the risk \(1\) of the conditional expectation function plus the excess \(4\) from using \(f_1\).










LemTheorem 13 (Conditional mean minimizes squared-error risk)






Theorem 13 (Conditional mean minimizes squared-error risk) Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be jointly distributed random variables with \({\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[Y^2\right]\mathclose{}} < \infty\). Let \({\mu\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}} \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}{\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[Y\mid X\right]\mathclose{}}\) be the conditional expectation function of \(Y\) given \(X\). Write \(f^*\stackrel{\text{def}}{=}\mu\) for the prediction function that uses it. Then for any prediction function \({f\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}}\) with \({\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[{f\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}}^2\right]\mathclose{}} < \infty\):
\[{R\mathopen{}\left(f\right)\mathclose{}} \ge {R\mathopen{}\left(f^*\right)\mathclose{}}\]
with equality if and only if \(\mathbb{P}({f\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}} = {f^*\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}}) = 1\). That is, \(f^*\) minimizes the squared-error risk among all prediction functions of \(X\).










ProofProof






Proof. By Theorem 12:
\[
\begin{aligned}
{R\mathopen{}\left(f\right)\mathclose{}} - {R\mathopen{}\left(f^*\right)\mathclose{}}
&= {\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[{\mathopen{}\left({f\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}} - {f^*\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}}\right)\mathclose{}}^{2}\right]\mathclose{}}
&& \text{(squared-error risk decomposition)} \\
&\ge 0
&& \text{(the expectation of a non-negative variable)}
\end{aligned}
\]
The expectation of the non-negative variable \({\mathopen{}\left({f\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}} - {f^*\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}}\right)\mathclose{}}^{2}\) is zero if and only if the variable is \(0\) with probability \(1\), meaning \(\mathbb{P}({f\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}} = {f^*\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}}) = 1\).










ExmExample 35 (The best predictor in the best-predictor exercise)






Example 35 (The best predictor in the best-predictor exercise) In Exercise 7, consider the constant prediction \(f_1\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{} = 3\). Its squared-error risk is \({R\mathopen{}\left(f_1\right)\mathclose{}} = 5\). The risk of the conditional mean is \({R\mathopen{}\left(f^*\right)\mathclose{}} = 1\). So \(f_1\) has the larger risk. The inequality is strict because \(f_1\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{} \ne {f^*\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}}\).










DefDefinition 19 (Irreducible risk)






Definition 19 (Irreducible risk) In the squared-error risk decomposition of Theorem 12, the minimum squared-error risk
\[{\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[{\mathopen{}\left(Y- {\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[Y\mid X\right]\mathclose{}}\right)\mathclose{}}^{2}\right]\mathclose{}} = {\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[{\operatorname{Var}\mathopen{}\left(Y\mid X\right)\mathclose{}}\right]\mathclose{}}\]
is the irreducible risk.










RemarkRemark 6 (The irreducible risk does not depend on the prediction function)






Remark 6 (The irreducible risk does not depend on the prediction function). The irreducible risk depends only on the joint distribution of \((X, Y)\) and not on the prediction function \(f\), so no choice of \(f\) can achieve a smaller risk.










ExmExample 36 (Irreducible risk in the best-predictor exercise)






Example 36 (Irreducible risk in the best-predictor exercise) In Exercise 7, \({\operatorname{Var}\mathopen{}\left(Y\mid X= 0\right)\mathclose{}} = 1\) and \({\operatorname{Var}\mathopen{}\left(Y\mid X= 1\right)\mathclose{}} = 1\), so the irreducible risk is \({\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[{\operatorname{Var}\mathopen{}\left(Y\mid X\right)\mathclose{}}\right]\mathclose{}} = 1\).










DefDefinition 20 (Reducible risk)






Definition 20 (Reducible risk) In the squared-error risk decomposition of Theorem 12, the excess risk from choosing the prediction function \(f\) instead of the conditional mean,
\[{\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[{\mathopen{}\left({\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[Y\mid X\right]\mathclose{}} - {f\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}}\right)\mathclose{}}^{2}\right]\mathclose{}} \ge 0\]
is the reducible risk.










RemarkRemark 7 (When the reducible risk is zero)






Remark 7 (When the reducible risk is zero). The reducible risk is zero if and only if \(\mathbb{P}({f\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}} = {\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[Y\mid X\right]\mathclose{}}) = 1\).










ExmExample 37 (Reducible risk in the best-predictor exercise)






Example 37 (Reducible risk in the best-predictor exercise) In Exercise 7, the constant prediction \(f_1\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{} = 3\) has reducible risk \(5 - 1 = 4\), and the prediction \(f_2\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{} = 4X\) has reducible risk \(2 - 1 = 1\).










RemarkRemark






Remark. This characterization of the best predictor under squared error loss follows Hastie et al. [13, Sec. 2.4], eq. 2.11. The risk identity in Theorem 12
\[{\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[{\mathopen{}\left(Y- {f\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}}\right)\mathclose{}}^{2}\right]\mathclose{}} = {\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[{\mathopen{}\left(Y- {\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[Y\mid X\right]\mathclose{}}\right)\mathclose{}}^{2}\right]\mathclose{}} + {\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[{\mathopen{}\left({\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[Y\mid X\right]\mathclose{}} - {f\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}}\right)\mathclose{}}^{2}\right]\mathclose{}}\]
shows that the total squared-error risk is the sum of the irreducible risk (Definition 19) and the reducible risk (Definition 20).










CorCorollary 4 (Conditional mean as the minimizer of squared-error risk)






Corollary 4 (Conditional mean as the minimizer of squared-error risk) Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be jointly distributed random variables with \({\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[Y^2\right]\mathclose{}} < \infty\). Among prediction functions \({f\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}}\) with \({\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[{f\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}}^2\right]\mathclose{}} < \infty\), the conditional expectation function is a minimizer of the squared-error risk:
\[{\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[Y\mid X\right]\mathclose{}} \in \arg \min_{f} {\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[{\mathopen{}\left(Y- {f\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}}\right)\mathclose{}}^{2}\right]\mathclose{}},\]
where \(\arg \min\) is the set of minimizers.










ProofProof






Proof. By Theorem 13, \({f^*\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}} = {\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[Y\mid X\right]\mathclose{}}\) has risk no larger than that of any prediction function \(f\), so it is a minimizer.










ExmExample 38 (The minimizer in the best-predictor exercise)






Example 38 (The minimizer in the best-predictor exercise) In Exercise 7, the conditional expectation function \({f^*\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}}\) has risk \(1\). The constant prediction \(f_1\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{} = 3\) has risk \(5\) and \(f_2\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{} = 4X\) has risk \(2\), both larger than \(1\). So \(f^*\) is the minimizer among the three.










CorCorollary 5 (The minimizer of squared-error risk is unique up to probability-1 equality)






Corollary 5 (The minimizer of squared-error risk is unique up to probability-1 equality) Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be jointly distributed random variables with \({\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[Y^2\right]\mathclose{}} < \infty\). Every prediction function \({f\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}}\) with \({\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[{f\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}}^2\right]\mathclose{}} < \infty\) that is a minimizer of the squared-error risk (see Corollary 4) satisfies:
\[\mathbb{P}({f\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}} = {\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[Y\mid X\right]\mathclose{}}) = 1\]










ProofProof






Proof. If \(f\) is a minimizer, its risk equals that of \(f^*\), so the equality case of Theorem 13 gives \(\mathbb{P}({f\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}} = {f^*\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}}) = 1\).










ExmExample 39 (Uniqueness in the best-predictor exercise)






Example 39 (Uniqueness in the best-predictor exercise) In Exercise 7, \(f_2\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{} = 4X\) differs from \({f^*\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}}\) when \(X= 0\), which has probability \(0.5\). So \(f_2\) is not a minimizer, which matches its risk \(2\) being larger than \(1\).

title: Expectation
text:
4 Entropy and cross-entropy







DefDefinition 21 (Entropy)






Definition 21 (Entropy) The entropy of a discrete random variable \(X\) with probability mass function \(\mathbb{P}(X=x)\) is the expectation of \(-\log \mathbb{P}(X)\) [15]:
\[H(X) \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}{\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[-\log \mathbb{P}(X)\right]\mathclose{}} = -\sum_{x \in \mathcal{R}(X)} \mathbb{P}(X=x) \log \mathbb{P}(X=x)\]
A term with \(\mathbb{P}(X=x) = 0\) is taken to be \(0\), because \(p \log p \to 0\) as \(p \to 0\).










RemarkRemark 8 (The base of the logarithm is a unit)






Remark 8 (The base of the logarithm is a unit). With the natural logarithm, entropy is measured in nats. With base 2, it is measured in bits. Changing the base multiplies every entropy by the same positive constant. It does not change which distribution has the larger entropy.










ExmExample 40 (Entropy of a coin flip)






Example 40 (Entropy of a coin flip) Let \(X\) be the result of one flip of a coin with \(\mathbb{P}(X=1) = \pi\) and \(\mathbb{P}(X=0) = 1 - \pi\) (Bernoulli distribution). Using logarithms to base 2,
\[H(X) = -\pi\log_2 \pi- (1 - \pi) \log_2 (1 - \pi).\]
For a fair coin, \(\pi= 1/2\), and
\[
\begin{aligned}
H(X)
&= -\tfrac{1}{2} \log_2 \tfrac{1}{2} - \tfrac{1}{2} \log_2 \tfrac{1}{2} \\
&= \tfrac{1}{2} + \tfrac{1}{2} \\
&= 1 \text{ bit}.
\end{aligned}
\]
For a coin that always lands heads, \(\pi= 1\), and
\[
\begin{aligned}
H(X) &= -1 \cdot \log_2 1 - 0 \\
&= 0.
\end{aligned}
\]
The outcome is known in advance, so there is no uncertainty to measure. An entropy of \(0\) means that all of the probability is on one outcome.










RemarkRemark 9 (Where the definition comes from)






Remark 9 (Where the definition comes from). Murphy [16, Sec. 2.8.1], p. 56 defines entropy this way, and notes that among distributions on \(K\) outcomes it is largest, \(\log K\), for the uniform distribution.










DefDefinition 22 (Cross-entropy)






Definition 22 (Cross-entropy) Let \(p\) and \(q\) be probability mass functions on the same finite set of outcomes \({\mathopen{}\left\{1, \ldots, K\right\}\mathclose{}}\), with \(p_k\) and \(q_k\) the probabilities of outcome \(k\). The cross-entropy of \(q\) relative to \(p\) [17] is
\[H(p, q) \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}-\sum_{k=1}^{K} p_k \log q_k.\]
When \(q_k = 0\) for an outcome with \(p_k > 0\), the cross-entropy is infinite.










RemarkRemark 10 (Cross-entropy as an expected negative log probability)






Remark 10 (Cross-entropy as an expected negative log probability). The cross-entropy is the expectation of \(-\log q(X)\) when \(X\) has probability mass function \(p\).










RemarkRemark 11 (Entropy is the cross-entropy of a distribution with itself)






Remark 11 (Entropy is the cross-entropy of a distribution with itself). Setting \(q = p\) gives \(H(p, p) = -\sum_k p_k \log p_k\), which is the entropy of a random variable with mass function \(p\).










DefDefinition 23 (Kullback–Leibler divergence (KL divergence, relative entropy))






Definition 23 (Kullback–Leibler divergence (KL divergence, relative entropy)) For \(p\) and \(q\) as in Definition 22, the Kullback–Leibler divergence (KL divergence, or relative entropy) of \(q\) from \(p\) is
\[D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p \,\|\, q) \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}\sum_{k=1}^{K} p_k \log \frac{p_k}{q_k} = H(p, q) - H(p, p).\]










RemarkRemark 12 (The divergence is not symmetric)






Remark 12 (The divergence is not symmetric). In general, \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p \,\|\, q) \ne D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q \,\|\, p)\), so it is not a distance between \(p\) and \(q\).










ExmExample 41 (Cross-entropy and divergence for two coins)






Example 41 (Cross-entropy and divergence for two coins) Let \(p = (\tfrac{1}{2}, \tfrac{1}{2})\) be a fair coin and \(q = (\tfrac{1}{4}, \tfrac{3}{4})\) a coin biased toward the second outcome. Using logarithms to base 2, \(\log_2 \tfrac{1}{4} = -2\) and \(\log_2 \tfrac{3}{4} = \log_2 3 - 2\), so
\[
\begin{aligned}
H(p, q) &= -\tfrac{1}{2} \log_2 \tfrac{1}{4} - \tfrac{1}{2} \log_2 \tfrac{3}{4} \\
&= 1 + \tfrac{1}{2} \mathopen{}\left(2 - \log_2 3\right)\mathclose{} \\
&= 2 - \tfrac{1}{2} \log_2 3 \\
&\approx 1.208, \\
H(p, p) &= -\tfrac{1}{2} \log_2 \tfrac{1}{2} - \tfrac{1}{2} \log_2 \tfrac{1}{2} \\
&= 1, \\
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p \,\|\, q) &= H(p, q) - H(p, p) = 1 - \tfrac{1}{2} \log_2 3 \approx 0.208.
\end{aligned}
\]
Here the cross-entropy is larger than the entropy of \(p\), and the divergence is the difference.










RemarkRemark 13 (Where the definitions come from)






Remark 13 (Where the definitions come from). Murphy [16, Sec. 2.8.2], pp. 57–58 defines the KL divergence and the cross-entropy as above, and gives the coding interpretation: the cross-entropy is the average number of bits needed to encode data from a source with distribution \(p\) using a code designed for \(q\).

title: Probability for Data Science
text:
Probability theory is the branch of mathematics concerned with formalizing and quantifying uncertainty. It is the foundation on which statistical inference is built: before we can reason about what data tell us about the world, we need a precise language for describing random phenomena.
These notes collect the probability that data science courses assume. Some key results are listed here, organized by topic:

Notation
Probability basics: sample spaces and events, probability axioms, conditional probability, and Bayes’ theorem
Random variables: PMF, PDF, CDF, quantile function, and survival, hazard, and cumulative hazard functions
Independence: independence, conditional independence, and (conditionally) IID random variables
Expectation: expectation, LOTUS, conditional expectation, Fubini-Tonelli, and the law of iterated expectations
Variance and covariance: deviation, variance, conditional variance, homoskedasticity, and covariance
Key distributions: Bernoulli, binomial, Poisson, negative binomial, and Weibull distributions
Limit theorems: the Central Limit Theorem

Most of this material should be review from an introductory probability or mathematical statistics course (e.g., UC Davis’s Epi 202). These notes began as the probability chapter of the Morrison Lab’s Regression Models for Epidemiology, which applies them to regression and survival models (see Additional resources).

section: Using these notes in another site
text:
Using these notes in another site
Course sites link to these pages by URL; they do not include this repository as a git submodule. A host site that keeps a copy of this repository at its root, named pds, can still include fragments with paths that start with pds/, for example {{< include pds/_subfiles/_thm-bayes.qmd >}}. This site includes its own fragments the same way, through a pds symlink that points at the repository root.
Quarto resolves @id cross-references only within one rendered page, so a host site that links to a result here uses an explicit link, [text](expectation.qmd#thm-lotus).

title: Probability for Data Science
text:
Additional resources

Comparable courses
Several universities offer open-access courses with comparable or complementary coverage of probability for data science, computer science, and statistics:

Stanford University CS 109: Probability for Computer Scientists (Chris Piech, Mehran Sahami, and David Varodayan) introduces counting, probability axioms, random variables, joint distributions, limit theorems, and machine learning applications.
Stanford University STATS 116: Theory of Probability (John Duchi) provides a rigorous mathematical treatment of probability spaces, conditioning, random variables, transform methods, and limit theorems (see also lecture notes by Amir Dembo).
UC Berkeley Data 140 / Stat 140: Probability for Data Science (Ani Adhikari and Jim Pitman) blends mathematical probability theory with Python simulations and computational data science applications.
Stanford University EE 278: Probability and Statistical Inference (Ayfer Özgür and Tsachy Weissman) builds on probability for hypothesis testing, empirical risk minimization, concentration inequalities (Markov, Chebyshev, Hoeffding), Gaussian random vectors and minimum mean-square error estimation; its previous notes are handwritten lectures on these topics. The prerequisite probability course has open lecture notes by David Tse and Abbas El Gamal.
Harvard University Stat 110: Introduction to Probability (Joseph K. Blitzstein; companion textbook Blitzstein and Hwang [1], online at probabilitybook.net) covers conditioning, distributions, transform methods, and Markov chains with an emphasis on intuitive storytelling.
MIT 18.05: Introduction to Probability and Statistics (Jeremy Orloff and Jonathan Bloom, MIT OpenCourseWare) bridges probability, discrete and continuous random variables, and both Bayesian and frequentist statistical inference.
MIT 6.041 / 6.431: Probabilistic Systems Analysis and Applied Probability (John Tsitsiklis, MIT OpenCourseWare) covers probability spaces, conditioning, independence, transform methods, and Bernoulli and Poisson processes.
Cal Poly / Kevin Ross: An Introduction to Probability and Simulation (Ross [2]) develops probability concepts through simulation in R and Python, providing intuitive frameworks including conditioning as “slicing and renormalizing” and “taking out what is known” in conditional expectation.



Textbooks and companion notes

Miller [3]

Hastie et al. [4]
James et al. [5]
Amir Dembo and Kevin Ross, Stochastic Processes lecture notes (Dembo and Ross [6], Stanford MATH 136 / STAT 219)
Amir Dembo, Probability Theory lecture notes (Stanford STAT 310 / MATH 230, the measure-theoretic sequel to this material; used in STATS 310B)
John Duchi, Lecture Notes on Statistics and Information Theory (Stanford STATS 311), which develops entropy and divergences beyond the definitions here
Morrison Lab’s Regression Models for Epidemiology, which applies this material to regression and survival analysis



Video channels
The DATA 571 (Machine Learning) course notes keep a curated list of online video channels, with levels, for probability and statistics as well as machine learning, AI, computer science and mathematics.

title: Notation
text:
1 Stochastic vs. probabilistic vs. random






RemarkRemark






Remark. The terms “stochastic”, “probabilistic”, and “random” are frequently used in statistics and probability theory, often interchangeably in everyday conversation, but they carry nuanced technical distinctions.





1.1 Key distinction: modeling approach vs. phenomena






RemarkRemark






Remark. As noted in Wikipedia:

Stochasticity and randomness are technically distinct concepts: the former refers to a modeling approach, while the latter describes phenomena; in everyday conversation these terms are often used interchangeably.












DefDefinition 1 (Random)






Definition 1 (Random) Something is random when it occurs by chance, without a deterministic pattern: its outcome cannot be predicted precisely, only probabilistically. It is the most general of the three terms, used to describe variables or occurrences rather than whole processes or modeling approaches.










RemarkRemark






Remark. The term “random” is sometimes used as shorthand for a uniform distribution (especially the discrete uniform distribution), but it can refer to any probability distribution.










ExmExample 1 (A random variable)






Example 1 (A random variable) The result of a single die roll is random: it cannot be predicted with certainty, only described by the probability \(1/6\) for each face. We speak of a “random variable” and a “random event” for exactly this kind of single outcome.










DefDefinition 2 (Stochastic process (random process))






Definition 2 (Stochastic process (random process)) A stochastic process is a collection of random variables indexed by a set, most often a set of times or locations. In probability theory, “stochastic process” and “random process” are synonyms [1], [2], [3].










RemarkRemark 1 (The word “stochastic”)






Remark 1 (The word “stochastic”). The word “stochastic” comes from the Greek \(\sigma\tau\acute{o}\chi o\varsigma\) (stókhos), meaning “aim” or “guess” (see etymology). The term is almost always used for processes or systems evolving in time or space under uncertain rules, rather than for a single variable or event.










ExmExample 2 (Stock price evolution)






Example 2 (Stock price evolution) The sequence of a stock’s daily closing prices is a stochastic process: a random variable (the price) indexed by a set (the trading days).










DefDefinition 3 (Probabilistic)






Definition 3 (Probabilistic) A model, method, or line of reasoning is probabilistic when it explicitly involves probability theory: it assigns probabilities to events or outcomes, and focuses on quantifying and reasoning about uncertainty based on known or estimated distributions. While every stochastic model is probabilistic (since it uses probabilities), not every probabilistic model needs to describe a process evolving in time.










ExmExample 3 (A linear regression model)






Example 3 (A linear regression model) A linear regression model with Gaussian errors, \(Y = \beta_{0} + \beta_{1} x + \varepsilon\) with \(\varepsilon\sim {\operatorname{N}\mathopen{}\left(0, \sigma^2\right)\mathclose{}}\), is probabilistic: for each value of the covariate \(x\), it assigns a probability distribution to the outcome \(Y\). It is not a stochastic process, because it describes the outcome at a given covariate value rather than a process evolving in time.










RemarkRemark






Remark. The model is probabilistic because of its error distribution, not because of the method used to fit it. The same model is probabilistic whether its parameters are estimated by maximum likelihood or by Bayesian inference. Bayesian inference additionally assigns a probability distribution to the parameters themselves, which makes the inference method probabilistic too.






1.2 Summary of usage









Table 1: Comparison of “random”, “stochastic”, and “probabilistic”











Term
What it describes
Typical use
Example




Random
Single variable or event
Random variable, random outcome
Coin toss, die roll


Stochastic
System or process in time/space
Stochastic process
Stock price evolution, Markov chain


Probabilistic
Approach/model using probability
Probabilistic model/reasoning
Regression model, Bayesian inference















RemarkRemark






Remark. While some sources treat “stochastic” and “random” as practically synonymous, a common convention is to use “random” for variables and events, and “stochastic” for processes, especially to highlight temporal or spatial structure in the modeling.

title: Random variables
text:
DefDefinition 1 (Random variable)






Definition 1 (Random variable) A random variable is a function from a sample space \(\Omega\) to the real numbers \(\mathbb{R}\) [1]: it assigns a number to each possible outcome of a random experiment.










RemarkRemark






Remark. We use uppercase letters (\(X\), \(Y\), \(Z\), …) for random variables, and lowercase letters (\(x\), \(y\), \(z\), …) for their realized (observed) values. We write \(\{X = x\}\) for the event \(\{\omega\in \Omega: X(\omega) = x\}\), and similarly for \(\{X \le x\}\) and other conditions on \(X\). A fully rigorous definition also requires the function to be measurable, so that every such set is an event with a probability; that requirement never binds in these notes.










ExmExample 1 (Number of heads in two coin flips)






Example 1 (Number of heads in two coin flips) Flip a fair coin twice. The sample space is \(\Omega= {\mathopen{}\left\{HH, HT, TH, TT\right\}\mathclose{}}\), each outcome with probability \(1/4\). Let \(X\) be the number of heads:
\[
\begin{aligned}
X(HH) &= 2, \\
X(HT) &= 1, \\
X(TH) &= 1, \\
X(TT) &= 0
\end{aligned}
\]
Then \(\{X = 1\} = {\mathopen{}\left\{HT, TH\right\}\mathclose{}}\), so
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Pr(X = 1) &= 1/4 + 1/4 \\
&= 1/2.
\end{aligned}
\]










DefDefinition 2 (Range of a random variable)






Definition 2 (Range of a random variable) The range of a random variable \(X\), denoted \(\mathcal{R}(X)\), is the set of values \(X\) can take:
\[\mathcal{R}(X) \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}{\mathopen{}\left\{X(\omega) : \omega\in \Omega\right\}\mathclose{}}\]










RemarkRemark






Remark. The range of \(X\) is the image of \(X\) as a function on \(\Omega\). For a general function, these notes say “image”, because some sources use “range” for the codomain instead; for a random variable, “range” is the standard term.










ExmExample 2 (Range of the number of heads)






Example 2 (Range of the number of heads) In Example 1, \(\mathcal{R}(X) = {\mathopen{}\left\{0, 1, 2\right\}\mathclose{}}\).










DefDefinition 3 (Discrete random variable)






Definition 3 (Discrete random variable) A random variable \(X\) is discrete if its range \(\mathcal{R}(X)\) is countable.










ExmExample 3 (Discrete random variables)






Example 3 (Discrete random variables) The number of heads in Example 1 is discrete, with a finite range. A count with no upper bound, such as the number of emergency-department visits in a day, is discrete with a countably infinite range, \({\mathopen{}\left\{0, 1, 2, \dots\right\}\mathclose{}}\).










DefDefinition 4 (Continuous random variable)






Definition 4 (Continuous random variable) A random variable \(X\) is continuous if \(\Pr(X = x) = 0\) for every \(x \in \mathbb{R}\).










RemarkRemark






Remark. Every continuous random variable in these notes also has a probability density function. Continuous random variables without a density exist, but they do not arise in applications.










ExmExample 4 (A continuous random variable)






Example 4 (A continuous random variable) Let \(X\) satisfy \(\Pr(a \le X \le b) = b - a\) for all \(0 \le a \le b \le 1\). Taking
\[
\begin{aligned}
a &= b \\
&= x
\end{aligned}
\]
gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Pr(X = x) &= x - x \\
&= 0
\end{aligned}
\]
for every \(x \in [0,1]\). Taking \(a = 0\) and \(b = 1\) gives \(\Pr(0 \le X \le 1) = 1\), so by the complement rule \(X\) falls outside \([0, 1]\) with probability 0, and \(\Pr(X = x) = 0\) for every \(x\) outside \([0, 1]\) as well. So \(X\) is continuous. Its range, \([0, 1]\), is uncountable.










ExmExample 5 (A random variable that is neither discrete nor continuous)






Example 5 (A random variable that is neither discrete nor continuous) Some random variables are neither discrete nor continuous: a time to event that equals exactly \(0\) with positive probability, and otherwise spreads over \((0, \infty)\), is one. For instance, let \(U\) be the continuous random variable of Example 4, and let \(T = 1/(1 - U) - 2\) when \(1/2 < U < 1\), and \(T = 0\) otherwise. On \({\mathopen{}\left\{1/2 < U < 1\right\}\mathclose{}}\), \(T\) is increasing in \(U\) and takes values in \((0, \infty)\), and solving \(t = 1/(1 - u) - 2\) for \(u\) gives \(u = 1 - 1/(t + 2)\). So \({\mathopen{}\left\{T > 0\right\}\mathclose{}} = {\mathopen{}\left\{1/2 < U < 1\right\}\mathclose{}}\), and \({\mathopen{}\left\{T = t\right\}\mathclose{}} = {\mathopen{}\left\{U = 1 - 1/(t + 2)\right\}\mathclose{}}\) for each \(t > 0\). Since \(U\) is continuous (Example 4), single points have probability zero:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Pr(U = 1/2) &= \Pr(U = 1) \\
&= 0
\end{aligned}
\]
Using these values:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Pr(T > 0)
&= \Pr(1/2 < U < 1)
&& \text{(} {\mathopen{}\left\{T > 0\right\}\mathclose{}} = {\mathopen{}\left\{1/2 < U < 1\right\}\mathclose{}} \text{)} \\
&= \Pr(1/2 \le U \le 1) - \Pr(U = 1/2) - \Pr(U = 1)
&& \text{(additivity)} \\
&= \tfrac{1}{2} - 0 - 0
&& \text{(} \Pr(a \le U \le b) = b - a \text{)} \\
&= \tfrac{1}{2}
&& \text{(simplify)}
\end{aligned}
\]
\(T\) is not continuous, because
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Pr(T = 0) &= 1 - \Pr(T > 0) \\
&= 1/2
\end{aligned}
\]
by the complement rule.
\(T\) is not discrete either. If it were, its range would be countable, so \({\mathopen{}\left\{T > 0\right\}\mathclose{}}\) would be the disjoint union of the countably many events \({\mathopen{}\left\{T = t\right\}\mathclose{}}\) with \(t \in \mathcal{R}(T)\) and \(t > 0\), and:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Pr(T > 0)
&= \sum_{t \in \mathcal{R}(T),\, t > 0} \Pr(T = t)
&& \text{(countable additivity)} \\
&= \sum_{t \in \mathcal{R}(T),\, t > 0} {\Pr\mathopen{}\left(U = 1 - \tfrac{1}{t + 2}\right)\mathclose{}}
&& \text{(} {\mathopen{}\left\{T = t\right\}\mathclose{}} = {\mathopen{}\left\{U = 1 - 1/(t + 2)\right\}\mathclose{}} \text{)} \\
&= 0
&& \text{(} U \text{ is continuous)}
\end{aligned}
\]
which contradicts \(\Pr(T > 0) = 1/2\).

title: Random variables
text:
DefDefinition 1 (Random variable)






Definition 1 (Random variable) A random variable is a function from a sample space \(\Omega\) to the real numbers \(\mathbb{R}\) [1]: it assigns a number to each possible outcome of a random experiment.










RemarkRemark






Remark. We use uppercase letters (\(X\), \(Y\), \(Z\), …) for random variables, and lowercase letters (\(x\), \(y\), \(z\), …) for their realized (observed) values. We write \(\{X = x\}\) for the event \(\{\omega\in \Omega: X(\omega) = x\}\), and similarly for \(\{X \le x\}\) and other conditions on \(X\). A fully rigorous definition also requires the function to be measurable, so that every such set is an event with a probability; that requirement never binds in these notes.










ExmExample 1 (Number of heads in two coin flips)






Example 1 (Number of heads in two coin flips) Flip a fair coin twice. The sample space is \(\Omega= {\mathopen{}\left\{HH, HT, TH, TT\right\}\mathclose{}}\), each outcome with probability \(1/4\). Let \(X\) be the number of heads:
\[
\begin{aligned}
X(HH) &= 2, \\
X(HT) &= 1, \\
X(TH) &= 1, \\
X(TT) &= 0
\end{aligned}
\]
Then \(\{X = 1\} = {\mathopen{}\left\{HT, TH\right\}\mathclose{}}\), so
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Pr(X = 1) &= 1/4 + 1/4 \\
&= 1/2.
\end{aligned}
\]










DefDefinition 2 (Range of a random variable)






Definition 2 (Range of a random variable) The range of a random variable \(X\), denoted \(\mathcal{R}(X)\), is the set of values \(X\) can take:
\[\mathcal{R}(X) \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}{\mathopen{}\left\{X(\omega) : \omega\in \Omega\right\}\mathclose{}}\]










RemarkRemark






Remark. The range of \(X\) is the image of \(X\) as a function on \(\Omega\). For a general function, these notes say “image”, because some sources use “range” for the codomain instead; for a random variable, “range” is the standard term.










ExmExample 2 (Range of the number of heads)






Example 2 (Range of the number of heads) In Example 1, \(\mathcal{R}(X) = {\mathopen{}\left\{0, 1, 2\right\}\mathclose{}}\).










DefDefinition 3 (Discrete random variable)






Definition 3 (Discrete random variable) A random variable \(X\) is discrete if its range \(\mathcal{R}(X)\) is countable.










ExmExample 3 (Discrete random variables)






Example 3 (Discrete random variables) The number of heads in Example 1 is discrete, with a finite range. A count with no upper bound, such as the number of emergency-department visits in a day, is discrete with a countably infinite range, \({\mathopen{}\left\{0, 1, 2, \dots\right\}\mathclose{}}\).










DefDefinition 4 (Continuous random variable)






Definition 4 (Continuous random variable) A random variable \(X\) is continuous if \(\Pr(X = x) = 0\) for every \(x \in \mathbb{R}\).










RemarkRemark






Remark. Every continuous random variable in these notes also has a probability density function. Continuous random variables without a density exist, but they do not arise in applications.










ExmExample 4 (A continuous random variable)






Example 4 (A continuous random variable) Let \(X\) satisfy \(\Pr(a \le X \le b) = b - a\) for all \(0 \le a \le b \le 1\). Taking
\[
\begin{aligned}
a &= b \\
&= x
\end{aligned}
\]
gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Pr(X = x) &= x - x \\
&= 0
\end{aligned}
\]
for every \(x \in [0,1]\). Taking \(a = 0\) and \(b = 1\) gives \(\Pr(0 \le X \le 1) = 1\), so by the complement rule \(X\) falls outside \([0, 1]\) with probability 0, and \(\Pr(X = x) = 0\) for every \(x\) outside \([0, 1]\) as well. So \(X\) is continuous. Its range, \([0, 1]\), is uncountable.










ExmExample 5 (A random variable that is neither discrete nor continuous)






Example 5 (A random variable that is neither discrete nor continuous) Some random variables are neither discrete nor continuous: a time to event that equals exactly \(0\) with positive probability, and otherwise spreads over \((0, \infty)\), is one. For instance, let \(U\) be the continuous random variable of Example 4, and let \(T = 1/(1 - U) - 2\) when \(1/2 < U < 1\), and \(T = 0\) otherwise. On \({\mathopen{}\left\{1/2 < U < 1\right\}\mathclose{}}\), \(T\) is increasing in \(U\) and takes values in \((0, \infty)\), and solving \(t = 1/(1 - u) - 2\) for \(u\) gives \(u = 1 - 1/(t + 2)\). So \({\mathopen{}\left\{T > 0\right\}\mathclose{}} = {\mathopen{}\left\{1/2 < U < 1\right\}\mathclose{}}\), and \({\mathopen{}\left\{T = t\right\}\mathclose{}} = {\mathopen{}\left\{U = 1 - 1/(t + 2)\right\}\mathclose{}}\) for each \(t > 0\). Since \(U\) is continuous (Example 4), single points have probability zero:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Pr(U = 1/2) &= \Pr(U = 1) \\
&= 0
\end{aligned}
\]
Using these values:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Pr(T > 0)
&= \Pr(1/2 < U < 1)
&& \text{(} {\mathopen{}\left\{T > 0\right\}\mathclose{}} = {\mathopen{}\left\{1/2 < U < 1\right\}\mathclose{}} \text{)} \\
&= \Pr(1/2 \le U \le 1) - \Pr(U = 1/2) - \Pr(U = 1)
&& \text{(additivity)} \\
&= \tfrac{1}{2} - 0 - 0
&& \text{(} \Pr(a \le U \le b) = b - a \text{)} \\
&= \tfrac{1}{2}
&& \text{(simplify)}
\end{aligned}
\]
\(T\) is not continuous, because
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Pr(T = 0) &= 1 - \Pr(T > 0) \\
&= 1/2
\end{aligned}
\]
by the complement rule.
\(T\) is not discrete either. If it were, its range would be countable, so \({\mathopen{}\left\{T > 0\right\}\mathclose{}}\) would be the disjoint union of the countably many events \({\mathopen{}\left\{T = t\right\}\mathclose{}}\) with \(t \in \mathcal{R}(T)\) and \(t > 0\), and:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Pr(T > 0)
&= \sum_{t \in \mathcal{R}(T),\, t > 0} \Pr(T = t)
&& \text{(countable additivity)} \\
&= \sum_{t \in \mathcal{R}(T),\, t > 0} {\Pr\mathopen{}\left(U = 1 - \tfrac{1}{t + 2}\right)\mathclose{}}
&& \text{(} {\mathopen{}\left\{T = t\right\}\mathclose{}} = {\mathopen{}\left\{U = 1 - 1/(t + 2)\right\}\mathclose{}} \text{)} \\
&= 0
&& \text{(} U \text{ is continuous)}
\end{aligned}
\]
which contradicts \(\Pr(T > 0) = 1/2\).
