2 Characteristics of probability distributions







DefDefinition 5 (Probability mass function (PMF))






Definition 5 (Probability mass function (PMF)) If \(X\) is a discrete random variable, the probability mass function of \(X\) at value \(x\), denoted \(f(x)\), \(f_X(x)\), \(\mathbb{P}(x)\), \(\mathbb{P}_X(x)\), or \(\mathbb{P}(X=x)\), is the probability that \(X\) takes exactly the value \(x\) [2]:
\[\mathbb{P}(X=x) \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}\Pr(\{X=x\})\]










ExmExample 6 (PMF of the number of heads)






Example 6 (PMF of the number of heads) For the number of heads \(X\) in two fair coin flips (Example 1):
\[\mathbb{P}(X = 0) = \tfrac{1}{4}, \quad \mathbb{P}(X = 1) = \tfrac{1}{2}, \quad \mathbb{P}(X = 2) = \tfrac{1}{4}\]










DefDefinition 6 (Bernoulli distribution)






Definition 6 (Bernoulli distribution) A discrete random variable \(X\) has the Bernoulli distribution with parameter \(\pi\in [0, 1]\), written \(X \sim \operatorname{Ber}(\pi)\) [3], if:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Pr(X=x) &\stackrel{\text{def}}{=}\text{1}_{x\in {\mathopen{}\left\{0,1\right\}\mathclose{}}}\pi^x(1-\pi)^{1-x}\\
&= \begin{cases}
\pi, & x=1\\
1-\pi, & x=0
\end{cases}
\end{aligned}
\]










ExmExample 7 (The first of two coin flips)






Example 7 (The first of two coin flips) In Example 1, let \(X_1\) indicate heads on the first flip, so
\[
\begin{aligned}
X_1(HH) &= X_1(HT) \\
&= 1
\end{aligned}
\]
and
\[
\begin{aligned}
X_1(TH) &= X_1(TT) \\
&= 0.
\end{aligned}
\]
Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(X_1 = 1) &= \Pr({\mathopen{}\left\{HH, HT\right\}\mathclose{}}) \\
&= 1/2
\end{aligned}
\]
and
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(X_1 = 0) &= \Pr({\mathopen{}\left\{TH, TT\right\}\mathclose{}}) \\
&= 1/2,
\end{aligned}
\]
so \(X_1 \sim \operatorname{Ber}(1/2)\).










DefDefinition 7 (Probability density function (PDF))






Definition 7 (Probability density function (PDF)) If \(X\) is a continuous random variable, a probability density function of \(X\), denoted \(f(x)\), \(f_X(x)\), \(\operatorname{p}(x)\), \(\operatorname{p}_X(x)\), or \(\operatorname{p}(X=x)\), is a function \(f\) that satisfies [4]:

\(f(x) \ge 0\) for every \(x\).
The integral of \(f\) over any interval is the probability that \(X\) falls in that interval: \[\Pr(a \le X \le b) = \int_a^b f(x)\,dx \quad \text{for all } a \le b\]











DefDefinition 8 (Uniform distribution on a set)






Definition 8 (Uniform distribution on a set) Let \(S\) be a set with a measure \(\mu\) such that \(0 < \mu(S) < \infty\). The uniform distribution on \(S\) is the probability measure
\[\Pr(A) \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}\frac{\mu(A)}{\mu(S)}, \quad A \subseteq S.\]










DefDefinition 9 (Uniform distribution on an interval)






Definition 9 (Uniform distribution on an interval) The uniform distribution on an interval \([\alpha, \beta]\) (Definition 8 with \(\mu\) the length), with \(\alpha< \beta\), is the distribution of a random variable \(X\), written \(X \sim \text{Uniform}(\alpha, \beta)\), that is continuous with density [5]:
\[
f(x) \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}\begin{cases}
\frac{1}{\beta- \alpha}, & \alpha\le x \le \beta\\
0, & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
\]










ExmExample 8 (Subinterval probabilities of a uniform random variable)






Example 8 (Subinterval probabilities of a uniform random variable) For \(X \sim \text{Uniform}(\alpha, \beta)\) (Definition 9) and any subinterval \([a, b] \subseteq [\alpha, \beta]\) (so \(\alpha\le a \le b \le \beta\)):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Pr(a \le X \le b)
&= \int_a^b f(x)\,dx
&& \text{(definition of a probability density function)} \\
&= \int_a^b \frac{1}{\beta- \alpha}\,dx
&& \text{(} f(x) = \tfrac{1}{\beta- \alpha} \text{ on } [\alpha, \beta] \text{)} \\
&= \frac{b - a}{\beta- \alpha}
&& \text{(integrate)}
\end{aligned}
\]
In particular, the probability that \(X\) falls in any subinterval is proportional to that subinterval’s length. For the standard uniform distribution on \([0, 1]\), \(f(x) = 1\) for \(x \in [0, 1]\) and \(f(x) = 0\) otherwise, giving \(\Pr(a \le X \le b) = b - a\) for all \(0 \le a \le b \le 1\). An interval reaching outside \([\alpha, \beta]\) adds nothing to the probability, because \(f = 0\) there.










LemTheorem 1 (A density is not unique)






Theorem 1 (A density is not unique) If \(f\) is a density of a continuous random variable \(X\), and \(g \ge 0\) differs from \(f\) at only finitely many points, then \(g\) is also a density of \(X\).










ProofProof






Proof. For \(a \le b\), the difference \(g - f\) is \(0\) at all but finitely many points, so:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\int_a^b g(x)\,dx
&= \int_a^b f(x)\,dx + \int_a^b \mathopen{}\left(g(x) - f(x)\right)\mathclose{}\,dx
&& \text{(linearity of the integral)} \\
&= \int_a^b f(x)\,dx + 0
&& \text{(a function that is 0 at all but finitely many points integrates to 0)} \\
&= \Pr(a \le X \le b)
&& \text{(} f \text{ is a density of } X \text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]
Together with \(g \ge 0\), this is Definition 7 for \(g\).










RemarkRemark






Remark. So the value of a density at a single point carries no probability by itself. These notes use the version that is continuous wherever possible.










LemTheorem 2 (Some continuous random variables have no density)






Theorem 2 (Some continuous random variables have no density) There exist continuous random variables that have no probability density function.










RemarkRemark






Remark. The proof needs measure theory beyond these notes. The standard example is the Cantor distribution, which puts no probability on any single point, but puts all of its probability on a set of total length 0, so any candidate density would integrate to 0 over a set of probability 1.
Every continuous random variable in these notes also has a probability density function. Continuous random variables without a density do not arise in applications.










DefDefinition 10 (Normal distribution (Gaussian distribution))






Definition 10 (Normal distribution (Gaussian distribution)) A random variable \(X\) has the normal distribution (or Gaussian distribution) with mean parameter \(\mu\in \mathbb{R}\) and variance parameter \(\sigma^2> 0\), written \(X \sim {\operatorname{N}\mathopen{}\left(\mu, \sigma^2\right)\mathclose{}}\) [6], if \(X\) is continuous with density:
\[\operatorname{p}(X=x) \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}\frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}} \text{e}^{-\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}}, \quad x \in \mathbb{R}\]










ExmExample 9 (Normal densities at their centers)






Example 9 (Normal densities at their centers) For \(X \sim {\operatorname{N}\mathopen{}\left(0, 1\right)\mathclose{}}\), the density at \(x = 0\) is:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{p}(X=0)
&= \frac{1}{1 \cdot\sqrt{2\pi}} \text{e}^{-\frac{(0-0)^2}{2 \cdot 1}}
&& \text{(normal density with } \mu= 0, \sigma^2= 1 \text{)} \\
&= \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}
&& \text{(} \text{e}^0 = 1 \text{)} \\
&\approx 0.399
&& \text{(evaluate)}
\end{aligned}
\]
For \(X \sim {\operatorname{N}\mathopen{}\left(0, 0.1^2\right)\mathclose{}}\), the same steps give \(\operatorname{p}(X=0) = 1 / (0.1\sqrt{2\pi}) \approx 3.99\), a density greater than 1.










RemarkRemark






Remark. A density is not a probability: it can exceed 1, as the second density in Example 9 does.










LemTheorem 3 (The normal density integrates to 1)






Theorem 3 (The normal density integrates to 1) If \(X \sim {\operatorname{N}\mathopen{}\left(\mu, \sigma^2\right)\mathclose{}}\) (Definition 10), then:
\[\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}} \text{e}^{-\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}}\,dx = 1\]










LemTheorem 4 (The mean and variance of the normal distribution)






Theorem 4 (The mean and variance of the normal distribution) If \(X \sim {\operatorname{N}\mathopen{}\left(\mu, \sigma^2\right)\mathclose{}}\) (Definition 10), then \(X\) has mean \({\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[X\right]\mathclose{}} = \mu\) and variance \({\operatorname{Var}\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}} = \sigma^2\).










RemarkRemark






Remark. The proofs of these two theorems evaluate three integrals by calculus: the total of the density, the mean integral and the variance integral. The total is the Gaussian integral. This page omits the proofs [7]. These facts are where the parameters’ names come from.










DefDefinition 11 (Standard normal distribution)






Definition 11 (Standard normal distribution) The standard normal distribution is the normal distribution with mean parameter 0 and variance parameter 1, \({\operatorname{N}\mathopen{}\left(0, 1\right)\mathclose{}}\).










ExmExample 10 (Half of a standard normal lies below 0)






Example 10 (Half of a standard normal lies below 0) If \(Z\) has the standard normal distribution, its density \(\operatorname{p}(Z=z) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \text{e}^{-z^2/2}\) takes the same value at \(z\) and \(-z\), so \(\Pr(Z \le 0) = \Pr(Z \ge 0)\). Those two probabilities sum to 1, because \(\Pr(Z = 0) = 0\) for a continuous \(Z\), so each is \(\tfrac{1}{2}\).










DefDefinition 12 (Exponential distribution)






Definition 12 (Exponential distribution) A random variable \(T\) has the exponential distribution with rate \({\lambda}> 0\) [8] if \(T\) is continuous with density:
\[
f(t) \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}\begin{cases}
{\lambda}\text{e}^{-{\lambda}t}, & t \ge 0 \\
0, & t < 0
\end{cases}
\]










ExmExample 11 (Probability of an event within one time unit)






Example 11 (Probability of an event within one time unit) Let \(T\) be exponential with rate \({\lambda}\). The probability that \(T\) falls in \([0, 1]\) is:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Pr(0 \le T \le 1)
&= \int_0^1 {\lambda}\text{e}^{-{\lambda}t}\,dt
&& \text{(definition of a density)} \\
&= \mathopen{}\left[-\text{e}^{-{\lambda}t}\right]\mathclose{}_{t=0}^{1}
&& \text{(antiderivative of } {\lambda}\text{e}^{-{\lambda}t} \text{)} \\
&= 1 - \text{e}^{-{\lambda}}
&& \text{(evaluate at the bounds)}
\end{aligned}
\]
With \({\lambda}= 0.5\), for example, \(\Pr(0 \le T \le 1) = 1 - \text{e}^{-0.5} \approx 0.393\).










DefDefinition 13 (Cumulative distribution function (CDF))






Definition 13 (Cumulative distribution function (CDF)) For a random variable \(X\) (discrete or continuous), its cumulative distribution function [9] is:
\[{\operatorname{F}\mathopen{}\left(t\right)\mathclose{}} \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}\Pr(X\le t), \quad t\in\mathbb{R}.\]










RemarkRemark






Remark. The CDF is always defined, whether \(X\) is discrete or continuous.










ExmExample 12 (CDF of the number of heads)






Example 12 (CDF of the number of heads) Summing the PMF in Example 6 over values at or below \(t\):
\[
{\operatorname{F}\mathopen{}\left(t\right)\mathclose{}} = \begin{cases}
0, & t < 0 \\
\tfrac{1}{4}, & 0 \le t < 1 \\
\tfrac{3}{4}, & 1 \le t < 2 \\
1, & t \ge 2
\end{cases}
\]










LemTheorem 5 (Properties of a CDF)






Theorem 5 (Properties of a CDF) The CDF \(\operatorname{F}\) of any random variable \(X\) is non-decreasing, and:
\[\lim_{t \to -\infty} {\operatorname{F}\mathopen{}\left(t\right)\mathclose{}} = 0, \qquad \lim_{t \to \infty} {\operatorname{F}\mathopen{}\left(t\right)\mathclose{}} = 1\]










ProofProof






Proof. Non-decreasing. For \(s < t\), \(\{X \le t\}\) is the disjoint union of \(\{X \le s\}\) and \(\{s < X \le t\}\), so finite additivity gives:
\[
\begin{aligned}
{\operatorname{F}\mathopen{}\left(t\right)\mathclose{}}
&= \Pr(X \le s) + \Pr(s < X \le t)
&& \text{(additivity, and the definition of the CDF)} \\
&\ge \Pr(X \le s)
&& \text{(probabilities are non-negative)} \\
&= {\operatorname{F}\mathopen{}\left(s\right)\mathclose{}}
&& \text{(definition of the CDF)}
\end{aligned}
\]
Limit at \(-\infty\). The events \(A_n = \{X \le -n\}\), \(n = 1, 2, \ldots\), are decreasing, and their intersection is empty, because every outcome \(\omega\) has \(X(\omega) > -n\) once \(n > -X(\omega)\). By continuity of probability, \({\operatorname{F}\mathopen{}\left(-n\right)\mathclose{}} = \Pr(A_n) \to 0\). For \(t \le -n\), \(0 \le {\operatorname{F}\mathopen{}\left(t\right)\mathclose{}} \le {\operatorname{F}\mathopen{}\left(-n\right)\mathclose{}}\), because \(\operatorname{F}\) is non-decreasing, so \({\operatorname{F}\mathopen{}\left(t\right)\mathclose{}} \to 0\) as \(t \to -\infty\).
Limit at \(\infty\). The events \(B_n = \{X > n\}\) are decreasing, and their intersection is empty, because every outcome \(\omega\) has \(X(\omega) \le n\) once \(n \ge X(\omega)\). By continuity of probability, \(\Pr(B_n) \to 0\), so, by the complement rule:
\[
\begin{aligned}
{\operatorname{F}\mathopen{}\left(n\right)\mathclose{}}
&= 1 - \Pr(X > n)
&& \text{(complement rule)} \\
&\to 1 - 0
&& \text{(} \Pr(B_n) \to 0 \text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]
For \(t \ge n\), \({\operatorname{F}\mathopen{}\left(n\right)\mathclose{}} \le {\operatorname{F}\mathopen{}\left(t\right)\mathclose{}} \le 1\), because \(\operatorname{F}\) is non-decreasing, so \({\operatorname{F}\mathopen{}\left(t\right)\mathclose{}} \to 1\) as \(t \to \infty\).










LemTheorem 6 (The CDF determines the distribution)






Theorem 6 (The CDF determines the distribution) If random variables \(X\) and \(Y\) have the same CDF, then \(\Pr(X \in B) = \Pr(Y \in B)\) for every Borel set \(B \subseteq \mathbb{R}\), which includes every interval, and every set built from intervals by countably many unions, intersections, and complements.










RemarkRemark






Remark. The proof needs measure theory beyond these notes [9], [10].










DefDefinition 14 (Quantile function (population inverse CDF))






Definition 14 (Quantile function (population inverse CDF)) For a random variable \(X\) with cumulative distribution function (CDF) \(\operatorname{F}\), its population quantile function (generalized inverse of \(\operatorname{F}\)) is [11]:
\[{\operatorname{Q}\mathopen{}\left(p\right)\mathclose{}} \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}\inf {\mathopen{}\left\{t : {\operatorname{F}\mathopen{}\left(t\right)\mathclose{}} \ge p\right\}\mathclose{}}, \quad p \in (0, 1).\]










RemarkRemark






Remark. The restriction to \(p \in (0, 1)\) keeps \({\operatorname{Q}\mathopen{}\left(p\right)\mathclose{}}\) finite: for \(p = 1\), the set \({\mathopen{}\left\{t : {\operatorname{F}\mathopen{}\left(t\right)\mathclose{}} \ge 1\right\}\mathclose{}}\) is empty whenever \({\operatorname{F}\mathopen{}\left(t\right)\mathclose{}} < 1\) for every \(t\), as for a normal distribution, and the infimum of the empty set is \(+\infty\).










ExmExample 13 (Median of the number of heads)






Example 13 (Median of the number of heads) From Example 12, \({\operatorname{F}\mathopen{}\left(t\right)\mathclose{}} \ge 0.5\) first holds at \(t = 1\), so the median of the number of heads is \({\operatorname{Q}\mathopen{}\left(0.5\right)\mathclose{}} = 1\).










RemarkRemark






Remark. Figure 1 shows the mass function, CDF and quantile function of the number of heads in two fair coin flips (top row), beside the density, CDF and quantile function of a standard normal variable (bottom row).











Show code
# One ggplot2 figure serves every format:
# qnp::interactive_plot() turns it into an interactive plotly widget
# in HTML formats,
# with the alt text as the aria-label,
# and the handout and other formats draw it as it is.
# Top row: X = number of heads in two fair coin flips,
# so the pmf is 1/4, 1/2, 1/4 on 0, 1, 2, as in the examples above.
# Bottom row: the standard normal distribution;
# the density is shaded up to t = 1
# to show that the CDF at t is the area to its left.
local({
  library(ggplot2)

  heads <- 0:2
  pmf <- c(1, 2, 1) / 4
  cdf_steps <- cumsum(pmf)
  shade_at <- 1
  z <- seq(-3.5, 3.5, length.out = 300)
  p_grid <- seq(0.005, 0.995, length.out = 300)
  z_shade <- z[z <= shade_at]
  blue <- "#1f77b4"

  panel_names <- c(
    "Coin flips: mass function",
    "Coin flips: CDF",
    "Coin flips: quantile function",
    "Normal: density",
    "Normal: CDF",
    "Normal: quantile function"
  )
  panel_data <- function(panel, x, y) {
    data.frame(
      panel = factor(panel, levels = panel_names),
      x = x,
      y = y
    )
  }

  bars <- panel_data(panel_names[1], heads, pmf)
  steps <- rbind(
    panel_data(panel_names[2], c(-1, heads, 3), c(0, cdf_steps, 1)),
    panel_data(panel_names[3], c(0, 0.25, 0.75, 1), c(0, 1, 2, 2))
  )
  curves <- rbind(
    panel_data(panel_names[4], z, dnorm(z)),
    panel_data(panel_names[5], z, pnorm(z)),
    panel_data(panel_names[6], p_grid, qnorm(p_grid))
  )
  shaded <- panel_data(
    panel_names[4],
    c(z_shade, shade_at),
    c(dnorm(z_shade), 0)
  )
  marked <- panel_data(panel_names[5], shade_at, pnorm(shade_at))

  pmf_cdf_quantile <- ggplot(mapping = aes(x = x, y = y)) +
    geom_col(
      data = bars,
      fill = blue,
      width = 0.6
    ) +
    geom_step(
      data = steps,
      colour = blue
    ) +
    geom_line(
      data = curves,
      colour = blue
    ) +
    geom_ribbon(
      data = shaded,
      mapping = aes(ymin = 0, ymax = y),
      fill = blue,
      alpha = 0.3
    ) +
    geom_point(
      data = marked,
      colour = blue
    ) +
    facet_wrap(
      ~panel,
      nrow = 2,
      scales = "free"
    ) +
    labs(
      x = NULL,
      y = NULL
    ) +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(panel.spacing = unit(2, "lines"))

  qnp::interactive_plot(
    plot = pmf_cdf_quantile,
    alt = fig_alt
  )
})




Figure 1: A probability mass function, cumulative distribution function and quantile function for a discrete random variable (top row: the number of heads in two fair coin flips) and a continuous one (bottom row: the standard normal distribution). The shaded area under the normal density up to a point equals the CDF at that point. The quantile function reverses the CDF: its axes are the CDF’s, swapped.






















LemTheorem 7 (A density integrates to the CDF)






Theorem 7 (A density integrates to the CDF) If \(X\) is a continuous random variable with density \(f\) and CDF \(\operatorname{F}\), then for every \(t\):
\[{\operatorname{F}\mathopen{}\left(t\right)\mathclose{}} = \int_{-\infty}^{t} f(x)\,dx\]










ProofProof






Proof. For any \(a < t\), \(\{X \le t\}\) is the disjoint union of \(\{X \le a\}\) and \(\{a < X \le t\}\), and \(\Pr(X = a) = 0\) because \(X\) is continuous. So:
\[
\begin{aligned}
{\operatorname{F}\mathopen{}\left(t\right)\mathclose{}}
&= \Pr(X \le a) + \Pr(a < X \le t)
&& \text{(additivity, and the definition of the CDF)} \\
&= {\operatorname{F}\mathopen{}\left(a\right)\mathclose{}} + \Pr(a \le X \le t)
&& \text{(definition of the CDF; } \Pr(X = a) = 0 \text{)} \\
&= {\operatorname{F}\mathopen{}\left(a\right)\mathclose{}} + \int_a^t f(x)\,dx
&& \text{(definition of the density)}
\end{aligned}
\]
Letting \(a \to -\infty\), \({\operatorname{F}\mathopen{}\left(a\right)\mathclose{}} \to 0\) (Theorem 5), which gives \({\operatorname{F}\mathopen{}\left(t\right)\mathclose{}} = \int_{-\infty}^{t} f(x)\,dx\).










LemTheorem 8 (The derivative of the CDF is the density where the density is continuous)






Theorem 8 (The derivative of the CDF is the density where the density is continuous) If \(X\) is a continuous random variable with density \(f\) and CDF \(\operatorname{F}\), then at every \(t\) where \(f\) is continuous:
\[f(t) = \frac{\partial}{\partial t} {\operatorname{F}\mathopen{}\left(t\right)\mathclose{}}\]










ProofProof






Proof. By Theorem 7, \({\operatorname{F}\mathopen{}\left(t\right)\mathclose{}} = \int_{-\infty}^{t} f(x)\,dx\). The fundamental theorem of calculus then gives \(\frac{\partial}{\partial t} \int_{-\infty}^{t} f(x)\,dx = f(t)\) at every \(t\) where \(f\) is continuous.










CorCorollary 1 (A CDF has its density as derivative at all but finitely many points)






Corollary 1 (A CDF has its density as derivative at all but finitely many points) If \(X\) is a continuous random variable with CDF \(\operatorname{F}\) and a density \(f\) that is continuous at all but finitely many points, then \(\operatorname{F}\) is differentiable with \(\operatorname{F}' = f\) at all but finitely many points.










ProofProof






Proof. At every point \(t\) where \(f\) is continuous, Theorem 8 gives \(\operatorname{F}'(t) = f(t)\), and by assumption those are all but finitely many points.










RemarkRemark






Remark. Every density in these notes is continuous at all but finitely many points, so Corollary 1 applies to each of them.










ExmExample 14 (CDF and density of a uniform random variable)






Example 14 (CDF and density of a uniform random variable) For \(X \sim \text{Uniform}(0, 1)\) with the density \(f\) of Definition 9, and \(t \in [0, 1]\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
{\operatorname{F}\mathopen{}\left(t\right)\mathclose{}}
&= \int_{-\infty}^{t} f(x)\,dx
&& \text{(the CDF is the integral of the density)} \\
&= \int_{-\infty}^{0} 0\,dx + \int_{0}^{t} 1\,dx
&& \text{(split at 0, and substitute } f \text{)} \\
&= t
&& \text{(integrate)}
\end{aligned}
\]
For \(t \in (0, 1)\), where \(f\) is continuous,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial}{\partial t} {\operatorname{F}\mathopen{}\left(t\right)\mathclose{}} &= 1 \\
&= f(t).
\end{aligned}
\]
At \(t = 1\), \(f\) jumps from 1 to 0, and \(\operatorname{F}\) has no derivative: its slope is 1 on the left and 0 on the right.










LemTheorem 9 (A piecewise-smooth CDF has its derivative as a density)






Theorem 9 (A piecewise-smooth CDF has its derivative as a density) If the CDF \(\operatorname{F}\) of a random variable \(X\) is continuous everywhere, and has a continuous derivative at all but finitely many points, then \(X\) is continuous, and \(\operatorname{F}'\) (given any values at the finitely many exceptional points) is a density of \(X\).










ProofProof






Proof. For events \(A \subseteq B\), \(B\) is the disjoint union of \(A\) and \(B \setminus A\), so additivity gives \(\Pr(A) \le \Pr(B)\). For any \(x\) and \(\Delta> 0\), \(\{X = x\} \subseteq \{x - \Delta< X \le x\}\), so:
\[
\begin{aligned}
0
&\le \Pr(X = x)
&& \text{(probabilities are non-negative)} \\
&\le \Pr(x - \Delta< X \le x)
&& \text{(} \{X = x\} \subseteq \{x - \Delta< X \le x\} \text{)} \\
&= {\operatorname{F}\mathopen{}\left(x\right)\mathclose{}} - {\operatorname{F}\mathopen{}\left(x - \Delta\right)\mathclose{}}
&& \text{(additivity, and the definition of the CDF)}
\end{aligned}
\]
and \({\operatorname{F}\mathopen{}\left(x\right)\mathclose{}} - {\operatorname{F}\mathopen{}\left(x - \Delta\right)\mathclose{}} \to 0\) as \(\Delta\downarrow 0\), because \(\operatorname{F}\) is continuous. So \(\Pr(X = x) = 0\) for every \(x\), and \(X\) is continuous. Then, for \(a \le b\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Pr(a \le X \le b)
&= \Pr(a < X \le b)
&& \text{(} \Pr(X = a) = 0 \text{)} \\
&= {\operatorname{F}\mathopen{}\left(b\right)\mathclose{}} - {\operatorname{F}\mathopen{}\left(a\right)\mathclose{}}
&& \text{(additivity, and the definition of the CDF)} \\
&= \int_a^b \operatorname{F}'(x)\,dx
&& \text{(fundamental theorem of calculus)}
\end{aligned}
\]
The last step applies the fundamental theorem of calculus on each piece of \([a, b]\) between exceptional points, where \(\operatorname{F}'\) is continuous, and joins the pieces using the continuity of \(\operatorname{F}\) at the exceptional points. Finally, \(\operatorname{F}' \ge 0\) wherever it exists, because \(\operatorname{F}\) is non-decreasing (Theorem 5).










ExmExample 15 (A density from a CDF with a corner)






Example 15 (A density from a CDF with a corner) Let \(X\) have CDF \({\operatorname{F}\mathopen{}\left(t\right)\mathclose{}} = 0\) for \(t < 0\), \({\operatorname{F}\mathopen{}\left(t\right)\mathclose{}} = t^2\) for \(0 \le t \le 1\), and \({\operatorname{F}\mathopen{}\left(t\right)\mathclose{}} = 1\) for \(t > 1\). This \(\operatorname{F}\) is continuous everywhere, and has a continuous derivative everywhere except \(t = 1\), where its slope drops from 2 to 0. By Theorem 9, \(X\) is continuous with density \(f(t) = 2t\) for \(0 \le t < 1\) and \(f(t) = 0\) otherwise. As a check, \(\int_0^1 2t\,dt = 1\).










LemTheorem 10 (A density as a limit of interval probabilities)






Theorem 10 (A density as a limit of interval probabilities) If \(X\) is a continuous random variable with density \(f\), and \(f\) is continuous at \(x\), then \(f(x)\) is the limit of the probability that \(X\) falls in an interval starting at \(x\), divided by the width of that interval, as that width shrinks to 0:
\[f(x) = \lim_{\Delta\downarrow 0} \frac{\Pr(x \le X < x + \Delta)}{\Delta}\]










ProofProof






Proof. For \(\Delta> 0\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\Pr(x \le X < x + \Delta)}{\Delta}
&= \frac{\Pr(x < X \le x + \Delta)}{\Delta}
&& \text{(} \Pr(X = x) = 0 \text{ and } \Pr(X = x + \Delta) = 0 \text{)} \\
&= \frac{{\operatorname{F}\mathopen{}\left(x + \Delta\right)\mathclose{}} - {\operatorname{F}\mathopen{}\left(x\right)\mathclose{}}}{\Delta}
&& \text{(additivity, and the definition of the CDF)}
\end{aligned}
\]
By Theorem 8, \(\operatorname{F}\) is differentiable at \(x\) with \(\operatorname{F}'(x) = f(x)\), so this difference quotient converges to \(f(x)\) as \(\Delta\downarrow 0\).










RemarkRemark






Remark. For small \(\Delta> 0\), \(f(x) \cdot\Delta\approx \Pr(x \le X < x + \Delta)\). Although a density is not unique (Theorem 1), this limit pins down its value at every point where it is continuous.
See also Rothman et al. [12] (Chapter 22, p. 535).










ExmExample 16 (The uniform density as a limit)






Example 16 (The uniform density as a limit) For \(X \sim \text{Uniform}(0, 1)\) and \(x \in [0, 1)\), \(\Pr(x \le X < x + \Delta) = \Delta\) once \(\Delta\le 1 - x\), so:
\[
\begin{aligned}
f(x)
&= \lim_{\Delta\downarrow 0} \frac{\Delta}{\Delta} \\
&= 1
\end{aligned}
\]
For \(x < 0\) or \(x > 1\), the interval eventually misses \([0, 1]\), so the limit is \(0\). Both agree with the density of Definition 9.










PrpProposition 1 (The density limit is the right derivative of the CDF)






Proposition 1 (The density limit is the right derivative of the CDF) If \(X\) is a continuous random variable with CDF \(\operatorname{F}\), then for every \(x\):
\[\lim_{\Delta\downarrow 0} \frac{\Pr(x \le X < x + \Delta)}{\Delta}
= \lim_{\Delta\downarrow 0} \frac{{\operatorname{F}\mathopen{}\left(x + \Delta\right)\mathclose{}} - {\operatorname{F}\mathopen{}\left(x\right)\mathclose{}}}{\Delta}\]
whenever either limit exists; the right-hand side is the right derivative of \(\operatorname{F}\) at \(x\).










ProofProof






Proof. The first two lines of the proof of Theorem 10 use only that \(X\) is continuous, so for every \(\Delta> 0\) the two quotients are equal. Equal functions of \(\Delta\) have the same limit as \(\Delta\downarrow 0\), or both have none.










ExmExample 17 (The density limit at a jump)






Example 17 (The density limit at a jump) At a point where \(f\) is not continuous, the limit can differ from the chosen value \(f(x)\). For \(X \sim \text{Uniform}(0, 1)\) with the density \(f\) of Definition 9, which sets \(f(1) = 1\) and \(f(x) = 0\) for \(x > 1\), and for \(\Delta> 0\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Pr(1 \le X < 1 + \Delta)
&= \Pr(1 \le X \le 1 + \Delta)
&& \text{(} \Pr(X = 1 + \Delta) = 0 \text{)} \\
&= \int_1^{1 + \Delta} f(x)\,dx
&& \text{(definition of the density)} \\
&= 0
&& \text{(} f = 0 \text{ on } (1, 1 + \Delta] \text{; one point does not change an integral)}
\end{aligned}
\]
So the limit of \(\Pr(1 \le X < 1 + \Delta) / \Delta\) at \(x = 1\) is 0, although \(f(1) = 1\). By Proposition 1, 0 is also the right derivative of \(\operatorname{F}\) at 1, matching the slope of 0 on the right in Example 14.










LemTheorem 11 (Density functions integrate to 1)






Theorem 11 (Density functions integrate to 1) If \(X\) is a continuous random variable with density \(f\):
\[\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x)\, dx = 1\]










ProofProof






Proof. \[
\begin{aligned}
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x)\, dx
&= \lim_{b \to \infty} \int_{-\infty}^{b} f(x)\, dx
&& \text{(definition of an improper integral)} \\
&= \lim_{b \to \infty} {\operatorname{F}\mathopen{}\left(b\right)\mathclose{}}
&& \text{(the CDF is the integral of the density)} \\
&= 1
&& \text{(limit of a CDF)}
\end{aligned}
\]
The last step is Theorem 5.










ExmExample 18 (The uniform density integrates to 1)






Example 18 (The uniform density integrates to 1) For \(X \sim \text{Uniform}(0, 1)\) (Definition 9),
\[
\begin{aligned}
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x)\,dx &= \int_0^1 1\,dx \\
&= 1.
\end{aligned}
\]










DefDefinition 15 (Jointly distributed random variables)






Definition 15 (Jointly distributed random variables) Random variables \(X_1, \ldots, X_n\) are jointly distributed when they are defined on the same sample space \(\Omega\), so that an event about several of them at once, such as \(\{X_1 \le x_1\} \cap \{X_2 \le x_2\}\), has a probability.










RemarkRemark






Remark. We write \(\Pr(X \in A, Y \in B)\) for \(\Pr(\{X \in A\} \cap \{Y \in B\})\), and similarly for more variables.










ExmExample 19 (The first flip and the total)






Example 19 (The first flip and the total) In Example 1, let \(X_1\) indicate heads on the first flip (as in Example 7), and let \(X\) be the total number of heads. Both are functions on the same sample space, \({\mathopen{}\left\{HH, HT, TH, TT\right\}\mathclose{}}\), so they are jointly distributed, and, for example:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Pr(X_1 = 1, X = 1)
&= \Pr({\mathopen{}\left\{HH, HT\right\}\mathclose{}} \cap {\mathopen{}\left\{HT, TH\right\}\mathclose{}}) \\
&= \Pr({\mathopen{}\left\{HT\right\}\mathclose{}}) \\
&= \tfrac{1}{4}
\end{aligned}
\]










DefDefinition 16 (Joint distribution)






Definition 16 (Joint distribution) The joint distribution of jointly distributed random variables \(X_1, \ldots, X_n\) is the function that assigns to each set \(A \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n\) for which \(\{(X_1, \ldots, X_n) \in A\}\) is an event the probability \(\Pr((X_1, \ldots, X_n) \in A)\) [13].










ExmExample 20 (Joint distribution of the first flip and the total)






Example 20 (Joint distribution of the first flip and the total) In Example 19, the joint distribution of \(X_1\) and \(X\) assigns to the set \(A = {\mathopen{}\left\{(x_1, x) : x_1 = 1,\, x \ge 1\right\}\mathclose{}}\) the probability
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Pr((X_1, X) \in A)
&= \Pr({\mathopen{}\left\{HH, HT\right\}\mathclose{}}) \\
&= \tfrac{1}{2}
\end{aligned}
\]
since the first flip is heads exactly on \(HH\) and \(HT\), and each of those outcomes has at least one head.










LemTheorem 12 (A joint distribution is determined by its rectangle probabilities)






Theorem 12 (A joint distribution is determined by its rectangle probabilities) If jointly distributed random variables \(X_1, \ldots, X_n\), and jointly distributed random variables \(Y_1, \ldots, Y_n\), satisfy
\[\Pr(X_1 \in A_1, \ldots, X_n \in A_n) = \Pr(Y_1 \in A_1, \ldots, Y_n \in A_n)\]
for all sets \(A_1, \ldots, A_n\) of real numbers for which these are events, then \((X_1, \ldots, X_n)\) and \((Y_1, \ldots, Y_n)\) have the same joint distribution.










RemarkRemark






Remark. The proof needs measure theory beyond these notes: the sets \(A_1 \times \cdots \times A_n\) form a \(\pi\)-system, and two probability measures that agree on a \(\pi\)-system agree on the \(\sigma\)-algebra it generates [10].










DefDefinition 17 (Joint probability mass function (joint PMF))






Definition 17 (Joint probability mass function (joint PMF)) For jointly distributed discrete random variables \(X\) and \(Y\), the joint probability mass function (joint PMF) of \(X\) and \(Y\) is the probability that \(X\) takes the value \(x\) and \(Y\) takes the value \(y\):
\[\mathbb{P}(X = x,\, Y = y) \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}\Pr(\{X = x\} \cap \{Y = y\})\]










ExmExample 21 (Joint PMF of the first flip and the total)






Example 21 (Joint PMF of the first flip and the total) Continuing Example 19, each outcome of the two flips fixes both \(X_1\) and \(X\), so the joint PMF puts probability \(1/4\) on each outcome’s pair of values:




\(X = 0\)
\(X = 1\)
\(X = 2\)




\(X_1 = 0\)
\(1/4\) (\(TT\))
\(1/4\) (\(TH\))
\(0\)


\(X_1 = 1\)
\(0\)
\(1/4\) (\(HT\))
\(1/4\) (\(HH\))













DefDefinition 18 (Marginal distribution)






Definition 18 (Marginal distribution) When a random variable \(X\) is one of several jointly distributed random variables, the distribution of \(X\) by itself (its CDF, and its PMF or density) is called the marginal distribution of \(X\) [14].










RemarkRemark






Remark. The word “marginal” only says that the other variables are being set aside; the marginal distribution of \(X\) is the same object as the distribution of \(X\).










ExmExample 22 (Marginal distribution of the total)






Example 22 (Marginal distribution of the total) In Example 21, the marginal distribution of the total \(X\) is the PMF of Example 6: \(\mathbb{P}(X = 0) = 1/4\), \(\mathbb{P}(X = 1) = 1/2\), \(\mathbb{P}(X = 2) = 1/4\).










LemTheorem 13 (Marginal PMF from a joint PMF)






Theorem 13 (Marginal PMF from a joint PMF) If \(X\) and \(Y\) are jointly distributed discrete random variables, then for every \(x\):
\[\mathbb{P}(X = x) = \sum_{y \in \mathcal{R}(Y)} \mathbb{P}(X = x,\, Y = y)\]










ProofProof






Proof. The event \(\{X = x\}\) is the disjoint union of the events \(\{X = x\} \cap \{Y = y\}\) over the countably many values \(y \in \mathcal{R}(Y)\), so:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(X = x)
&= {\Pr\mathopen{}\left(\bigcup_{y \in \mathcal{R}(Y)} \mathopen{}\left(\{X = x\} \cap \{Y = y\}\right)\mathclose{}\right)\mathclose{}}
&& \text{(the events partition } \{X = x\} \text{)} \\
&= \sum_{y \in \mathcal{R}(Y)} \Pr(\{X = x\} \cap \{Y = y\})
&& \text{(countable additivity)} \\
&= \sum_{y \in \mathcal{R}(Y)} \mathbb{P}(X = x,\, Y = y)
&& \text{(definition of the joint PMF)}
\end{aligned}
\]










ExmExample 23 (Summing a row of the joint PMF)






Example 23 (Summing a row of the joint PMF) In Example 21, summing the \(X_1 = 1\) row:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(X_1 = 1)
&= \mathbb{P}(X_1 = 1, X = 0) + \mathbb{P}(X_1 = 1, X = 1) + \mathbb{P}(X_1 = 1, X = 2)
&& \text{(marginal PMF from the joint PMF)} \\
&= 0 + \tfrac{1}{4} + \tfrac{1}{4}
&& \text{(read the table)} \\
&= \tfrac{1}{2}
&& \text{(add)}
\end{aligned}
\]
which matches \(X_1 \sim \operatorname{Ber}(1/2)\) from Example 7.










DefDefinition 19 (Joint probability density function (joint density))






Definition 19 (Joint probability density function (joint density)) For jointly distributed continuous random variables \(X\) and \(Y\), a joint probability density function (joint density) of \(X\) and \(Y\), denoted \(f_{X,Y}(x, y)\) or \(\operatorname{p}(X = x,\, Y = y)\), is a function \(f_{X,Y}\) on \(\mathbb{R}^2\) that satisfies:

\(f_{X,Y}(x, y) \ge 0\) for every \((x, y)\).
The integral of \(f_{X,Y}\) over any region \(A \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2\) is the probability that the pair \((X, Y)\) falls in \(A\): \[\Pr((X, Y) \in A) = \iint_A f_{X,Y}(x, y)\,dx\,dy\]











RemarkRemark






Remark. As with events, a fully rigorous version restricts \(A\) to a designated collection of regions; every region that arises in these notes is in it.










ExmExample 24 (A joint density on a triangle)






Example 24 (A joint density on a triangle) Let \(f_{X,Y}(x, y) = 2\) for \(0 \le x \le y \le 1\), and \(0\) otherwise. The triangle \(\{(x, y) : 0 \le x \le y \le 1\}\) has area \(1/2\), so \(f_{X,Y}\) gives the whole plane probability \(2 \cdot\tfrac{1}{2} = 1\), and it is the joint density of a pair \((X, Y)\) with \(X \le Y\) always. For example, the probability that both are at most \(1/2\) is \(2\) times the area of the smaller triangle \(\{0 \le x \le y \le 1/2\}\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Pr(X \le \tfrac{1}{2}, Y \le \tfrac{1}{2})
&= 2 \cdot\tfrac{1}{8} \\
&= \tfrac{1}{4}
\end{aligned}
\]










LemTheorem 14 (Not every pair of continuous random variables has a joint density)






Theorem 14 (Not every pair of continuous random variables has a joint density) If \(X\) is a continuous random variable, then the pair \((X, X)\) has no joint density.










ProofProof






Proof. Suppose \(f\) were a joint density of \((X, X)\), and let \(L = {\mathopen{}\left\{(x, y) : y = x\right\}\mathclose{}}\) be the diagonal line. Every outcome \(\omega\) has \(X(\omega) = X(\omega)\), so \({\mathopen{}\left\{(X, X) \in L\right\}\mathclose{}} = \Omega\). For each \(x\), the function \(y \mapsto \text{1}_{y = x} f(x, y)\) is \(0\) except at the single point \(y = x\), so its integral over \(y\) is \(0\). Then:
\[
\begin{aligned}
1
&= \Pr((X, X) \in L)
&& \text{(} {\mathopen{}\left\{(X, X) \in L\right\}\mathclose{}} = \Omega\text{, and } \Pr(\Omega) = 1 \text{)} \\
&= \iint_L f(x, y)\,dx\,dy
&& \text{(definition of a joint density)} \\
&= \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \mathopen{}\left(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \text{1}_{y = x} f(x, y)\,dy\right)\mathclose{}\,dx
&& \text{(iterate the integral; Tonelli's theorem)} \\
&= \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} 0\,dx
&& \text{(the inner integrand is 0 except at } y = x \text{)} \\
&= 0
&& \text{(integrate)}
\end{aligned}
\]
which is a contradiction. Tonelli’s theorem allows the iterated integral because \(f \ge 0\) (Fubini–Tonelli theorem; Billingsley [10], Theorem 18.3).










LemTheorem 15 (Marginal density from a joint density)






Theorem 15 (Marginal density from a joint density) If \(X\) and \(Y\) have joint density \(f_{X,Y}\), then \(X\) has the density:
\[f_X(x) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f_{X,Y}(x, y)\,dy\]










ProofProof






Proof. For \(a \le b\), the event \(\{a \le X \le b\}\) is the event that \((X, Y)\) falls in the strip \([a, b] \times \mathbb{R}\), so:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Pr(a \le X \le b)
&= \Pr((X, Y) \in [a, b] \times \mathbb{R})
&& \text{(same event)} \\
&= \iint_{[a, b] \times \mathbb{R}} f_{X,Y}(x, y)\,dx\,dy
&& \text{(definition of a joint density)} \\
&= \int_a^b \mathopen{}\left(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f_{X,Y}(x, y)\,dy\right)\mathclose{}\,dx
&& \text{(iterate the integral; Tonelli's theorem)} \\
&= \int_a^b f_X(x)\,dx
&& \text{(definition of } f_X \text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]
Tonelli’s theorem allows the iterated integral because \(f_{X,Y} \ge 0\) (Fubini–Tonelli theorem; Billingsley [10], Theorem 18.3). So \(f_X\) satisfies Definition 7.










ExmExample 25 (Marginal densities on the triangle)






Example 25 (Marginal densities on the triangle) For the joint density of Example 24 and \(x \in [0, 1]\), \(f_{X,Y}(x, y) = 2\) exactly when \(x \le y \le 1\), so:
\[
\begin{aligned}
f_X(x)
&= \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f_{X,Y}(x, y)\,dy
&& \text{(marginal density from a joint density)} \\
&= \int_x^1 2\,dy
&& \text{(} f_{X,Y}(x, y) = 2 \text{ for } x \le y \le 1 \text{, else } 0 \text{)} \\
&= 2(1 - x)
&& \text{(integrate)}
\end{aligned}
\]
The same steps with the roles swapped give
\[
\begin{aligned}
f_Y(y) &= \int_0^y 2\,dx \\
&= 2y
\end{aligned}
\]
for \(y \in [0, 1]\).










DefDefinition 20 (Joint density-mass function)






Definition 20 (Joint density-mass function) Let \(X\) be a discrete random variable and \(Y\) a continuous random variable, jointly distributed. A joint density-mass function of \(X\) and \(Y\), denoted \(\operatorname{p}(X = x,\, Y = y)\), is a function \(\operatorname{p}(X = x,\, Y = y) \ge 0\) that is a probability mass in \(x\) and a probability density in \(y\): for every \(x\) and every set \(B \subseteq \mathbb{R}\),
\[\Pr(X = x,\, Y \in B) = \int_{B} \operatorname{p}(X = x,\, Y = y)\,dy\]










RemarkRemark






Remark. When \(X\) is continuous and \(Y\) is discrete, the roles swap: \(\Pr(X \in B,\, Y = y) = \int_B \operatorname{p}(X = x,\, Y = y)\,dx\).










CorCorollary 2 (Marginal PMF from a joint density-mass function)






Corollary 2 (Marginal PMF from a joint density-mass function) If \(X\) and \(Y\) have joint density-mass function \(\operatorname{p}(X = x,\, Y = y)\), then for every \(x\):
\[\mathbb{P}(X = x) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \operatorname{p}(X = x,\, Y = y)\,dy\]










ProofProof






Proof. Every outcome has \(Y(\omega) \in \mathbb{R}\), so \({\mathopen{}\left\{Y \in \mathbb{R}\right\}\mathclose{}} = \Omega\), and:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(X = x)
&= \Pr({\mathopen{}\left\{X = x\right\}\mathclose{}} \cap \Omega)
&& \text{(} {\mathopen{}\left\{X = x\right\}\mathclose{}} \subseteq \Omega\text{)} \\
&= \Pr(X = x,\, Y \in \mathbb{R})
&& \text{(} {\mathopen{}\left\{Y \in \mathbb{R}\right\}\mathclose{}} = \Omega\text{)} \\
&= \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \operatorname{p}(X = x,\, Y = y)\,dy
&& \text{(definition of a joint density-mass function, with } B = \mathbb{R}\text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]










ExmExample 26 (A coin flip and a waiting time)






Example 26 (A coin flip and a waiting time) Let \(\operatorname{p}(X = 0,\, Y = y) = 1/2\) for \(y \in [0, 1]\), \(\operatorname{p}(X = 1,\, Y = y) = 1/4\) for \(y \in [0, 2]\), and \(0\) otherwise. Integrating over \(y\) gives \(\mathbb{P}(X = 0) = 1/2\) and \(\mathbb{P}(X = 1) = 1/2\), which add to 1. For example, the probability that \(X = 1\) and \(Y \le 1\) is:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Pr(X = 1,\, Y \le 1)
&= \int_0^1 \tfrac{1}{4}\,dy \\
&= \tfrac{1}{4}
\end{aligned}
\]





2.1 Joint distributions and marginalization
For a discrete random variable \(X\) taking values in \(\mathbb{X}\), a probability mass function (PMF) \(\mathbb{P}(x) : \mathbb{X} \to [0, 1]\) gives the probability that \(X\) takes the value \(x\):
\[\sum_{x \in \mathbb{X}} \mathbb{P}(x) = 1\]
The support of the distribution is the subset of values where the probability is strictly positive: \(\{x \in \mathbb{X} : \mathbb{P}(x) > 0\}\). When \(\mathbb{X}\) is finite, \(\mathbb{P}(x)\) can be written as a probability vector.
For two discrete variables \(X \in \mathbb{X}\) and \(Y \in \mathbb{Y}\), their joint probability distribution \(\mathbb{P}(x, y) : \mathbb{X} \times \mathbb{Y} \to [0, 1]\) satisfies:
\[\sum_{x \in \mathbb{X}} \sum_{y \in \mathbb{Y}} \mathbb{P}(x, y) = 1\]
For two variables, the joint probabilities can be laid out in a matrix or table. Summing across a row or column collapses that variable away, a process called marginalization:
\[\mathbb{P}(x) = \sum_{y \in \mathbb{Y}} \mathbb{P}(x, y), \qquad \mathbb{P}(y) = \sum_{x \in \mathbb{X}} \mathbb{P}(x, y)\]
The resulting distributions \(\mathbb{P}(x)\) and \(\mathbb{P}(y)\) are the marginal distributions of \(X\) and \(Y\).






ExmExample 27 (Joint probabilities and marginalization)






Example 27 (Joint probabilities and marginalization) Consider an example adapted from Brian Hutchinson’s notes [15]. Let \(m \in \{0, 1\}\) indicate whether a meteorite hits your house on a given day (\(m = 1\)), and let \(d \in \{0, 1\}\) indicate whether you have a good day (\(d = 1\)). In this distribution, 9 out of 10 days are good days (\(\mathbb{P}(d=1) = 0.9\)), and the probability of a meteorite strike is 1 in a million (\(\mathbb{P}(m=1) = 10^{-6}\)):









Table 1: Joint distribution of a meteorite strike (\(m\)) and day quality (\(d\)), with marginals.












\(d=0\) (bad day)
\(d=1\) (good day)
Marginal \(\mathbb{P}(m)\)




\(m=0\) (no meteorite)
\(0.09999902\)
\(0.89999998\)
\(0.999999\)


\(m=1\) (meteorite hit)
\(0.00000098\)
\(0.00000002\)
\(0.000001\)


Marginal \(\mathbb{P}(d)\)
\(0.10000000\)
\(0.90000000\)
\(1.000000\)









Summing each row yields the marginal distribution of \(m\); summing each column yields the marginal distribution of \(d\). Conditioning inverts the perspective:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(d=0 \mid m=1)
&= \frac{\mathbb{P}(m=1, d=0)}{\mathbb{P}(m=1)} \\
&= \frac{0.00000098}{0.000001} \\
&= 0.98
\end{aligned}
\]
Given that a meteorite struck your house, you have a 98% chance of having a bad day. In reverse:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(m=1 \mid d=0)
&= \frac{\mathbb{P}(m=1, d=0)}{\mathbb{P}(d=0)} \\
&= \frac{0.00000098}{0.1} \\
&= 0.0000098
\end{aligned}
\]
Given that you are having a bad day, the probability of a meteorite hit is roughly 1 in 100,000. Bad days are common (\(\mathbb{P}(d=0) = 0.1\)), so having one is very weak evidence that an astronomical rarity occurred.






2.2 Continuous distributions and densities
When a random variable \(X\) takes values in a continuous space \(\mathcal{R}(X) \subseteq \mathbb{R}\), its behavior is described by a probability density function (PDF) \(\operatorname{p}(x) : \mathcal{R}(X) \to \mathbb{R}_+\) satisfying:
\[\int_{\mathcal{R}(X)} \operatorname{p}(x)\,\mathrm{d}x = 1\]
Probabilities are assigned to subsets \(A \subseteq \mathcal{R}(X)\) by integrating the density over that set:
\[\Pr(X \in A) = \int_{A} \operatorname{p}(x)\,\mathrm{d}x\]






LemTheorem 16 (Points have zero probability in continuous distributions)






Theorem 16 (Points have zero probability in continuous distributions) For any continuous random variable and any specific value \(a \in \mathbb{R}\):
\[\Pr(X = a) = 0\]




Why? As Brian Hutchinson notes [15], what is the probability that someone’s height is exactly \(6.0000000000\dots\) feet? Zero. A single real point has width zero, so the integral over a single point is zero.
Non-zero probabilities attach to intervals or regions of non-zero width:
\[\Pr(6 - \varepsilon\le X \le 6 + \varepsilon) = \int_{6-\varepsilon}^{6+\varepsilon} \operatorname{p}(x)\,\mathrm{d}x > 0 \qquad (\text{for } \varepsilon> 0)\]
Every rule developed for discrete variables carries over to continuous variables by replacing sums \(\sum_{x \in \mathcal{R}(X)}\) with integrals \(\int_{\mathcal{R}(X)} \mathrm{d}x\). For example, marginalizing out \(X\) from a joint density \(\operatorname{p}(x, y)\) to find the marginal density \(\operatorname{p}(y)\) becomes:
\[\operatorname{p}(y) = \int_{\mathcal{R}(X)} \operatorname{p}(x, y)\,\mathrm{d}x\]

3 Survival, hazard, and cumulative hazard functions







DefDefinition 21 (Survival function (survivor function))






Definition 21 (Survival function (survivor function)) The survival function (or survivor function) of a random variable \(T\), denoted \(\operatorname{S}(t)\), is the probability that \(T\) exceeds \(t\) [18]:
\[\operatorname{S}(t) \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}\Pr(T > t)\]










RemarkRemark






Remark. The name comes from time-to-event analysis: if \(T\) is the time at which a participant dies, then \(\operatorname{S}(t)\) is the probability that the participant is still alive at time \(t\). The definition itself applies to any random variable.










LemTheorem 17 (Survival function and CDF)






Theorem 17 (Survival function and CDF) For any random variable \(T\) with CDF \(F(t)\):
\[\operatorname{S}(t) = 1 - F(t)\]
If \(T\) is continuous with density \(f(t)\), then also:
\[\operatorname{S}(t) = \int_{u=t}^{\infty} f(u)\,du\]










ProofProof






Proof. The event \(\{T > t\}\) is the complement of the event \(\{T \le t\}\), so the complement rule gives:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{S}(t)
&\stackrel{\text{def}}{=}\Pr(T > t)
&& \text{(definition of the survival function)} \\
&= 1 - \Pr(T \le t)
&& \text{(complement rule)} \\
&= 1 - F(t)
&& \text{(definition of the CDF)}
\end{aligned}
\]
For continuous \(T\), the density integrates to 1 over the real line (Theorem 11), and \(F\) is the integral of the density up to \(t\) (Theorem 7), so:
\[
\begin{aligned}
1 - F(t)
&= \int_{u=-\infty}^{\infty} f(u)\,du - \int_{u=-\infty}^{t} f(u)\,du
&& \text{(total integral is 1; } F \text{ is the integral of } f \text{)} \\
&= \int_{u=t}^{\infty} f(u)\,du
&& \text{(split the first integral at } t \text{ and cancel)}
\end{aligned}
\]










ExmExample 28 (Survival function of an exponential distribution)






Example 28 (Survival function of an exponential distribution) Let \(T\) be exponential with rate \({\lambda}> 0\) (Definition 12), so \(T\) has density \(f(t) = {\lambda}\text{e}^{-{\lambda}t}\) for \(t \ge 0\). For \(t \ge 0\), by Theorem 17:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{S}(t)
&= \int_{u=t}^{\infty} {\lambda}\text{e}^{-{\lambda}u}\,du
&& \text{(integral form of the survival function)} \\
&= \mathopen{}\left[-\text{e}^{-{\lambda}u}\right]\mathclose{}_{u=t}^{\infty}
&& \text{(antiderivative of } {\lambda}\text{e}^{-{\lambda}u} \text{)} \\
&= 0 - \mathopen{}\left(-\text{e}^{-{\lambda}t}\right)\mathclose{}
&& \text{(evaluate at the bounds; } \text{e}^{-{\lambda}u} \to 0 \text{ as } u \to \infty \text{)} \\
&= \text{e}^{-{\lambda}t}
&& \text{(simplify)}
\end{aligned}
\]
For \(t < 0\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{S}(t) &= \Pr(T > t) \\
&= 1,
\end{aligned}
\]
since \(T \ge 0\). With \({\lambda}= 0.5\), for example, \(\operatorname{S}(2) = \text{e}^{-1} \approx 0.368\).










DefDefinition 22 (Hazard function (hazard rate, hazard rate function))






Definition 22 (Hazard function (hazard rate, hazard rate function)) The hazard function (also called the hazard rate or hazard rate function) of a continuous random variable \(T\) at a value \(t\) with \(\Pr(T \ge t) > 0\), typically denoted \({\lambda}(t)\) or \(\operatorname{h}(t)\), is the limit of the conditional probability that \(T\) falls in an interval starting at \(t\), given \(T \ge t\), divided by the width of that interval, as that width shrinks to 0 [19]:
\[{\lambda}(t) \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}\lim_{\Delta\downarrow 0} \frac{\Pr(t \le T < t + \Delta\mid T \ge t)}{\Delta}\]










RemarkRemark






Remark. Sources differ on the symbol: \(\operatorname{h}(t)\) appears in Dobson and Barnett [20], Vittinghoff et al. [21], Klein and Moeschberger [22], and Kleinbaum and Klein [23], while \(\lambda(t)\) appears in Rothman et al. [12] and Kalbfleisch and Prentice [24].
If \(T\) is the time at which an event occurs, then \({\lambda}(t)\) is a rate, not a probability: for a small interval width \(\Delta> 0\), \({\lambda}(t) \cdot\Delta\) is approximately the probability that the event occurs in \([t, t + \Delta)\), given that it has not occurred before \(t\). Many sources write the hazard as \({\lambda}(t) = \operatorname{p}(T = t \mid T \ge t)\), reading it as the density of \(T\) at \(t\), conditional on the event \(T \ge t\); that notation abbreviates the limit in Definition 22. For a discrete \(T\), the analogous quantity is the discrete-time hazard.
The name “hazard” carries a connotation that the event is undesirable — death, relapse, equipment failure, and so on. When the event in question is neutral or desirable (recovery, conception, graduation, response to treatment), the same quantity \({\lambda}(t)\) is often called the event incidence rate instead. This terminology parallels the convention that conditional probabilities of undesirable events are called risks, while the same conditional probabilities for neutral or desirable events are simply called probabilities. The math is identical; only the name changes with the valence of the event.










ExmExample 29 (A hazard greater than 1)






Example 29 (A hazard greater than 1) A hazard can exceed 1, just as a density can (Example 9). Let \(T\) be exponential with rate \({\lambda}= 2\), so \(\operatorname{S}(t) = \text{e}^{-2t}\) for \(t \ge 0\) (Example 28). Since \(T\) is continuous, \(\Pr(T = s) = 0\) for every \(s\), so
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Pr(T \ge s) &= \Pr(T > s) \\
&= \operatorname{S}(s).
\end{aligned}
\]
For \(t \ge 0\) and \(\Delta> 0\), \(\{T \ge t\}\) is the disjoint union of \(\{t \le T < t + \Delta\}\) and \(\{T \ge t + \Delta\}\), so:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Pr(t \le T < t + \Delta\mid T \ge t)
&= \frac{\Pr(\{t \le T < t + \Delta\} \cap \{T \ge t\})}{\Pr(T \ge t)}
&& \text{(definition of conditional probability)} \\
&= \frac{\Pr(t \le T < t + \Delta)}{\Pr(T \ge t)}
&& \text{(subset property)} \\
&= \frac{\Pr(T \ge t) - \Pr(T \ge t + \Delta)}{\Pr(T \ge t)}
&& \text{(additivity)} \\
&= \frac{\operatorname{S}(t) - \operatorname{S}(t + \Delta)}{\operatorname{S}(t)}
&& \text{(} \Pr(T \ge s) = \operatorname{S}(s) \text{)} \\
&= \frac{\text{e}^{-2t} - \text{e}^{-2(t + \Delta)}}{\text{e}^{-2t}}
&& \text{(exponential survival function)} \\
&= 1 - \text{e}^{-2\Delta}
&& \text{(divide by } \text{e}^{-2t} \text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]
The subset property applies because \(\{t \le T < t + \Delta\} \subseteq \{T \ge t\}\). Then:
\[
\begin{aligned}
{\lambda}(t)
&= \lim_{\Delta\downarrow 0} \frac{1 - \text{e}^{-2\Delta}}{\Delta}
&& \text{(definition of the hazard function)} \\
&= \left.{\frac{\partial}{\partial \Delta} \mathopen{}\left(1 - \text{e}^{-2\Delta}\right)\mathclose{}}\right|_{\Delta= 0}
&& \text{(definition of the derivative; } 1 - \text{e}^{0} = 0 \text{)} \\
&= 2\text{e}^{0}
&& \text{(chain rule)} \\
&= 2
&& \text{(} \text{e}^{0} = 1 \text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]
So \({\lambda}(t) = 2 > 1\) at every \(t \ge 0\): a hazard is a rate, not a probability.










DefDefinition 23 (Discrete-time hazard)






Definition 23 (Discrete-time hazard) The discrete-time hazard of a discrete random variable \(T\) at a value \(t\) with \(\Pr(T \ge t) > 0\) is the conditional probability that \(T\) equals \(t\), given \(T \ge t\):
\[\Pr(T = t \mid T \ge t)\]










ExmExample 30 (Rolling until the first six)






Example 30 (Rolling until the first six) Roll a fair die repeatedly, and let \(T\) be the number of the roll that first shows a six. Then \(T \ge t\) exactly when the first \(t - 1\) rolls are not sixes, which has probability \((5/6)^{t-1}\), and \(T = t\) when, in addition, roll \(t\) is a six. So, for each \(t = 1, 2, \ldots\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Pr(T = t \mid T \ge t)
&= \frac{\Pr(T = t,\, T \ge t)}{\Pr(T \ge t)}
&& \text{(definition of conditional probability)} \\
&= \frac{\Pr(T = t)}{\Pr(T \ge t)}
&& \text{(} T = t \text{ implies } T \ge t \text{)} \\
&= \frac{(5/6)^{t-1} \cdot(1/6)}{(5/6)^{t-1}}
&& \text{(rolls are independent)} \\
&= \frac{1}{6}
&& \text{(cancel)}
\end{aligned}
\]
The discrete-time hazard is the same at every roll: having gone without a six so far does not change the chance of a six on the next roll.










CorCorollary 3 (A discrete-time hazard lies in \({[0, 1]}\))






Corollary 3 (A discrete-time hazard lies in \({[0, 1]}\)) The discrete-time hazard of a discrete random variable \(T\) at a value \(t\) with \(\Pr(T \ge t) > 0\) satisfies:
\[0 \le \Pr(T = t \mid T \ge t) \le 1\]










ProofProof






Proof. \(\{T \ge t\}\) is the disjoint union of \(\{T = t\}\) and \(\{T > t\}\), so, by additivity, \(\Pr(T \ge t) = \Pr(T = t) + \Pr(T > t) \ge \Pr(T = t)\). Since \(\{T = t\} \subseteq \{T \ge t\}\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Pr(T = t \mid T \ge t)
&= \frac{\Pr(\{T = t\} \cap \{T \ge t\})}{\Pr(T \ge t)}
&& \text{(definition of conditional probability)} \\
&= \frac{\Pr(T = t)}{\Pr(T \ge t)}
&& \text{(subset property)}
\end{aligned}
\]
The numerator is non-negative and at most the positive denominator, so the ratio lies in \([0, 1]\).










RemarkRemark






Remark. Unlike the continuous-time hazard function, which is a rate and can exceed 1 (Example 29), the discrete-time hazard is a probability.










LemTheorem 18 (Hazard equals density over survival)






Theorem 18 (Hazard equals density over survival) If \(T\) is a continuous random variable with density \(f(t)\) and survival function \(\operatorname{S}(t)\), then for every \(t\) with \(\operatorname{S}(t) > 0\) at which \(f\) is continuous:
\[{\lambda}(t) = \frac{f(t)}{\operatorname{S}(t)}\]










ProofProof






Proof. The proof uses three facts. First, for \(\Delta> 0\) the event \(\{t \le T < t + \Delta\}\) is a subset of the event \(\{T \ge t\}\), so intersecting them leaves \(\{t \le T < t + \Delta\}\) (the subset property). Second, \(\Pr(T = t) = 0\) for a continuous \(T\), so
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Pr(T \ge t) &= \Pr(T > t) \\
&= \operatorname{S}(t),
\end{aligned}
\]
which is positive. Third, because \(f\) is continuous at \(t\), Theorem 10 gives \(f(t)\) as the limit of \(\Pr(t \le T < t + \Delta) / \Delta\).
\[
\begin{aligned}
{\lambda}(t)
&\stackrel{\text{def}}{=}\lim_{\Delta\downarrow 0} \frac{\Pr(t \le T < t + \Delta\mid T \ge t)}{\Delta}
&& \text{(definition of the hazard function)} \\
&= \lim_{\Delta\downarrow 0} \frac{1}{\Delta} \cdot\frac{\Pr(\{t \le T < t + \Delta\} \cap \{T \ge t\})}{\Pr(T \ge t)}
&& \text{(definition of conditional probability)} \\
&= \lim_{\Delta\downarrow 0} \frac{1}{\Delta} \cdot\frac{\Pr(t \le T < t + \Delta)}{\Pr(T \ge t)}
&& \text{(subset property)} \\
&= \frac{1}{\Pr(T \ge t)} \cdot\lim_{\Delta\downarrow 0} \frac{\Pr(t \le T < t + \Delta)}{\Delta}
&& \text{(} \Pr(T \ge t) \text{ does not depend on } \Delta\text{)} \\
&= \frac{f(t)}{\Pr(T \ge t)}
&& \text{(density as a limit; } f \text{ is continuous at } t \text{)} \\
&= \frac{f(t)}{\operatorname{S}(t)}
&& \text{(} \Pr(T = t) = 0 \text{ for continuous } T \text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]










ExmExample 31 (Hazard function of an exponential distribution)






Example 31 (Hazard function of an exponential distribution) Continuing Example 28, for \(t > 0\), where \(f\) is continuous:
\[
\begin{aligned}
{\lambda}(t)
&= \frac{f(t)}{\operatorname{S}(t)}
&& \text{(hazard equals density over survival)} \\
&= \frac{{\lambda}\text{e}^{-{\lambda}t}}{\text{e}^{-{\lambda}t}}
&& \text{(substitute the exponential density and survival function)} \\
&= {\lambda}
&& \text{(cancel } \text{e}^{-{\lambda}t} \text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]
At \(t = 0\), where \(f\) jumps from \(0\) to \({\lambda}\), Definition 22 gives the same value directly: \(\Pr(0 \le T < \Delta\mid T \ge 0) / \Delta= \mathopen{}\left(1 - \text{e}^{-{\lambda}\Delta}\right)\mathclose{} / \Delta\to {\lambda}\) as \(\Delta\downarrow 0\). So the exponential distribution has a constant hazard for \(t \ge 0\), equal to its rate parameter; for \(t < 0\), \(f(t) = 0\), so \({\lambda}(t) = 0\).










DefDefinition 24 (Cumulative hazard function)






Definition 24 (Cumulative hazard function) The cumulative hazard function of a continuous random variable \(T\), often denoted \({\Lambda}(t)\) or \(\operatorname{H}(t)\), is the integral of its hazard function up to \(t\):
\[{\Lambda}(t) \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}\int_{u=-\infty}^{t} {\lambda}(u)\,du\]










ExmExample 32 (Cumulative hazard function of an exponential distribution)






Example 32 (Cumulative hazard function of an exponential distribution) Continuing Example 31, the hazard is \({\lambda}(u) = {\lambda}\) for \(u \ge 0\) and \(0\) for \(u < 0\), so for \(t \ge 0\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
{\Lambda}(t)
&= \int_{u=-\infty}^{0} 0\,du + \int_{u=0}^{t} {\lambda}\,du
&& \text{(split the integral at } 0 \text{)} \\
&= 0 + {\lambda}t
&& \text{(integrate each piece)} \\
&= {\lambda}t
&& \text{(simplify)}
\end{aligned}
\]
and \({\Lambda}(t) = 0\) for \(t < 0\).










CorCorollary 4 (Cumulative hazard of a non-negative random variable)






Corollary 4 (Cumulative hazard of a non-negative random variable) If \(T\) is a continuous random variable with \(T \ge 0\), such as a time to event, then \({\lambda}(u) = 0\) for every \(u < 0\), and for every \(t \ge 0\):
\[{\Lambda}(t) = \int_{u=0}^{t} {\lambda}(u)\,du\]










ProofProof






Proof. Let \(u < 0\). Every outcome has \(T(\omega) \ge 0 > u\), so \(\{T \ge u\} = \Omega\), which has probability \(1 > 0\), and \({\lambda}(u)\) is defined. For \(0 < \Delta\le -u\), the event \(\{u \le T < u + \Delta\}\) is empty, because \(u + \Delta\le 0\), so:
\[
\begin{aligned}
{\lambda}(u)
&= \lim_{\Delta\downarrow 0} \frac{\Pr(u \le T < u + \Delta\mid T \ge u)}{\Delta}
&& \text{(definition of the hazard function)} \\
&= \lim_{\Delta\downarrow 0} \frac{\Pr(\{u \le T < u + \Delta\} \cap \{T \ge u\})}{\Delta\cdot\Pr(T \ge u)}
&& \text{(definition of conditional probability)} \\
&= \lim_{\Delta\downarrow 0} \frac{\Pr(\emptyset \cap \Omega)}{\Delta\cdot\Pr(\Omega)}
&& \text{(the two events found above)} \\
&= \lim_{\Delta\downarrow 0} \frac{0}{\Delta\cdot 1}
&& \text{(} \emptyset \cap \Omega= \emptyset \text{; } \Pr(\emptyset) = 0 \text{; } \Pr(\Omega) = 1 \text{)} \\
&= 0
&& \text{(simplify)}
\end{aligned}
\]
Then, for \(t \ge 0\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
{\Lambda}(t)
&= \int_{u=-\infty}^{t} {\lambda}(u)\,du
&& \text{(definition of the cumulative hazard)} \\
&= \int_{u=-\infty}^{0} {\lambda}(u)\,du + \int_{u=0}^{t} {\lambda}(u)\,du
&& \text{(split the integral at } 0 \text{)} \\
&= \int_{u=-\infty}^{0} 0\,du + \int_{u=0}^{t} {\lambda}(u)\,du
&& \text{(} {\lambda}(u) = 0 \text{ for } u < 0 \text{)} \\
&= \int_{u=0}^{t} {\lambda}(u)\,du
&& \text{(integrate)}
\end{aligned}
\]










RemarkRemark






Remark. The form in Corollary 4, with lower limit \(0\), is the form most survival-analysis texts use.










CorCorollary 5 (Survival function from the cumulative hazard)






Corollary 5 (Survival function from the cumulative hazard) If \(T\) is a continuous random variable whose density \(f\) is continuous at all but finitely many points, then for every \(t\) with \(\operatorname{S}(t) > 0\):
\[{\Lambda}(t) = -{\operatorname{log}\mathopen{}\left\{\operatorname{S}(t)\right\}\mathclose{}}\]
and therefore:
\[\operatorname{S}(t) = {\operatorname{exp}\mathopen{}\left\{-{\Lambda}(t)\right\}\mathclose{}} \tag{1}\]










ProofProof






Proof. Since \(\operatorname{S}(t) = 1 - F(t)\) (Theorem 17) and \(F\) has derivative \(f\) wherever \(f\) is continuous (Theorem 8), \(\operatorname{S}\) has derivative \(-f\) at those points. At each such \(u\) with \(\operatorname{S}(u) > 0\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{d}{du}\mathopen{}\left(-{\operatorname{log}\mathopen{}\left\{\operatorname{S}(u)\right\}\mathclose{}}\right)\mathclose{}
&= -\frac{1}{\operatorname{S}(u)} \cdot\frac{d}{du}\operatorname{S}(u)
&& \text{(chain rule)} \\
&= -\frac{1}{\operatorname{S}(u)} \cdot\mathopen{}\left(-f(u)\right)\mathclose{}
&& \text{(} \operatorname{S}' = -f \text{)} \\
&= \frac{f(u)}{\operatorname{S}(u)}
&& \text{(simplify)} \\
&= {\lambda}(u)
&& \text{(hazard equals density over survival)}
\end{aligned}
\]
The function \(-{\operatorname{log}\mathopen{}\left\{\operatorname{S}(u)\right\}\mathclose{}}\) is continuous, because \(\operatorname{S}\) is continuous for a continuous \(T\), and it has derivative \({\lambda}(u)\) at all but finitely many points, so it is an antiderivative of \({\lambda}\) for the fundamental theorem of calculus. As \(u \to -\infty\), \(\operatorname{S}(u) \to 1\), so \(-{\operatorname{log}\mathopen{}\left\{\operatorname{S}(u)\right\}\mathclose{}} \to 0\). Therefore:
\[
\begin{aligned}
{\Lambda}(t)
&\stackrel{\text{def}}{=}\int_{u=-\infty}^{t} {\lambda}(u)\,du
&& \text{(definition of the cumulative hazard)} \\
&= \mathopen{}\left[-{\operatorname{log}\mathopen{}\left\{\operatorname{S}(u)\right\}\mathclose{}}\right]\mathclose{}_{u=-\infty}^{t}
&& \text{(} -\log \operatorname{S}\text{ is an antiderivative of } {\lambda}\text{)} \\
&= -{\operatorname{log}\mathopen{}\left\{\operatorname{S}(t)\right\}\mathclose{}} - 0
&& \text{(evaluate at the bounds)} \\
&= -{\operatorname{log}\mathopen{}\left\{\operatorname{S}(t)\right\}\mathclose{}}
&& \text{(simplify)}
\end{aligned}
\]
Exponentiating both sides of \(-{\Lambda}(t) = {\operatorname{log}\mathopen{}\left\{\operatorname{S}(t)\right\}\mathclose{}}\) gives Equation 1.










ExmExample 33 (Recovering the exponential survival function from its cumulative hazard)






Example 33 (Recovering the exponential survival function from its cumulative hazard) Continuing Example 32, for \(t \ge 0\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{S}(t)
&= {\operatorname{exp}\mathopen{}\left\{-{\Lambda}(t)\right\}\mathclose{}}
&& \text{(survival function from the cumulative hazard)} \\
&= {\operatorname{exp}\mathopen{}\left\{-{\lambda}t\right\}\mathclose{}}
&& \text{(substitute } {\Lambda}(t) = {\lambda}t \text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]
which matches the survival function computed directly in Example 28.













Table 2: Probability distribution functions of a continuous random variable \(T\)





Name
Symbols
Definition




Probability density function (PDF)
\(f(t), \operatorname{p}(t)\)
\(f \ge 0\) with \(\int_a^b f(u)\,du = \Pr(a \le T \le b)\)


Cumulative distribution function (CDF)
\(F(t)\)
\(\Pr(T\leq t)\)


Survival function
\(\operatorname{S}(t), \bar{F}(t)\)
